AI.method: KG2Code converts knowledge graphs to code-based representations, KG2Code-QA formulates KGQA as code generation task, and creates automated pipeline to train LLMs on large-scale code corpus.
AI.result: The approach significantly outperforms existing KG-enhanced LLM methods for KGQA, enables zero-shot KGQA, and exhibits strong generalization to unseen knowledge graphs.
AI.conclusion: KG2Code provides an effective solution that preserves KG structure while aligning with LLMs' code-aware pretraining, addressing hallucinations and improving KGQA performance and generalization.

title: FILLER: Feature Imputation via Latent Location Exploration and Retrieval
summary: In real-world machine learning applications, incomplete observations create a fundamental challenge. Researchers have come up with several ideas to address this crucial problem. However, current models still face challenges in balancing scalability and structural consistency. This study proposes a feature imputation method, called FILLER, that deliberately searches the two-dimensional latent space produced by a generative model and fills the missing values with appropriate entries. The generative model is trained on fully observed data to generate samples from the latent space, and FILLER uses this trained model to impute the values missing in the corrupted test samples. In this study, G-NeuroDAVIS serves the purpose of the generative model. This work also presents a mathematical proof on the convergence of the iterative search. Finally, FILLER has been evaluated on several image datasets under random and structured missingness patterns with varying levels of imputation complexities. In order to justify the efficacy of FILLER, it has been compared against existing state-of-the-art solution strategies in terms of RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM. In addition, Wilcoxon signed-rank test has been carried out to validate statistical significance. Moreover, downstream analyses (classification and clustering) have also established the quality of imputation in terms of standard metrics.

AI.tldr: FILLER is a feature imputation method that searches a 2D latent space from a generative model to fill missing values, showing better performance than state-of-the-art methods on image datasets.
AI.motivation: In real-world ML applications, incomplete observations create fundamental challenges. Existing models struggle to balance scalability and structural consistency when handling missing data.
AI.method: Proposes FILLER method that uses a generative model (G-NeuroDAVIS) trained on complete data to create a 2D latent space. It then searches this space iteratively to impute missing values in corrupted test samples, with mathematical proof of convergence.
AI.result: FILLER outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple image datasets under random and structured missingness patterns. Evaluated using RMSE, PSNR, SSIM metrics with statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Downstream classification and clustering tasks also confirm imputation quality.
AI.conclusion: FILLER provides an effective solution for missing data imputation by leveraging generative models and latent space search, demonstrating superior performance and practical utility for real-world ML applications.

title: Do Language Models Converge to Themselves? Recursive Self-Refinement as Textual Relaxation
summary:
Large language models are increasingly used in recursive refinement workflows, where an initial draft is repeatedly revised by the same model. Despite their growing use, the long-term dynamics of such workflows remain poorly understood. Does repeated refinement continue to improve outputs indefinitely, or does it converge toward a stable textual form?
  We study recursive self-refinement as a dynamical process in which repeated LLM revision drives text toward a model-preferred soft fixed-point region. Using GPT-5.5, we generate 10-step refinement trajectories for 50 ICML 2025 abstracts under both default-temperature and deterministic decoding, and additionally evaluate 15 ICML 2020 abstracts. We analyze normalized edit distance, exact and approximate fixed points, word-count stability, exponential relaxation, and external LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
  Across all settings, refinement trajectories rapidly saturate. Most edits occur within the first few iterations, after which trajectories enter a soft fixed-point region with only minor surface-level changes. Deterministic decoding reaches exact fixed points earlier and exhibits smaller residual fluctuations than default-temperature decoding, while both achieve universal approximate convergence. The average edit magnitude follows a consistent exponential relaxation pattern, suggesting convergence toward a model-preferred textual equilibrium rather than open-ended optimization. External evaluation indicates that converged abstracts improve clarity, conciseness, and scientific style while preserving technical meaning.
  These findings support a dynamical-systems view of LLM self-refinement and motivate practical stopping criteria based on edit-magnitude saturation.

AI.tldr: LLM self-refinement saturates quickly, reaching a "soft fixed-point region" where further revisions make only minor changes rather than indefinite improvement.
AI.motivation: To understand the long-term dynamics of LLM recursive refinement workflows - whether repeated revisions lead to indefinite improvement or convergence to stable text forms.
AI.method: Generated 10-step refinement trajectories for 50 ICML 2025 abstracts using GPT-5.5 under default-temperature and deterministic decoding, plus 15 ICML 2020 abstracts. Analyzed normalized edit distance, exact/approximate fixed points, word-count stability, exponential relaxation, and external LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
AI.result: Refinement trajectories rapidly saturate, with most edits in first few iterations before entering a soft fixed-point region with only minor changes. Deterministic decoding reaches exact fixed points earlier with smaller fluctuations. Edit magnitude follows exponential relaxation pattern. Converged abstracts improve clarity, conciseness, and style while preserving technical meaning.
AI.conclusion: LLM self-refinement converges toward model-preferred textual equilibrium rather than open-ended optimization, supporting a dynamical-systems view and enabling practical stopping criteria based on edit-magnitude saturation.

title: AlloBench: Measuring Online Tool Allocation Capability in LLM Agents
summary: Creating a reusable tool is an investment: an agent pays a fixed cost now in exchange for the potential of future reuse. Therefore, a user should prefer an agent that creates a small number of highly reusable tools, rather than many one-offs. We introduce a paired benchmark that tests whether LLM agents exhibit conscious allocation behavior under a fixed budget in two contexts: an abstract text-based formulation and a code-construction task. We find that every frontier model we test---Claude Haiku, Claude Opus, GPT-5.4-mini, and GPT-5.6 Sol---acts near-optimally in the abstract framing but fails to transfer this ability to script-writing. Through further experiments, we identify the particular failure modes for each model. Notably, the first three models fail even when the scripts are not evaluated, while GPT-5.6 Sol stays selective under that weaker manipulation and collapses only at full construction. Furthermore, an open-source Qwen model policy-trained for abstract allocation generalizes this ability across held-out lexical variations, but sees no improvement at script allocation. Together, these results establish online tool allocation as a significant capability boundary, even for modern frontier models.

AI.tldr: LLM agents perform well on abstract tool allocation tasks but fail to transfer this ability to practical code construction, revealing a significant capability boundary even for frontier models.
AI.motivation: The research investigates whether LLM agents exhibit conscious allocation behavior when creating reusable tools under fixed budgets, testing if they can strategically invest in fewer highly reusable tools versus many one-off tools.
AI.method: Researchers introduced a paired benchmark testing LLM agents in two contexts: (1) abstract text-based formulation, and (2) code-construction tasks. They tested frontier models (Claude Haiku, Claude Opus, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.6 Sol) and also experimented with an open-source Qwen model policy-trained for abstract allocation to test generalization.
AI.result: All frontier models performed near-optimally in abstract framing but failed to transfer this ability to script-writing. Failure modes differed by model: first three models failed even when scripts weren't evaluated, while GPT-5.6 Sol stayed selective in weaker conditions but collapsed at full construction. Policy-trained Qwen generalized across lexical variations but showed no improvement at script allocation.
AI.conclusion: Online tool allocation represents a significant capability boundary for modern LLMs, even frontier models, highlighting the gap between abstract reasoning and practical implementation, especially in code construction contexts.

title: MINT-V2X: A Mobility-Integrated Network Trajectory Dataset for Predictive Resource Management
summary: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication systems are based on datasets that not only contain vehicle trajectory data but also wireless network parameters with a realistic level of fidelity, enabling the creation of prediction and optimization models. There is a very critical research infrastructure gap today, and publicly available datasets are likely to be limited to one of the two: mobility or network parameters, and rarely provide a single, integrated view that combines both. This paper introduces MINT-V2X, a comprehensive dataset generated by coupling SUMO traffic dynamics with OMNeT++/Simu5G network simulation. The validation framework is composed of 14 standardized tests based on 3GPP Release 14 (C-V2X), ETSI standards and Shannon capacity theory. The resulting dataset contains 9.87 million synchronized data points from 1,386 vehicles from 15 roadside units (RSUs) during 3 hours of urban traffic simulation. We demonstrate strict algorithmic consistency through network metric correlations (CQI-SINR: 0.993; SINR-PDR: 0.946). Finally, we demonstrate the value of the dataset by conducting an RSU load prediction case study, showing that using trajectory data yields better predictive performance than network-history-only baselines. The dataset, experiments, and complete SUMO configuration files are available in the GitHub repository to facilitate reproduction on alternative simulation stacks.

AI.tldr: MINT-V2X is a comprehensive V2X dataset that integrates realistic vehicle mobility data from SUMO with network simulation from OMNeT++/Simu5G, providing synchronized trajectory and wireless network parameters for V2X research.
AI.motivation: Current publicly available V2X datasets are limited to either mobility or network parameters, creating a critical research infrastructure gap. There's a need for integrated datasets that combine both realistic vehicle trajectory data and wireless network parameters with high fidelity.
AI.method: Coupled SUMO traffic dynamics with OMNeT++/Simu5G network simulation, validated using 14 standardized tests based on 3GPP Release 14 (C-V2X), ETSI standards, and Shannon capacity theory.
AI.result: Generated 9.87 million synchronized data points from 1,386 vehicles across 15 RSUs over 3 hours of urban traffic simulation. Demonstrated strong network metric correlations (CQI-SINR: 0.993; SINR-PDR: 0.946). Case study showed trajectory data improves RSU load prediction over network-history-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: MINT-V2X fills a critical gap in V2X research infrastructure by providing an integrated, validated dataset combining realistic mobility and network parameters, enabling better prediction and optimization models for V2X systems.

title: Training with (Swap) Regret Loss in a Single-Layer Self-Attention Model: A Case Study on the Probability Simplex
summary: We revisit the regret loss framework introduced in Park et al. (2025), which uses decision-theoretic regret as a direct loss function for training models to make better decisions, through the lens of probability-simplex policies. Our first result shows that a single-layer self-attention model trained with regret loss admits a stationary point whose forward-pass exactly matches smoothed fictitious play with the appropriate stepsize that ensures no-regret behavior-i.e., for any given policy input, the model outputs the same update that smoothed fictitious play would produce. In parallel, we also newly introduce a swap-regret loss function, which extends the regret-loss framework beyond external regret and enables models to directly optimize for swap-deviation robustness. We further show that this swap-regret loss admits a stationary point whose forward pass implements the corresponding swap-regret update induced by classical Blum-Mansour no-pass implementation algorithm, with each head implementing an external-regret update via smoothed fictitious play. Together, these results show that regret-trained attention can realize differentiable mechanisms whose deployment induces equilibrium behavior in games: external-regret dynamics lead to coarse correlated equilibrium, while swap-regret dynamics lead to correlated equilibrium. Thus, regret-based objectives steer minimal attention architectures toward online-learning dynamics with game-theoretic guarantees, without supervised traces of those algorithms.

AI.tldr: Regret-trained self-attention models can implement no-regret learning dynamics like smoothed fictitious play and Blum-Mansour algorithms, achieving game-theoretic equilibria without supervised training on those algorithms.
AI.motivation: To develop models that learn to make better decisions using regret-based loss functions rather than traditional supervised learning, enabling models to implement no-regret online learning algorithms and achieve game-theoretic equilibrium behavior.
AI.method: 1) Extends regret loss framework from Park et al. (2025) using probability-simplex policies. 2) Shows single-layer self-attention trained with regret loss yields stationary point matching smoothed fictitious play. 3) Introduces swap-regret loss function for swap-deviation robustness. 4) Shows swap-regret loss yields stationary point implementing Blum-Mansour no-pass algorithm.
AI.result: 1) Regret-trained attention models implement differentiable versions of no-regret dynamics. 2) External-regret dynamics lead to coarse correlated equilibrium in games. 3) Swap-regret dynamics lead to correlated equilibrium. 4) Models achieve these game-theoretic guarantees without supervised training on algorithm traces.
AI.conclusion: Regret-based objectives can steer minimal attention architectures to implement online-learning dynamics with provable game-theoretic guarantees, providing a way to train models that naturally converge to equilibrium behavior in strategic settings.

title: EventOD: Event-Aware OD Flow Generation via LLM-Guided Semantic Modulation
summary: Estimating origin-destination (OD) flows under disruptive events is important for disaster response and urban resilience. Existing deep OD models trained on routine mobility often degrade when extreme events abruptly alter regional functions and population activities, while retraining a new generator for each event is impractical under limited event-time supervision. We propose EventOD, an event-adaptive OD generation framework that steers a pretrained OD generator using structured event semantics. EventOD first uses a large language model to infer region-level functional and demographic control vectors from coarse event observations. It then learns two lightweight adaptation modules, AlphaNet and BetaNet, to calibrate the magnitude of these semantic shifts, and further introduces a retrieval-augmented fallback pathway for scenarios with sparse supervision. The resulting event-conditioned features are injected into a pretrained graph diffusion OD model through input-level modulation, enabling event-aware adaptation without updating generator parameters. Experiments on hurricane- and pandemic-induced mobility across U.S. counties show that EventOD consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and distributional fidelity over strong baselines. Source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EventOD-5C11/.

AI.tldr: EventOD is an event-adaptive framework that uses structured event semantics to steer a pretrained OD generator for estimating origin-destination flows during disruptive events without retraining the generator.
AI.motivation: Existing deep OD models trained on routine mobility degrade during extreme events that abruptly alter regional functions and population activities. Retraining new generators for each event is impractical due to limited event-time supervision.
AI.method: EventOD uses an LLM to infer region-level functional and demographic control vectors from coarse event observations. It learns two lightweight adaptation modules (AlphaNet and BetaNet) to calibrate semantic shifts, and includes a retrieval-augmented fallback pathway for sparse supervision. The event-conditioned features are injected into a pretrained graph diffusion OD model through input-level modulation without updating generator parameters.
AI.result: Experiments on hurricane- and pandemic-induced mobility across U.S. counties show that EventOD consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and distributional fidelity over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: EventOD provides an effective event-adaptive OD generation framework that enables accurate estimation of mobility flows during disruptive events without requiring generator retraining, addressing the limitations of existing approaches for disaster response and urban resilience.

title: Neural operator discovery from heterogeneous trajectories
summary: Neural operators provide data-driven mappings for modeling dynamical systems. Extending them to families of systems typically requires explicit conditioning variables such as physical parameters, geometries, or boundary conditions. In many real-world settings, these quantities are unobserved. Here, we formulate neural operator discovery (NOD) as the problem of learning both shared solution operators and system-specific variation directly from heterogeneous trajectories without access to labeled governing factors. We introduce a factorized latent-conditioning formulation that jointly learns a neural operator and a low-dimensional latent representation through factorized prediction, trajectory-decoupled sampling, and dimension selection. Across diverse systems, the learned latent representation captures the intrinsic dimensionality of system variation and organizes system instances in a smooth and approximately invertible latent structure aligned with the underlying governing factors. This organization enables generalization to previously unseen system instances, including zero-shot extrapolation across regimes and stable long-horizon prediction. These results establish an interpretable paradigm for operator learning in the absence of explicit factor supervision.

AI.tldr: Neural operator discovery learns both shared solution operators and system-specific variation from heterogeneous trajectories without explicit conditioning variables like physical parameters.
AI.motivation: Traditional neural operators require explicit conditioning variables (physical parameters, geometries, boundary conditions), but in real-world settings these quantities are often unobserved. There's a need to learn operators from heterogeneous trajectories without access to labeled governing factors.
AI.method: Introduced a factorized latent-conditioning formulation that jointly learns a neural operator and low-dimensional latent representation through factorized prediction, trajectory-decoupled sampling, and dimension selection.
AI.result: The learned latent representation captures the intrinsic dimensionality of system variation and organizes system instances in a smooth, approximately invertible latent structure aligned with underlying governing factors. This enables generalization to unseen system instances, including zero-shot extrapolation across regimes and stable long-horizon prediction.
AI.conclusion: Establishes an interpretable paradigm for operator learning without explicit factor supervision, demonstrating that neural operators can discover both shared solution operators and system-specific variation directly from heterogeneous data.

title: StanceBench: A Benchmark for Audio LLM-Based Interpersonal Stance Evaluation from Speech
summary: Speech-to-speech dialogue models increasingly depend on prosody and interactional nuance to convey social intent, yet benchmarks for these cues remain limited. We introduce StanceBench, a benchmark for measuring interpersonal stance in conversational speech and evaluating audio-capable LLMs as automated judges. Using the Seamless Interaction corpus, StanceBench (1) specifies 9 stance dimensions via role-prompt poles, (2) standardizes single-speaker and interaction-based evaluations, and (3) reports LLM-as-a-judge robustness, bias, and stance inference. Across evaluated stances, empathy and politeness are the easiest. Warmth and assertiveness are moderately separable with positivity skew/asymmetry. Honesty is the hardest and shows high prompt order bias, consistent with needing cross-turn evidence. Attentiveness is separable but aligns weakly with humans. Interaction stances are more context-sensitive, with threshold gaps and high variance, especially conflict regulation.

AI.tldr: StanceBench is a benchmark for measuring interpersonal stance in conversational speech, using audio-capable LLMs as automated judges to evaluate 9 stance dimensions from the Seamless Interaction corpus.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for speech-to-speech dialogue models are limited in measuring prosody and interactional nuances that convey social intent. There's a need for standardized evaluation of interpersonal stance in conversational speech.
AI.method: Developed StanceBench using the Seamless Interaction corpus with three main components: 1) Specified 9 stance dimensions using role-prompt poles, 2) Standardized single-speaker and interaction-based evaluations, 3) Reported LLM-as-a-judge robustness, bias, and stance inference performance.
AI.result: Found that empathy and politeness are easiest to detect, warmth and assertiveness are moderately separable with positivity skew, honesty is hardest with high prompt order bias, attentiveness is separable but weakly aligned with humans. Interaction stances show high context-sensitivity with threshold gaps and high variance, especially for conflict regulation.
AI.conclusion: StanceBench provides a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating interpersonal stance in conversational speech, revealing systematic patterns in how well different stances can be detected by LLM judges and highlighting the challenges of measuring context-sensitive interactional nuances.

title: Does Graph Compression Preserve Signal Propagation?
summary: Graph compression reduces the computational cost of graph learning, but its effect on signal propagation remains largely underexplored. Existing work evaluates compression through downstream task performance or structural preservation, neither of which directly captures how propagation dynamics change after compression. We study two fundamental compression paradigms, coarsening and sparsification, and ask whether they preserve the propagation behavior of the original graph. Across five datasets, varying compression rates, and propagation depths, we measure signal behavior through three complementary metrics. Our results reveal a consistent tension between the two compression families. Sparsification retains higher signal diversity and mitigates oversmoothing, but its propagation trajectory progressively diverges from that of the original graph. Coarsening more faithfully preserves propagation behavior, but at the cost of stronger smoothing and rank collapse. These findings demonstrate that two propagation-centric objectives, preserving signal diversity and preserving propagation fidelity, are distinct and empirically at odds under graph compression, highlighting the need for evaluation protocols that jointly consider both dimensions. The code and results are available at: https://github.com/KawshikBanerjee/Compression-Propagation-Duality

AI.tldr: Graph compression alters signal propagation behavior differently based on method: sparsification preserves signal diversity but diverges from original propagation, while coarsening maintains propagation fidelity but causes stronger smoothing and rank collapse.
AI.motivation: Current graph compression evaluation focuses on downstream task performance or structural preservation, but doesn't directly measure how signal propagation dynamics change after compression, creating a gap in understanding compression's effects on fundamental graph behavior.
AI.method: The study examines two compression paradigms (coarsening and sparsification) across five datasets with varying compression rates and propagation depths. It measures signal behavior through three complementary metrics to evaluate how well each method preserves propagation behavior compared to original graphs.
AI.result: Sparsification retains higher signal diversity and mitigates oversmoothing but progressively diverges from original propagation trajectory. Coarsening preserves propagation behavior more faithfully but causes stronger smoothing and rank collapse. The two propagation-centric objectives (preserving signal diversity vs preserving propagation fidelity) are empirically at odds.
AI.conclusion: Graph compression creates a tension between preserving signal diversity and maintaining propagation fidelity, with different methods excelling at different objectives. This highlights the need for evaluation protocols that consider both dimensions when assessing compression methods, as current metrics don't capture this dual nature of propagation behavior.

title: TRE: Training-Free Hallucination Detection for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion large language models (D-LLMs) have recently gained increasing attention, yet their reliability is significantly hindered by the hallucination problem. Existing hallucination detection approaches for D-LLMs mainly follow a training-based paradigm, relying on data-driven training to optimize the detector. Such reliance not only limits their generalizability across domains models but also incurs additional training cost and deployment overhead. To address these limitations, we propose TRE, a training-free hallucination detection metric for D-LLMs. TRE is a parameter-free and single-run metric that estimates hallucination risk directly from the entropy signals of a single generation, without requiring any detector training or repeated sampling. TRE extracts entropy signals within the D-LLM decoding process along both the spatial and temporal dimensions. From a token-level spatial perspective, we focus on revealing tokens as the most informative carriers of uncertainty, capturing where uncertainty is actively committed. From a diffusion step-level temporal perspective, we empirically identify the dominance of late-step entropy and hence aggregate these signals with a simple linear weighting scheme to obtain TRE. Extensive experiments on multiple D-LLMs and QA datasets demonstrate that TRE achieves competitive performance, while enjoying strong generalizability, efficiency, and robustness.

AI.tldr: TRE is a training-free hallucination detection metric for Diffusion LLMs that uses entropy signals from a single generation without needing detector training or repeated sampling.
AI.motivation: Current hallucination detection approaches for Diffusion LLMs are training-based, which limits generalizability across domains/models and incurs additional training costs and deployment overhead.
AI.method: TRE extracts entropy signals from D-LLM decoding process along spatial (token-level) and temporal (diffusion step-level) dimensions. It focuses on revealing tokens as uncertainty carriers and aggregates late-step entropy with linear weighting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple D-LLMs and QA datasets show TRE achieves competitive performance while offering strong generalizability, efficiency, and robustness.
AI.conclusion: TRE provides an effective training-free solution for hallucination detection in D-LLMs that addresses the limitations of existing training-based approaches.

title: SPRKD: Effective Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks via Saddle Region Approximation
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Code and reproduction scripts: https://github.com/thetechdude124/SADDLE-POINT-RECRUITMENT-FOR-KNOWLEDGE-DISTILLATION. Awarded 2nd Place in Mathematical and Cybersecurity Research (NSA) at Regeneron ISEF 2023 and an Outstanding Research Award at WAICY (World AI Competition for Youth) 2022
summary: Modern deep neural networks are potent catalysts for scientific and industrial impact, yet excessive parameter counts impede deployment in low-compute settings such as hospital equipment and energy infrastructure. Predominant knowledge distillation (KD) methods favor replication: smaller students mimic teacher output logits, yet empirically yield low task performance, hamper convergence, and act merely as regularization rather than substantive knowledge transfer. We propose Saddle Point Recruitment for Knowledge Distillation (SPRKD), reframing distillation from replication to employing teachers as optimization-curvature and domain proxies, characterizing saddle points as regions of strong further-descent potential via embedding and basin-fractal properties. Using Hessian eigenvalue spectral density (ESD), SPRKD identifies low-loss saddle regions for student re-exploration; weak-teacher ensembles are aggregated into an Approximated Saddle Region (ASR), re-parameterized into the student via Transfer Learning by Injection, and approached with exponentially decaying Euclidean transformations, Negative Hessian Eigensteps, and Gaussian perturbations. On malaria blood smear classification with a 6,430-parameter CNN distilled from a weak 25,546-parameter teacher, SPRKD reaches 94.8% validation accuracy, outperforming Response KD by 24.70 percentage points (McNemar p = 6.3e-87) and matching scratch-trained baselines of the same architecture to statistical equivalence (p = 1.0). Across MNIST, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, SPRKD exceeds scratch-trained baselines by up to 8 percentage points on preliminary benchmarks. Hessian ESD and 2-D loss landscape analysis show convergence to wider minima with substantially smaller Hessian trace and spectral radius than Response KD and control students, indicating smoother descent and greater noise robustness.

AI.tldr: SPRKD is a new knowledge distillation method that reframes distillation from replication to using teachers as optimization-curvature proxies, identifying saddle points for student re-exploration to achieve better performance with small models.
AI.motivation: Modern deep neural networks have excessive parameters that impede deployment in low-compute settings like hospitals and energy infrastructure. Current knowledge distillation methods suffer from low task performance, hampered convergence, and act more as regularization than substantive knowledge transfer.
AI.method: SPRKD reframes distillation as using teachers as optimization-curvature and domain proxies. It identifies low-loss saddle regions via Hessian eigenvalue spectral density, aggregates weak-teacher ensembles into an Approximated Saddle Region, re-parameterizes this into the student via Transfer Learning by Injection, and uses Euclidean transformations, Negative Hessian Eigensteps, and Gaussian perturbations.
AI.result: On malaria blood smear classification with a 6,430-parameter CNN distilled from a weak teacher, SPRKD reached 94.8% validation accuracy, outperforming Response KD by 24.70 percentage points. Across MNIST, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, it exceeded scratch-trained baselines by up to 8 percentage points. Hessian analysis showed convergence to wider minima with smaller Hessian trace and spectral radius.
AI.conclusion: SPRKD successfully transforms knowledge distillation from mere replication to substantive knowledge transfer using teachers as optimization-curvature proxies, enabling better performance with smaller models suitable for low-compute environments while achieving smoother descent and greater noise robustness.

title: CuraWeb: Joint Optimization of Quality, Redundancy, and Diversity for Web-Scale Pretraining Data
summary: Open-web corpora curated via highly selective filters, such as FineWeb-Edu and DCLM, constitute the core of LLM pretraining data and have significantly advanced LLM performance. However, these pipelines typically rely on singular optimization objectives, which inevitably narrows distributional diversity and marginalizes long-tail knowledge, thereby restricting data coverage and underutilizing the vast potential of the open web. To address this limitation, we propose a novel curation paradigm that shifts from linear pruning to the joint optimization of quality, redundancy, and diversity. This framework synergizes dual-track cleaning (rule-based and model-driven) with hybrid deduplication (n-gram and semantic), while employing a multi-objective sampler to balance informational quality with distributional breadth. Applying this framework to Common Crawl, we construct CuraWeb, a 2T-token English corpus. Unlike existing resources, CuraWeb establishes an industrial-grade standard for data curation by recovering a more holistic data distribution with enhanced diversity and minimal redundancy, achieving broader coverage of long-tail knowledge across diverse domains. Experimental evaluations at the 3B scale demonstrate that CuraWeb significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, yielding an average performance gain of 1.8\% across a wide range of benchmarks, particularly in knowledge-intensive and reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: CuraWeb introduces a multi-objective web corpus curation framework balancing quality, redundancy, and diversity to recover holistic data distributions and long-tail knowledge, outperforming state-of-the-art curated corpora.
AI.motivation: Current LLM pretraining corpora use highly selective filters with singular optimization objectives, which narrow distributional diversity and marginalize long-tail knowledge, restricting data coverage and underutilizing the open web's potential.
AI.method: Proposes a joint optimization paradigm combining dual-track cleaning (rule-based and model-driven) with hybrid deduplication (n-gram and semantic), and employs a multi-objective sampler to balance informational quality with distributional breadth.
AI.result: Applied to Common Crawl to create CuraWeb, a 2T-token English corpus that establishes industrial-grade data curation standards, recovers holistic data distributions with enhanced diversity and minimal redundancy, and provides broader long-tail knowledge coverage.
AI.conclusion: CuraWeb significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at 3B scale, achieving 1.8% average performance gain across benchmarks, particularly excelling in knowledge-intensive and reasoning tasks, demonstrating the value of multi-objective curation for web-scale pretraining data.

title: Exploration of the generative capabilities of Boltzmann machines applied to social systems under the majority rule
summary: We study the generative capabilities of Boltzmann machines to recover systems governed by the majority rule under critical conditions. To this end, we train deep belief networks (DBNs) with different configurations, where the first layer can use Gaussian visible units with more than two states (i.e., non-binary units). We then allow the DBN to "dream" samples conditioned on visible units that we keep fixed, and we measure the deviation of this dreamed system from the real one. We also corroborate, using a discrete thermometer based on a convolutional network, that the reconstructions remain in a critical state. Across several training sessions with different architectures, we show that, despite the complexity of the problem, the DBN can recover samples that remain critical even under input noise, with a gradual degradation of physical observables relative to the original sample.

AI.tldr: Deep Belief Networks with Gaussian visible units can successfully recover and generate critical systems governed by majority rule, maintaining criticality even under input noise with gradual degradation of physical observables.
AI.motivation: To study the generative capabilities of Boltzmann machines in recovering complex physical systems governed by majority rule under critical conditions, particularly exploring whether neural networks can capture and reproduce critical behavior.
AI.method: Train deep belief networks (DBNs) with various configurations, using Gaussian visible units with multiple states (non-binary) in the first layer. The DBNs are allowed to "dream" samples conditioned on fixed visible units, and deviations from real systems are measured. Criticality of reconstructions is verified using a discrete thermometer based on a convolutional network.
AI.result: DBNs can successfully recover samples that remain critical even under input noise, though there is gradual degradation of physical observables relative to the original sample. Multiple training sessions with different architectures consistently demonstrate this capability despite the problem's complexity.
AI.conclusion: Deep Belief Networks with non-binary visible units possess strong generative capabilities for recovering critical systems governed by majority rule, maintaining critical state in reconstructions even with noisy inputs, making them promising for studying complex physical systems.

title: Beyond Block Boundaries: Multi-Block Editing for Diffusion Large Language Models
summary: Block diffusion has emerged as the dominant paradigm for scaling discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs), because decoding text in fixed-size blocks preserves parallel generation within each block while keeping the quadratic attention cost tractable. However, this efficiency comes with a structural limitation: tokens near the end of a block are generated without access to future cross-block context, and once a block is finalized, its uncertain predictions become irreversible context for all subsequent blocks. This creates a block boundary problem, in which uncertainty accumulates toward block boundaries and early mistakes propagate throughout later generation. To address this issue, we propose Multi-Block Editing (MBE), to mitigate this problem by editing decoded tokens based on cross-block context. Following this principle, MBE first proposes a training-free decoding algorithm to edit the decoded tokens in previous blocks, which is achieved by re-opening a full-attention window over selected blocks. Given the mismatched attention mechanism between block diffusion training and MBE inference, MBE further introduces a supervised Fine-tuning strategy, which equips the model with bidirectional attention masks that progressively expands the editing span. Furthermore, it also extends SGLang with a multi-shape CUDA Graph pool and fine-grained KV cache control to make these variable-length editing passes efficient in practice. Experiments on LLaDA2.1-Mini across 13 benchmarks show that training-free MBE outperforms all existing decoding baselines while maintaining comparable throughput, and MBE SFT further brings a performance gain of 2.7. The largest improvements appear on tasks requiring strong long-range consistency, including +13.3 on AIME 2025 and +5.9 on ZebraLogic, demonstrating the effectiveness of MBE.

AI.tldr: Multi-Block Editing (MBE) addresses the block boundary problem in block diffusion language models by enabling editing of previously decoded tokens using cross-block context, improving long-range consistency while maintaining efficiency.
AI.motivation: Block diffusion models face a structural limitation where tokens near block boundaries are generated without future cross-block context, and once a block is finalized, early uncertain predictions become irreversible context for subsequent blocks. This causes uncertainty accumulation at boundaries and error propagation throughout generation.
AI.method: MBE introduces a training-free decoding algorithm that edits decoded tokens in previous blocks by re-opening full-attention windows over selected blocks. To address attention mechanism mismatches, it adds supervised fine-tuning with bidirectional attention masks that progressively expand editing spans. The system is made efficient via SGLang extensions with multi-shape CUDA Graph pool and fine-grained KV cache control.
AI.result: Experiments on LLaDA2.1-Mini across 13 benchmarks show training-free MBE outperforms all existing decoding baselines with comparable throughput. MBE SFT provides additional 2.7 point performance gain. Largest improvements are on tasks requiring long-range consistency: +13.3 on AIME 2025 and +5.9 on ZebraLogic.
AI.conclusion: MBE effectively mitigates the block boundary problem in block diffusion language models by enabling token editing based on cross-block context, significantly improving long-range consistency while maintaining practical efficiency through optimized system implementations.

title: On the Impossibility of Unbiased and Length-Invariant Policy Optimization with Outcome Rewards
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is the dominant reinforcement learning algorithm for training reasoning capabilities in large language models, notably adopted by DeepSeek-R1. The recent improvement Dr. GRPO (COLM 2025) identifies the response-level length bias caused by per-trajectory length normalization in GRPO and proposes removing this normalization, claiming the resulting optimizer is "unbiased." We show that this claim is incomplete. Specifically, we establish an impossibility theorem: under the standard outcome reward + GRPO setting, no length-based weighting scheme can simultaneously achieve the following two properties. (P1) Gradient unbiasedness: the gradient estimator is an unbiased estimate of the true policy gradient. (P2) Length invariance: each trajectory's effective contribution to the gradient is independent of its token length. GRPO approximately satisfies P2 but violates P1; Dr. GRPO satisfies P1 but violates P2. We characterize the complete tradeoff spectrum via the parametric family f_alpha(L) = L^{alpha - 1}, where alpha = 0 recovers GRPO, alpha = 1 recovers Dr. GRPO, and provide quantitative analysis showing that Dr. GRPO's length bias can cause longer trajectories to dominate gradient updates by a factor proportional to the length ratio. Our results reveal that neither algorithm is universally "done right"; they occupy opposite ends of a fundamental and unavoidable tradeoff.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that neither GRPO nor Dr. GRPO is universally optimal - they occupy opposite ends of an unavoidable tradeoff between gradient unbiasedness and length invariance in RL for reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Dr. GRPO was recently proposed as an improvement to GRPO (the dominant RL algorithm for training reasoning capabilities in LLMs), claiming to remove length bias by eliminating per-trajectory length normalization. The authors found this claim incomplete and wanted to examine the fundamental tradeoffs involved.
AI.method: The authors establish an impossibility theorem showing that under standard outcome reward + GRPO setting, no length-based weighting scheme can simultaneously achieve gradient unbiasedness (P1) and length invariance (P2). They characterize the complete tradeoff spectrum using a parametric family f_alpha(L) = L^{alpha - 1}, where alpha = 0 recovers GRPO and alpha = 1 recovers Dr. GRPO.
AI.result: GRPO approximately satisfies length invariance (P2) but violates gradient unbiasedness (P1), while Dr. GRPO satisfies gradient unbiasedness (P1) but violates length invariance (P2). The authors quantitatively show that Dr. GRPO's length bias can cause longer trajectories to dominate gradient updates by a factor proportional to the length ratio.
AI.conclusion: Neither GRPO nor Dr. GRPO is universally "done right" - they represent opposite ends of a fundamental and unavoidable tradeoff between gradient unbiasedness and length invariance in RL algorithms for training reasoning capabilities in LLMs.

title: Obliviate: Efficient Unlearning in Recommender Systems
summary: Machine unlearning is becoming increasingly critical in the context of data privacy regulations, particularly for recommendation systems that are directly trained on user interaction data. The goal of this work is to remove requested interaction data and their downstream influence from trained model while preserving recommendation quality, and to do so without incurring the substantial computational cost of full retraining. Existing approaches exhibit several limitations, including limited unlearning completeness and degradation in recommendation performance, while having substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose Obliviate, an efficient two-stage unlearning framework for recommender systems that achieves high unlearning completeness while maintaining good utility. In the first stage, we introduce a Low-Rank Unlearning Adapter (LUA), which employs a lightweight Hessian proxy to enable curvature-aware and efficient unlearning through localized low-rank adapters rather than full parameters. In the second stage, we propose Locality-Aware Calibration (LAC), a lightweight refinement stage that updates only the adapter parameters to improve the performance by enforcing unlearning via ranking-based objectives while preserving utility through knowledge distillation. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that Obliviate achieves high level of forgetting with minimal loss in recommendation quality and at significantly reduced computational cost, offering a practical and scalable solution for large-scale recommender systems.

AI.tldr: Obliviate is a two-stage machine unlearning framework for recommender systems that efficiently removes user interaction data while preserving recommendation quality, using low-rank adapters and lightweight refinement instead of full retraining.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning is critical for data privacy compliance in recommendation systems, but existing approaches have limitations including poor unlearning completeness, degraded performance, and high computational overhead. There's a need for efficient solutions that can remove requested interaction data without full retraining costs.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: 1) Low-Rank Unlearning Adapter (LUA) uses a lightweight Hessian proxy for curvature-aware unlearning through localized low-rank adapters instead of full parameters. 2) Locality-Aware Calibration (LAC) refines adapter parameters using ranking-based objectives for unlearning and knowledge distillation for utility preservation.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show Obliviate achieves high forgetting levels with minimal recommendation quality loss, at significantly reduced computational cost compared to full retraining and other existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Obliviate provides a practical, scalable solution for large-scale recommender systems needing efficient machine unlearning, balancing privacy compliance (data removal) with maintained recommendation utility and computational efficiency.

title: Bitcoin Price Direction Prediction via Regime-Aware Multi-Modal Fusion of Social Sentiment and Technical Features
summary: Bitcoin price prediction on sub-daily timescales is a hard open problem in computational finance. Bitcoin exhibits fat-tailed returns, non-stationary dynamics, and a price discovery process influenced by social discourse on Reddit and Twitter. Conventional approaches fuse OHLCV technical features with sentiment via static concatenation, applying identical fusion weights regardless of market state. This is inconsistent with the behavioural finance literature, which shows that retail sentiment is most predictive during volatile periods and noisy during calm ones. This paper proposes Regime-Aware Multi-Modal Learning (RAML), which conditions fusion of sentiment and price features on a dynamically detected binary market regime. Rolling 24-hour volatility partitions observations into stable and volatile regimes; a learnable sigmoid gate adjusts the weight of the sentiment embedding relative to the price embedding, trusting sentiment more during volatility and price dynamics more during stable phases. The system is evaluated on 3,491 hourly observations (July 2024-September 2025), combining Bitcoin OHLCV data with Reddit /r/Bitcoin FinBERT sentiment. Four models are compared - price-only BiLSTM, sentiment-only classifier, static-concatenation BiLSTM, and RAML - across 3-hour and 6-hour horizons, with an ablation study isolating the sentiment branch, regime detection, and adaptive fusion. RAML achieves macro-F1 of 0.5474 (3h) and 0.5513 (6h), with the highest AUC at 3 hours (0.5084), indicating better calibration. Ablation confirms every component is necessary, and replacing adaptive weighting with concatenation causes recall collapse at 6 hours (F1: 0.14). These results establish regime-conditioned adaptive fusion as a necessary design principle for multi-modal financial forecasting.

AI.tldr: RAML proposes regime-aware adaptive fusion of Bitcoin price and sentiment data, outperforming static approaches by dynamically adjusting sentiment importance based on market volatility.
AI.motivation: Bitcoin price prediction is challenging due to fat-tailed returns, non-stationary dynamics, and social discourse influence. Conventional static fusion of price and sentiment data ignores behavioral finance insights that retail sentiment's predictive value varies with market states (most useful during volatility, noisy during calm periods).
AI.method: Regime-Aware Multi-Modal Learning (RAML) with three key components: 1) dynamic binary market regime detection using rolling 24-hour volatility to partition observations into stable/volatile states, 2) learnable sigmoid gate that adjusts sentiment embedding weight relative to price embedding, trusting sentiment more during volatility and price dynamics more during stable phases, and 3) evaluation on 3,491 hourly observations combining Bitcoin OHLCV data with Reddit /r/Bitcoin FinBERT sentiment.
AI.result: RAML achieves macro-F1 of 0.5474 (3h) and 0.5513 (6h), with highest AUC at 3 hours (0.5084), indicating better calibration. Ablation study confirms all components necessary. Replacing adaptive weighting with concatenation causes recall collapse at 6 hours (F1: 0.14), demonstrating superiority of adaptive fusion.
AI.conclusion: Regime-conditioned adaptive fusion is a necessary design principle for multi-modal financial forecasting, addressing limitations of static feature fusion by dynamically adjusting sentiment importance based on market volatility states.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Sensor Selection in Maritime Surveillance
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, submitted to the IEEE MetroSea 2026 Conference: Special Session 13: Object Detection, Tracking, and Sensor Fusion for Maritime Situational Awareness
summary: This paper presents an information-gain-guided reinforcement-learning sensor-selection framework for single-vessel tracking in heterogeneous maritime sensor networks. The proposed approach is motivated by information-theoretic sensor management: instead of activating all sensors or repeatedly performing computationally expensive online expected-information-gain evaluation, a learned policy selects one tracking-relevant sensor at each decision epoch. A Bayesian sequential Monte Carlo tracker estimates the vessel state from noisy measurements and provides a belief representation for scheduling under nonlinear and non-Gaussian conditions. A Proximal Policy Optimization agent selects one of five sensors deployed in a georeferenced simulation of the CMMI Smart Marina testbed at Ayia Napa Marina, Cyprus. The agent observes belief-state, detection-history, coverage, sensor-geometry, and realized-information-gain features. The reward is defined as a realized-information-gain term gated by an observability mask. Final-test simulations compare the proposed framework with random single-sensor selection, always-on sensing using all sensors simultaneously, and the expected-information-gain sensor-selection baseline proposed in our previous work. Results show that the learned policy achieves tracking performance close to always-on sensing while activating only one sensor per decision time step and avoiding the computationally expensive online entropy search required by expected-information-gain selection.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework for intelligent sensor selection in maritime tracking that uses information-gain guidance to select only one relevant sensor per time step, achieving near-optimal tracking with minimal computational cost.
AI.motivation: To address the computational inefficiency of activating all sensors or performing expensive online expected-information-gain evaluations in maritime tracking scenarios, while maintaining effective single-vessel tracking in heterogeneous sensor networks.
AI.method: Uses a Proximal Policy Optimization agent with Bayesian sequential Monte Carlo tracking that observes belief-state, detection history, coverage, sensor geometry, and realized information gain. The agent selects one of five sensors deployed in a georeferenced simulation of a marina testbed using information-theoretic rewards gated by observability.
AI.result: The learned policy achieves tracking performance close to always-on sensing while activating only one sensor per decision time step, avoiding the computationally expensive online entropy search required by expected-information-gain selection baselines.
AI.conclusion: The information-gain-guided reinforcement learning framework provides an effective and computationally efficient solution for sensor selection in maritime tracking, balancing tracking accuracy with resource constraints and computational overhead.

title: Directional Influence Function: Estimating Training Data Influence in Constrained Learning
summary: As constrained learning becomes increasingly common, models are trained under explicit feasibility requirements to enforce fairness, safety, robustness, regulariza- tion, and physics or logic constraints. Understanding how training samples in- fluence the model solution (e.g., learned parameters) is crucial for interpretability and robustness. The classical influence function (IF) estimates sample contribu- tions via local sensitivity analysis, measuring how the solution changes when a specific training sample is perturbed or removed. However, IF becomes unreli- able in constrained settings: data perturbations can reshape both the objective and the feasible region, leading to estimates that violate feasibility. In response, we propose the Directional Influence Function (DIF), a novel estimator that explicitly incorporates these constraints into influence estimation. DIF formulates the opti- mality conditions of constrained learning as a variational inequality (VI) and ana- lyzes how perturbing training data affects this VI. We validate DIF on constrained linear regression and demonstrate that it recovers leave-one-out retraining results, whereas IF and penalty-based IF exhibit significant bias. We further apply DIF to fairness-constrained CNNs, where DIF accurately predicts test loss changes under data removal and aligns closely with actual retraining. Our results establish DIF as an efficient and reliable tool for data attribution in constrained learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Directional Influence Function (DIF), a novel influence estimation method for constrained learning that explicitly accounts for constraints, unlike classical influence functions which become unreliable when constraints are present.
AI.motivation: As constrained learning becomes increasingly common for enforcing requirements like fairness, safety, and physics/logic constraints, understanding how training samples influence model solutions is crucial for interpretability and robustness. Classical influence functions become unreliable in constrained settings because data perturbations can reshape both the objective and feasible region, leading to estimates that violate feasibility.
AI.method: The authors propose Directional Influence Function (DIF), which formulates the optimality conditions of constrained learning as a variational inequality (VI) and analyzes how perturbing training data affects this VI. This explicitly incorporates constraints into influence estimation.
AI.result: DIF is validated on constrained linear regression where it recovers leave-one-out retraining results, while classical IF and penalty-based IF exhibit significant bias. In fairness-constrained CNNs, DIF accurately predicts test loss changes under data removal and aligns closely with actual retraining.
AI.conclusion: DIF establishes itself as an efficient and reliable tool for data attribution in constrained learning, addressing the limitations of classical influence functions in constrained settings.

title: AIR-BENCH Live: An Evolving Safety Benchmark for Foundation Models
summary: Foundation-model safety benchmarks capture the AI risks of their time of publication: as models improve and governments pass new AI-safety legislation, their risk taxonomies become incomprehensive and their attack prompts become ineffective. We present AIR-BENCH Live, a self-evolving successor to AIR-BENCH 2024. An automated update pipeline monitors government regulation and classifies new policies against the current four-tier risk taxonomy, either matching them to existing categories or proposing new granular categories. Then, a multi-agent, persona-driven prompt generation algorithm generates realistic, multilingual prompts with minimal human review, leaving room for improvement with modern jail breaking techniques. This algorithm is used to overhaul legacy prompts and generate prompts for new categories. In our current version, the pipeline has expanded the benchmark from 314 to 335 granular risks, with the 21 new categories drawing from 31 truly novel policy clauses across seven jurisdictions. Evaluating 14 recent models, we find a wide safety spread (from 0.17 to 0.89 among the models judged on their own behavior), that the modernized prompts are on average 0.06 points harder than the 2024 set, with the largest drops concentrated among the most compliant models, and that most models are modestly less safe on non-English prompts. By continuously absorbing new regulation and regenerating prompts, AIR-BENCH Live is designed to evolve alongside a fast-moving field.

AI.tldr: AIR-BENCH Live is a self-evolving AI safety benchmark that automatically updates by monitoring government regulations, expanding risk taxonomies, and generating multilingual attack prompts to keep pace with AI safety legislation and model advancements.
AI.motivation: Existing AI safety benchmarks become outdated as models improve and new regulations are passed, making their risk taxonomies incomplete and attack prompts ineffective against modern models. There's a need for benchmarks that continuously evolve alongside the fast-moving AI safety field.
AI.method: 1) Automated pipeline monitors government regulations and classifies new policies against existing 4-tier risk taxonomy or proposes new categories. 2) Multi-agent, persona-driven prompt generation algorithm creates realistic multilingual attack prompts with minimal human review. 3) Modern jailbreaking techniques are incorporated to improve prompt effectiveness. 4) The system overhauls legacy prompts and generates new ones for expanded risk categories.
AI.result: The pipeline expanded the benchmark from 314 to 335 granular risks, adding 21 new categories from 31 novel policy clauses across 7 jurisdictions. Evaluation of 14 recent models showed: wide safety spread (0.17-0.89 scores), modernized prompts are 0.06 points harder on average (with biggest drops for most compliant models), and most models are modestly less safe on non-English prompts.
AI.conclusion: AIR-BENCH Live successfully addresses the problem of outdated safety benchmarks by creating a self-evolving system that continuously absorbs new regulations and regenerates prompts, allowing it to remain relevant as AI safety standards and models advance over time.

title: When Can Depth Replace Precision? A Resource Theory of Quantized Neural Computation
comment: 141 pages, 26 figures, 15 tables. Includes complete proofs and documents the QReplace decision-support and Lean 4 verification companions. To be submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research
summary: When can additional low-bit residual computation replace missing numerical precision for a fixed input-output map? We model a quantized residual system over a fixed horizon as a pure schedule selecting fields from a declared low-bit operation library, and use relaxed controls to characterize its infinite-depth limit. The distance from the target to the closed relaxed reachable set is the exact structural floor: no increase in depth can remove it for that library. Pure schedules approach the relaxed class at rate $O(D^{-1})$ under bounded-variation time dependence and $O(D^{-\vartheta}+D^{-1})$ under Holder dependence of exponent $\vartheta$. Execution arithmetic can reverse this conclusion: full-state write-back introduces a $Dρ_z$ penalty and can freeze residual updates, whereas increment error feedback replaces this growth by a bounded carry term and obeys an exact common-lattice conservation law. A fixed-teacher converse makes this rate sharp: for coherent depth-$L$ first-order high-precision comparators, accuracy matching requires $D=Θ(L)$. Learned codebooks add a metadata resource, while state-dependent routing introduces hybrid event conditions. Verified primal and dual bounds yield feasible, impossible, or unresolved decisions before training. Companion software implements the workflow, and Lean 4 machine-checks the exact discrete core. Depth replaces precision only relative to a declared library, horizon, execution semantics, and routing model.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes when low-bit residual computation can replace missing numerical precision, establishing theoretical bounds on how depth in residual systems can compensate for limited precision relative to a target input-output map.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand the fundamental trade-offs between computation depth and numerical precision in quantized systems - specifically when deeper but lower-precision residual computations can achieve the same input-output mapping as shallower but higher-precision alternatives.
AI.method: Models quantized residual systems as pure schedules selecting from low-bit operation libraries, uses relaxed controls to characterize infinite-depth limits, analyzes distance to closed relaxed reachable sets as structural floors, studies convergence rates under different time dependencies, and examines execution semantics (write-back vs error feedback).
AI.result: Establishes exact structural floors for depth-precision trade-offs, proves convergence rates (O(D⁻¹) under bounded variation, O(D⁻ϑ + D⁻¹) under Hölder dependence), shows execution semantics dramatically affect outcomes (Dρ_z penalty for write-back vs bounded carry for error feedback), and demonstrates depth requirements scale as Θ(L) for first-order comparators.
AI.conclusion: Depth can replace precision, but only relative to specific parameters: the declared library, computation horizon, execution semantics, and routing model. Theoretical bounds can determine feasibility before training, with verified primal/dual bounds and machine-checked proofs.

title: How LLM Task-Adaptation Reshapes Alignment: A Multi-dimensional Study of Behavioral and Representational Drift
summary: Post-training is a key mechanism for adapting large language models to downstream tasks. While prior work suggests that task adaptation can alter a model's pre-existing alignment, especially its safety behavior, its broader effects across alignment domains remain poorly understood. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of representative task-adaptation methods, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT), KL-regularized SFT, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) across 15 alignment aspects spanning six key domains: safety, factuality, stance stability, social harm, controllability, and instructability. Our results reveal that post-training does not reshape alignment uniformly. RLVR improves task performance while inducing comparatively small, but non-zero, metric-specific shifts, while SFT leads to substantially larger alignment drift across domains. KL regularization mitigates this effect: stronger reference-model anchoring reduces alignment drift from the baseline, although KL-SFT still falls short of RLVR in preserving alignment. Representation-level analysis further supports this pattern, with shifts in alignment-relevant representations tracking behavioral drift. Together, these results show that task adaptation is not merely a capability-improving step, but an alignment intervention in its own right, motivating multi-dimensional alignment evaluation as a standard component of post-training pipelines.

AI.tldr: Post-training adaptation (SFT, KL-SFT, RLVR) affects LLM alignment across multiple domains: RLVR preserves alignment best, SFT causes significant drift, KL-SFT mitigates but doesn't fully prevent alignment changes.
AI.motivation: While prior work shows task adaptation can affect safety behavior, its broader effects across alignment domains remain poorly understood. The paper aims to systematically evaluate how different post-training methods impact various alignment aspects.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of three representative task-adaptation methods: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), KL-regularized SFT, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Evaluated across 15 alignment aspects spanning six domains: safety, factuality, stance stability, social harm, controllability, and instructability. Includes representation-level analysis to track behavioral drift.
AI.result: Post-training does not reshape alignment uniformly. RLVR improves task performance while inducing small but non-zero metric-specific shifts. SFT leads to substantially larger alignment drift across domains. KL regularization mitigates drift but still falls short of RLVR in preserving alignment. Representation-level analysis shows shifts in alignment-relevant representations track behavioral drift.
AI.conclusion: Task adaptation is not merely capability improvement but an alignment intervention that requires multi-dimensional evaluation. Should be standard in post-training pipelines to understand alignment effects across domains.

title: A Statistical Difference between Single-Layer Learning and Hierarchical Learning in Wide Neural Networks
summary:
Hierarchical neural networks are widely used in artificial intelligence, yet their mathematical properties remain incompletely understood. In the infinite-width limit, two different theoretical frameworks have been proposed. One reduces deep learning to kernel regression with a fixed kernel by assuming that the parameters remain close to their initialization, whereas the other allows the parameters to move away from their initialization, requiring the kernel itself to be optimized.
  In this paper, we study a three-layer neural network with a finite but large number of hidden units. We show that training the input-to-hidden weights yields a smaller generalization error than keeping them fixed. Furthermore, the latter setting exhibits singularities in the parameter space, whereas the former does not. These findings indicate that singularities play an essential role even in wide neural networks.

AI.tldr: Training input-to-hidden weights in wide neural networks leads to better generalization and avoids singularities that occur when keeping weights fixed at initialization.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the theoretical gap in understanding hierarchical neural networks, specifically comparing two frameworks in the infinite-width limit: one where parameters stay near initialization (fixed kernel) vs. where parameters can move away (optimized kernel). The authors investigate whether singularities in parameter space matter in practice for wide networks.
AI.method: The authors study a three-layer neural network with a finite but large number of hidden units. They compare two scenarios: training input-to-hidden weights versus keeping them fixed at initialization. They analyze generalization error and examine singularities in the parameter space for both approaches.
AI.result: Training input-to-hidden weights yields smaller generalization error than keeping them fixed. The fixed-weight setting exhibits singularities in parameter space, while the trained-weight setting does not. This indicates that singularities play an essential role even in wide neural networks.
AI.conclusion: The findings challenge the common assumption that wide networks can be reduced to kernel regression with fixed kernels. Instead, they demonstrate that allowing parameters to move from initialization (leading to kernel optimization) provides better generalization and avoids problematic singularities, suggesting singularities are relevant even in wide networks.

title: DOSA: A Tree-Guided, Self-Regressive Framework for Long Document Structure Analysis
summary: In visually-rich documents, information is encoded not only in individual page objects such as tables, headers, and text blocks, but also in the structural relations among them, making document structure analysis fundamental to information retrieval and document understanding. However, accurately inferring such relations remains challenging in multi-page documents with long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts. To address this, we propose a tree-guided and self-regressive framework, termed DOcument Structure Analyzer (DOSA), for inferring relations among page objects and reconstructing document-level semantic trees. DOSA processes documents chunk-by-chunk, fusing visual, textual, and layout features for each page object and predicting hierarchical and ordering relations. The predicted relations are used to incrementally construct a semantic tree, which is then leveraged as structural context to guide inference on subsequent chunks. Experimental results on five benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of DOSA, with improvements of up to 4 F1 points and 19 TEDS points on DocHieNet, the most challenging multi-page hierarchy benchmark.

AI.tldr: DOSA is a tree-guided self-regressive framework for document structure analysis that processes documents chunk-by-chunk, fuses multimodal features to predict hierarchical relations, and incrementally constructs semantic trees to guide subsequent inference.
AI.motivation: In visually-rich documents, information is encoded not only in individual page objects (tables, headers, text blocks) but also in structural relations among them. However, accurately inferring these relations remains challenging in multi-page documents due to long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts.
AI.method: Proposes DOSA (Document Structure Analyzer), a tree-guided self-regressive framework that processes documents chunk-by-chunk, fuses visual, textual, and layout features for each page object, predicts hierarchical and ordering relations, and uses predicted relations to incrementally construct semantic trees which then guide inference on subsequent chunks.
AI.result: Experimental results on five benchmarks show effectiveness of DOSA, with improvements of up to 4 F1 points and 19 TEDS points on DocHieNet, the most challenging multi-page hierarchy benchmark.
AI.conclusion: DOSA effectively addresses the challenge of document structure analysis in multi-page documents by combining tree-guided inference with self-regressive processing, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks through its ability to handle long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts.

title: Transfer Learning Architectures for Scalable Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
summary: Self-driving laboratories increasingly rely on multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) to balance cheap, approximate evaluations against scarce, expensive ones, with a predictive surrogate at its core. Gaussian processes (GPs) are the default choice, but they scale poorly as data accumulate and assume a smooth landscape that molecular and materials search spaces routinely violate. Transfer learning offers an alternative suited to this regime: it learns a representation from abundant cheap data and adapts it to sparse expensive data. Despite its use in property prediction, transfer learning has not been tested as the engine of a closed-loop optimization. Here we benchmark eleven transfer-learning surrogates against four GP methods under an identical selection rule, fidelity budget, and model size, across nine tasks spanning synthetic functions to real chemistry and materials problems. GPs win on smooth, low-dimensional functions but perform worst on molecular and materials problems, where transfer-learning surrogates reach substantially better solutions using far less computation. Because acquisition policy is held fixed across surrogates, this advantage is attributable to the surrogate itself. Uncertainty-driven exploration is not reliably beneficial, and calibration does not predict optimization performance, so greedy exploitation of the transfer-learned mean is the more robust default. Transfer learning is therefore the surrogate of choice for molecular and materials MFBO.

AI.tldr: Transfer learning surrogates outperform Gaussian processes for multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization in molecular and materials discovery, achieving better solutions with less computation despite identical acquisition policies.
AI.motivation: Gaussian processes, while standard for multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization in self-driving laboratories, have limitations: poor scaling with accumulating data and unrealistic smoothness assumptions that molecular/materials search spaces violate. Transfer learning offers a promising alternative that hasn't been tested in closed-loop optimization contexts.
AI.method: Benchmarked eleven transfer-learning surrogates against four GP methods using identical selection rules, fidelity budgets, and model sizes across nine tasks spanning synthetic functions to real chemistry/materials problems. Held acquisition policy constant to isolate surrogate effects.
AI.result: GPs perform well on smooth, low-dimensional functions but worst on molecular/materials problems. Transfer-learning surrogates reach substantially better solutions with far less computation. Uncertainty-driven exploration is not reliably beneficial, and calibration doesn't predict optimization performance, making greedy exploitation of transfer-learned mean the most robust approach.
AI.conclusion: Transfer learning is the surrogate of choice for molecular and materials multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, offering significant advantages over Gaussian processes in this domain.

title: Blood Pressure Estimation from PPG: A Comparative Study of Direct and ECG-Mediated Deep Learning Pipelines
summary:
Continuous cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is essential for connected health systems and wearable devices, enabling early detection, longitudinal tracking, and personalized management of cardiovascular disease. Many prior approaches attempt to estimate BP indirectly by reconstructing electrocardiography (ECG) from photoplethysmography (PPG), assuming ECG provides a stronger physiological link to BP. However, ECG sensing is less accessible in wearable settings and may introduce unnecessary complexity.
  In this work, we first perform a large-scale physiological correlation analysis on the MIMIC-III waveform database, revealing that PPG exhibits substantially stronger coupling with arterial blood pressure (ABP) ($|r|=0.247$, $p<0.001$) than ECG does ($r=0.018$, $p=0.187$), challenging the assumption that ECG provides a superior intermediate representation. Motivated by this insight, we conduct a systematic comparison between direct PPG-to-BP prediction and ECG-mediated pipelines using multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models.
  Across 1.74M segments from 3,127 patients, direct PPG-to-BP prediction achieves British Hypertension Society Grade A performance ($\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{SBP}} = 4.82 mmHg$, $\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{DBP}} = 4.31 mmHg$), outperforming all ECG-mediated approaches, which achieve only Grade B accuracy.
  Our findings suggest that accurate continuous BP monitoring can be achieved directly from wearable PPG signals, enabling simpler, more efficient pipelines for real-world connected health systems.

AI.tldr: Direct PPG-to-BP prediction outperforms ECG-mediated approaches for continuous cuffless blood pressure monitoring, achieving Grade A performance with simpler wearable implementation.
AI.motivation: Continuous cuffless BP monitoring is crucial for connected health systems, but previous methods rely on ECG as an intermediate representation, which is less accessible in wearable settings and adds unnecessary complexity. The authors challenge the assumption that ECG provides a superior physiological link to BP compared to PPG.
AI.method: 1) Large-scale physiological correlation analysis on MIMIC-III waveform database comparing PPG and ECG coupling with arterial blood pressure. 2) Systematic comparison between direct PPG-to-BP prediction and ECG-mediated pipelines using multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models. 3) Evaluation across 1.74M segments from 3,127 patients using British Hypertension Society grading criteria.
AI.result: Direct PPG-to-BP prediction achieved British Hypertension Society Grade A performance with MAE_SBP = 4.82 mmHg and MAE_DBP = 4.31 mmHg, outperforming all ECG-mediated approaches which only achieved Grade B accuracy. Physiological analysis showed PPG has substantially stronger coupling with ABP (|r|=0.247) than ECG does (r=0.018).
AI.conclusion: Accurate continuous BP monitoring can be achieved directly from wearable PPG signals, enabling simpler and more efficient pipelines for real-world connected health systems. This challenges conventional wisdom that ECG provides a superior intermediate representation for BP estimation.

title: Imprompt: A Language Framework for Prompt Programming
summary: With the unprecedented success of Language Models (LMs), the science of Prompt Engineering has evolved the powerful idea of Prompt Programming, where prompts are treated as a programmable control surface for describing complex tasks and leveraging LM capabilities.
