However, existing prompt programming frameworks suffer from various complexities and inelegances, which make them hard to utilize in practice for effectively describing tasks. We propose Imprompt, a new language framework for the study and practice of prompt programming. We undertake a foundational investigation of prompt programming, and contend that prompt programs must contain only the task descriptions and must be decoupled from lower-level 'execution' details. We further develop this position by illustrating structured prompting as a combination of prompt programming and prompt program 'compilation'. We exemplify this view by formally defining two compilers for Imprompt programs. We then explore the idea of typing for prompt programs and draw a correspondence between type checking and constrained decoding. Finally, we implement our compilers and type checkers and evaluate them on a variety of case studies. We believe our work contributes programming-language foundations toward the emerging area of prompt programming.

AI.tldr: Imprompt is a new language framework for prompt programming that separates task descriptions from execution details and introduces structured prompting with compilers and type checking for improved practicality.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt programming frameworks suffer from complexities and inelegances that make them hard to use effectively in practice for describing tasks, despite the success of Language Models and the evolution of Prompt Engineering.
AI.method: Proposes Imprompt framework based on the principle that prompt programs should contain only task descriptions and be decoupled from execution details. Introduces structured prompting as prompt programming combined with compilation, formally defines two compilers for Imprompt programs, explores typing for prompt programs with correspondence between type checking and constrained decoding, and implements compilers and type checkers.
AI.result: Developed the Imprompt framework with formal compilers and type checking capabilities, and evaluated them on various case studies to demonstrate practical application.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes programming-language foundations toward the emerging area of prompt programming by providing a structured framework that separates concerns and introduces compilation and type checking to make prompt programming more practical and elegant.

title: Harmonized Interpretable ECG Waveform Features for Robust Cross-Dataset Clinical Prediction
comment: Full version of the work presented as a 2-page paper at the 39th IEEE International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS 2026)
summary: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are widely used for cardiovascular risk prediction, yet models often fail to transfer across hospitals because of protocol, population, and measurement differences. We benchmark cross-dataset generalization on three tasks - heart failure classification, 30-day all-cause mortality, and 30-day mortality among sinus-rhythm ECGs - using two large cohorts (MIMIC-IV and the Alberta Cohort). To reduce vendor-specific measurement mismatch, we build a harmonized, interpretable feature representation computed directly from raw waveforms: FeatureDB morphology/heart-rate-variability summaries plus compact time-frequency descriptors (autoregressive and wavelet features). We train XGBoost models on this unified feature space and evaluate with patient-disjoint internal and bidirectional external testing. We pre-specify two hypotheses: (H1) external AUROC retains at least 90% of source-site internal AUROC under transfer, and (H2) internal AUROC of the harmonized feature set stays within 10% of dataset-native machine-measurement models. Across tasks, internal AUROC is 0.79-0.82 and cross-dataset AUROC is 0.74-0.78, with larger and direction-dependent AUPRC shifts under transfer. As an exploratory benchmark, an end-to-end ConvNeXt model trained directly on raw ECG waveforms with age and sex achieves higher internal AUROC, while the harmonized representation remains competitive in relative cross-dataset transfer stability. These findings show that a consistent waveform-derived feature interface preserves performance, supports realistic external validation, and provides a transparent alternative for cross-site clinical prediction.

AI.tldr: A harmonized ECG feature representation enables cross-hospital cardiovascular prediction with competitive performance and better generalization than dataset-specific models.
AI.motivation: ECG models often fail to transfer across hospitals due to protocol, population, and measurement differences, creating a need for robust cross-dataset generalization in cardiovascular risk prediction.
AI.method: Developed a harmonized feature representation from raw ECG waveforms using FeatureDB morphology/HRV summaries plus time-frequency descriptors (autoregressive and wavelet features), then trained XGBoost models and evaluated with patient-disjoint internal and bidirectional external testing on MIMIC-IV and Alberta Cohort datasets.
AI.result: Internal AUROC: 0.79-0.82; Cross-dataset AUROC: 0.74-0.78; H1 hypothesis met (external AUROC retained ≥90% of internal); H2 hypothesis met (harmonized features within 10% of dataset-native models). End-to-end ConvNeXt achieved higher internal AUROC, but harmonized representation showed competitive transfer stability.
AI.conclusion: A consistent waveform-derived feature interface preserves performance, supports realistic external validation, and provides a transparent alternative for cross-site clinical prediction, bridging the gap between interpretable features and deep learning performance.

title: Co-Harness: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Model Weights for LLM Agents
summary: Post-training agents for automated AI research requires optimizing not only model parameters, but also the runtime harness that shapes how research trajectories are generated, evaluated, and learned from. Existing pipelines typically train models under a fixed harness, including prompts, tools, skills, middleware, and memory, while leaving the data-generating process outside the optimization objective. This creates a mismatch between model updates and the static scaffolding that determines trajectory quality. We introduce Co-Harness, a framework that jointly optimizes the agent harness and model parameters during post-training. Co-Harness alternates between harness optimization and model optimization. An LLM-based HarnessCritic analyzes failed trajectories, identifies harness-level failure modes, and proposes validated local updates. The model is then fine-tuned on high-quality trajectories generated by the improved harness, distilling effective scaffolding into model parameters. A 200+ hour autonomous case study further shows that Co-Harness can recover from system crashes, improve inference efficiency, and discover ensemble strategies without human intervention. These results suggest that joint harness and model optimization is an effective way to improve agents beyond fixed-harness post-training.

AI.tldr: Co-Harness: A framework that jointly optimizes both AI agent models AND their runtime harness (prompts, tools, memory systems) during post-training, enabling recovery from failures, efficiency improvements, and autonomous strategy discovery.
AI.motivation: Current AI research agents are trained with fixed runtime harnesses while optimizing only model parameters, creating a mismatch between model updates and the static scaffolding that determines research trajectory quality.
AI.method: Co-Harness alternates between harness optimization and model optimization using an LLM-based HarnessCritic that analyzes failed trajectories, identifies harness-level failure modes, proposes validated updates, then fine-tunes models on improved trajectories.
AI.result: In a 200+ hour autonomous case study, Co-Harness demonstrated recovery from system crashes, improved inference efficiency, and discovered ensemble strategies without human intervention.
AI.conclusion: Joint harness and model optimization is more effective than fixed-harness post-training for improving AI research agents, enabling autonomous improvement of both the agent and its operational environment.

title: Short-Term Pain for Long-Term Gain: Adaptive Experiment with Post-Commitment Reward Shift
comment: A one-page abstract appeared in ACM EC'26
summary:
Decision-makers in learning environments face a dilemma when their short-term optimal actions may not favor their long-term benefits the most. To understand the fundamental tradeoff behind the dilemma, we study adaptive experimentation with post-commitment reward shifts. During an experiment phase, the decision-maker may adaptively test multiple options; during a subsequent commitment phase, the decision-maker must commit to a single option, whose reward may differ from its pre-commitment reward. We propose the Reserved Arm Eliminations for Commitment (RAEC) algorithm, which reserves a predetermined portion of the experiment phase to identify the best post-shift option while using the remaining rounds to minimize short-run regret. We establish regret upper bounds for RAEC across all parameter regimes and matching minimax lower bounds, providing a tight characterization of the cost of balancing short-term performance and long-term commitment.
  We also study two extensions. With prior structural knowledge linking pre- and post-shift rewards, we show that correctly identifying the ranking-changing component of the shift is more important than estimating its absolute magnitude. For settings with concave commitment rewards and portfolio choice, we develop the Reserved Online Stochastic Convex Optimization for Commitment (ROSCOC) algorithm, which directly converts its reserved exploration history into a commitment portfolio and achieves tight regret bound. Finally, we also conduct numerical experiments which confirm that our proposed algorithms achieve the desired regret predicted by our theory, and also outperform other baseline algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces algorithms for adaptive experimentation with post-commitment reward shifts, balancing short-term regret minimization with long-term commitment optimization.
AI.motivation: Decision-makers face a dilemma where short-term optimal actions may not align with long-term benefits, particularly when rewards can shift after commitment phases.
AI.method: Proposes RAEC algorithm that reserves a portion of experiment phase to identify best post-shift option while minimizing short-run regret. Also develops ROSCOC algorithm for concave commitment rewards and portfolio choice settings.
AI.result: Establishes tight regret upper bounds for RAEC across all parameter regimes with matching minimax lower bounds. Numerical experiments confirm algorithms achieve predicted regret and outperform baselines.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a fundamental understanding of the tradeoff between short-term performance and long-term commitment, with tight theoretical guarantees and practical algorithms for various settings including portfolio choice.

title: Beyond Sequential Interaction: Benchmarking Parallel Execution and Coordination for GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are systems powered by large multimodal models (LMMs). They perceive screen state and execute user instructions through GUI actions such as clicking, typing, and scrolling on desktops and mobile devices. However, current agents scale poorly to long-horizon tasks: actions incur costly LMM inferences, and performance degrades as context grows. Humans divide such workloads among collaborators who complete sub-tasks in parallel. Yet parallel coordination among GUI agents has received little attention. To close this gap, we introduce ParaGUIBench, to our knowledge, the first benchmark dedicated to parallel execution and coordination of multiple GUI agents on separate desktop instances. It consists of three components: a multi-device Docker infrastructure with a shared file system; a dataset of 233 tasks spanning six task categories; and an evaluation system with efficiency metrics, including step reduction ratio and token cost. We further introduce ParaGUI, a planner-worker agent that decomposes GUI tasks and dispatches sub-tasks to concurrent workers on separate desktop instances. On ParaGUIBench, ParaGUI reaches a 46.4% success rate, outperforming the strongest serial baseline (Claude Sonnet 4.6) by 12.9 points while using roughly half the steps and less than half the tokens. These results show that parallel execution can improve both success rate and efficiency on decomposable, long-horizon GUI tasks, pointing to a direction worth further study.

AI.tldr: ParaGUIBench is the first benchmark for parallel multi-GUI agents with shared file system, dataset of 233 tasks, and evaluation metrics. ParaGUI agent achieves 46.4% success rate using parallel execution, outperforming serial baselines with fewer steps and tokens.
AI.motivation: Current GUI agents scale poorly to long-horizon tasks due to expensive LMM inferences and performance degradation with growing context. Parallel coordination among GUI agents (inspired by human collaboration) has been largely overlooked, creating a research gap.
AI.method: Introduces ParaGUIBench benchmark with: 1) multi-device Docker infrastructure with shared file system, 2) dataset of 233 tasks across six categories, 3) evaluation system with efficiency metrics. Also introduces ParaGUI, a planner-worker agent that decomposes tasks and dispatches sub-tasks to concurrent workers on separate desktop instances.
AI.result: ParaGUI achieves 46.4% success rate on ParaGUIBench, outperforming the strongest serial baseline (Claude Sonnet 4.6) by 12.9 percentage points while using roughly half the steps and less than half the tokens.
AI.conclusion: Parallel execution can significantly improve both success rate and efficiency for decomposable, long-horizon GUI tasks. This approach represents a promising direction for future GUI agent research and development.

title: PerturbPFN: Probing the Limits of Synthetic Priors in Drug Perturbation Modelling
comment: 19 pages. Accepted at the 2nd ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data (FMSD 2026), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Predicting cellular responses to unseen chemical perturbations is challenging due to unknown targets and mechanisms, high-dimensional expression responses, and limited experimental coverage of the large small-molecule design space. We propose PerturbPFN, a PFN-style amortized model for unknown-target perturbation prediction under a hierarchical synthetic structural prior. Instead of directly regressing high-dimensional expression responses, PerturbPFN infers a latent system graph, sparse atomic intervention targets, and intervention strengths, then propagates their effects through an SCM decoder. The model is trained entirely on prior-predictive synthetic episodes generated from biologically motivated graph and expression simulators, enabling structured in-context learning without test-time gradient updates. We evaluate PerturbPFN on both real single-cell perturbation data and synthetic benchmarks, covering effect prediction, target identification, and regulatory structure discovery. Our results show that PerturbPFN offers a complementary trade-off to specialized baselines, achieving competitive perturbation prediction with low inference cost while exposing interpretable intermediate estimates of targets, strengths, and system structure.

AI.tldr: PerturbPFN is a PFN-style amortized model that predicts cellular responses to unseen chemical perturbations by inferring latent system graphs and intervention targets from synthetic data, enabling efficient prediction without test-time gradients.
AI.motivation: Predicting cellular responses to unseen chemical perturbations is challenging due to unknown targets/mechanisms, high-dimensional expression responses, and limited experimental coverage of the large small-molecule design space.
AI.method: PerturbPFN infers a latent system graph, sparse atomic intervention targets, and intervention strengths, then propagates their effects through an SCM (Structural Causal Model) decoder. The model is trained entirely on prior-predictive synthetic episodes from biologically motivated graph and expression simulators, enabling structured in-context learning without test-time gradient updates.
AI.result: The model was evaluated on real single-cell perturbation data and synthetic benchmarks for effect prediction, target identification, and regulatory structure discovery. It achieves competitive perturbation prediction with low inference cost while providing interpretable intermediate estimates of targets, strengths, and system structure.
AI.conclusion: PerturbPFN offers a complementary trade-off to specialized baselines, demonstrating that amortized models trained on synthetic data can effectively predict cellular responses to unseen perturbations with interpretable intermediate representations.

title: LazyMem: Retrieve Broadly, Construct Selectively for Efficient Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long-term memory lets LLM agents reuse past interactions, but raw dialogue histories are verbose and information-sparse. Retrieving broadly improves evidence coverage yet overwhelms downstream reasoning with noise; compressing at write time reduces noise but irreversibly discards details the future query may need. We introduce LazyMem, which sidesteps this dilemma by deferring all memory construction to query time. A lightweight 4B model processes the retrieved candidate pool in overlapping parallel windows, selectively retaining and compressing only query-relevant content. The model is trained through supervised fine-tuning followed by group-based reinforcement learning with a format-gated composite reward that combines a rule-based action signal measuring selection accuracy with an LLM-judged quality signal measuring source faithfulness and query utility. On the LongMemEval benchmark, LazyMem-4B achieves an LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 with only 213 memory tokens, 68.7$\times$ fewer than retrieval-only, and generalizes to LoCoMo (0.68) without target-domain training, while reducing mean latency over the prior query-time baseline. The 32B variant reaches 0.93, surpassing oracle-context references on aggregation-heavy question types. The code associated with this work is publicly available at https://github.com/allacnobug/LazyMem.

AI.tldr: LazyMem is a query-time memory processing system for LLM agents that uses a lightweight 4B model to selectively compress retrieved content, achieving high accuracy with dramatically fewer tokens while reducing latency.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent memory approaches face a dilemma: raw dialogue histories are verbose and information-sparse, broad retrieval improves evidence coverage but introduces noise, and compression at write time irreversibly discards details that future queries may need.
AI.method: LazyMem defers all memory construction to query time, using a lightweight 4B model to process retrieved candidate pools in overlapping parallel windows, selectively retaining and compressing only query-relevant content. The model is trained through supervised fine-tuning followed by group-based reinforcement learning with a format-gated composite reward combining rule-based action signals (selection accuracy) with LLM-judged quality signals (source faithfulness and query utility).
AI.result: On the LongMemEval benchmark, LazyMem-4B achieves LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 with only 213 memory tokens (68.7× fewer than retrieval-only), generalizes to LoCoMo (0.68) without target-domain training, reduces mean latency over prior query-time baselines, and the 32B variant reaches 0.93 accuracy, surpassing oracle-context references on aggregation-heavy questions.
AI.conclusion: Deferring memory construction to query time with selective compression via a lightweight trained model effectively resolves the retrieval-compression tradeoff, enabling efficient and accurate long-term memory for LLM agents while maintaining source faithfulness and query utility.

title: Local Regularization Does Not Characterize Multiclass PAC Learnability
summary: Local regularization assigns each hypothesis a test-point-dependent score and predicts with a minimum-score hypothesis consistent with the sample. Asilis et al. asked whether this principle characterizes multiclass PAC learnability. We give a negative answer. There is a countable class of Daniely--Shalev-Shwartz dimension at most two with realizable PAC sample complexity \[ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{1}δ\right), \] that no local regularizer learns. Hypotheses are edges of complete graphs and instances are tournaments. At a test tournament, the scores fix an edge ranking while the training sample independently removes competitors. Cyclic triangles force enough inversions that surviving competitors produce constant population error at arbitrarily large sample sizes.

AI.tldr: Local regularization doesn't characterize multiclass PAC learnability - there exists a countable class with dimension ≤2 and good sample complexity that no local regularizer can learn.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses an open question by Asilis et al. about whether local regularization characterizes multiclass PAC learnability. Local regularization assigns test-point-dependent scores to hypotheses and predicts with minimum-score consistent hypotheses.
AI.method: Constructs a counterexample using tournament graphs: hypotheses are edges of complete graphs, instances are tournaments. Uses cyclic triangles to force ranking inversions in local regularization scores, causing constant population error even with arbitrarily large training samples.
AI.result: Negative answer: there exists a countable class with Daniely-Shalev-Shwartz dimension at most 2 and realizable PAC sample complexity O(1/ε log 1/δ) that no local regularizer can learn. Shows local regularization is insufficient for characterizing multiclass PAC learnability.
AI.conclusion: Local regularization does not characterize multiclass PAC learnability, providing a separation between learnability principles in the multiclass setting.

title: HiLLTS: Zero-Shot Hierarchical LLM-Guided Traffic Signal Control for Sustainable Transportation
summary: Urban traffic congestion significantly increases fuel consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and commuter delays, resulting in substantial economic losses and environmental harm in modern cities. Traditional traffic signal control strategies such as fixed-time scheduling, actuated control, and reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods, offer different degrees of adaptability; however, RL-based methods can require extensive retraining, careful reward design, and substantial simulation data when transferred across networks or demand regimes. To address these challenges, we propose HiLLTS, an LLM-guided traffic signal control framework that employs a hierarchical three-layer architecture consisting of a central coordination agent, a district layer and multiple cluster-level intersection agents. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in both congestion and environmental performance. Compared with the strongest non-LLM baseline in each scenario, HiLLTS reduces average waiting time by 36.73% under the low-congestion scenario and 14.71% under the high-congestion scenario, while reducing average CO2 emissions by 7.87% and 8.57%, respectively. Larger gains are observed against weaker baselines: under low congestion, HiLLTS achieves reductions of up to 18.00% in emissions and 62.07% in waiting time relative to Fixed-Time control; under high congestion, reductions of up to 28.89% in emissions and 40.36% in waiting time are observed relative to Max Pressure. The ablation study further validates the contribution of LLM-guided coordination over rule-based control

AI.tldr: HiLLTS is an LLM-guided hierarchical traffic signal control framework that reduces congestion and emissions better than traditional methods across different traffic scenarios.
AI.motivation: Urban traffic congestion causes significant fuel waste, emissions, and economic losses. Traditional methods (fixed-time, actuated control, RL-based approaches) have limitations: RL methods need extensive retraining, careful reward design, and lots of simulation data when transferring across different traffic networks or demand conditions.
AI.method: Proposes HiLLTS (LLM-guided traffic signal control) with a hierarchical three-layer architecture: 1) central coordination agent, 2) district layer, and 3) multiple cluster-level intersection agents. Uses LLM guidance instead of rule-based coordination.
AI.result: HiLLTS consistently outperforms non-LLM baselines. Compared to strongest non-LLM baselines: reduces average waiting time by 36.73% (low congestion) and 14.71% (high congestion); reduces CO2 emissions by 7.87% and 8.57% respectively. Larger gains against weaker baselines: up to 62.07% waiting time reduction vs Fixed-Time (low congestion) and up to 40.36% vs Max Pressure (high congestion).
AI.conclusion: LLM-guided hierarchical coordination effectively addresses limitations of traditional traffic control methods, achieving significant improvements in both congestion reduction and environmental performance across varying traffic conditions.

title: Generalization bounds and sample complexity for remaining useful life prediction from complete degradation trajectories
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for publication in Measurement Science and Technology. The final Version of Record is available at https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6501/ae7109/meta
summary: Data-driven remaining useful life (RUL) prediction requires complete degradation trajectories for training, yet such run-to-failure data are scarce and expensive. Practitioners currently lack principled guidance on how many failure examples suffice for a given model and accuracy target. This paper develops a sample complexity framework for RUL prediction comprising seven main results organised around three themes. First, we establish fundamental learning rates: a distribution-free generalization bound shows that the uniform deviation of the mean squared error decreases as $O(B^{2}\sqrt{p/n})$, where $p$ is the model complexity and $n$ the number of trajectories, and a minimax lower bound proves that the $Θ(p/n)$ rate is unimprovable.} \rev{Second, we quantify how domain knowledge accelerates learning: incorporating degradation physics reduces data requirements by up to two orders of magnitude for deep networks, a Bernstein-type analysis achieves the minimax-optimal $O(p/n)$ rate under high signal-to-noise conditions, and closed-form penalties reveal when an incorrectly assumed physics model hurts rather than helps. Third, we characterise the impact of data quality: fleet variability induces an irreducible bias$-$variance tradeoff, while right-censored observations suffer an efficiency loss that depends critically on the degradation class.} Closed-form expressions are provided for exponential, power-law, and stretched-exponential degradation. \rev{Cross-domain validation against published turbofan, battery, and bearing benchmarks confirms the theoretical predictions within a factor of 2$-$3 on average. The results yield practical guidelines for planning data collection, selecting model complexity, and evaluating physics model assumptions in prognostics applications.

AI.tldr: Developed sample complexity framework for RUL prediction, showing data requirements depend on model complexity, physics knowledge, and degradation type, with practical guidelines for data collection.
AI.motivation: RUL prediction needs complete degradation trajectories, but run-to-failure data are scarce and expensive. Practitioners lack guidance on how much data is needed for given models and accuracy targets.
AI.method: Developed theoretical framework with generalization bounds, minimax analysis, Bernstein-type analysis, and closed-form expressions. Cross-domain validation on turbofan, battery, and bearing benchmarks.
AI.result: Established fundamental learning rates (Θ(p/n)), showed physics knowledge reduces data needs by 2 orders of magnitude for deep networks, quantified impact of fleet variability and censored data. Validation confirmed predictions within factor 2-3.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical guidelines for data collection planning, model complexity selection, and evaluating physics model assumptions in prognostics applications.

title: Risk Governance for Generative AI Mental Health Support: A Multi-Turn Safety Architecture
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for emotional support despite lacking mechanisms to safely govern evolving mental health risk. Existing safety approaches primarily detect risk but rarely shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds. We developed a model-agnostic safety governance architecture that combines contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation for multi-turn mental health interactions. Synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives were used to evaluate the architecture's performance, tested with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B, achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95\%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95\%CI: 0.88;0.95)) and increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6--59.2pp while preserving rapport and connection. Performance remained stable across conversation length and generalized across both proprietary and open-source models. These findings demonstrate that clinically-grounded safety governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a scalable framework for safer deployment across models.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a model-agnostic safety governance architecture for LLMs in mental health contexts, combining risk detection, verification, and protocol-guided responses to improve how models manage evolving mental health risks.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for emotional support but lack mechanisms to safely govern evolving mental health risks. Existing safety approaches primarily focus on risk detection rather than shaping how models respond as conversational risk unfolds, creating a gap in comprehensive safety management for mental health interactions.
AI.method: Developed a model-agnostic safety governance architecture with three components: contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation. Evaluated using synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives, tested with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B models.
AI.result: Achieved high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85, sensitivity: 0.92) and increased clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6-59.2 percentage points while preserving rapport and connection. Performance remained stable across conversation length and generalized across both proprietary and open-source models.
AI.conclusion: Clinically-grounded safety governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a scalable framework for safer deployment across different model architectures in mental health applications.

title: Extending Fourier Neural Operators for Modeling Parameterized and Coupled PDEs
summary: Parameterized and coupled partial differential equations (PDEs) are central to modeling phenomena in science and engineering, yet neural operator methods that address both aspects remain limited. We extend Fourier neural operators (FNOs) with minimal architectural modifications along two directions. For parameterized dynamics, we propose a hypernetwork-based modulation that conditions the operator on physical parameters. For coupled systems, we conduct a systematic exploration of architectural choices, examining how operator components can be adapted to balance shared structure with cross-variable interactions while retaining the efficiency of standard FNOs. Evaluations on benchmark PDEs, including the one-dimensional capacitively coupled plasma equations and the Gray-Scott system, show that our methods achieve up to 55-72% lower errors than strong baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of principled modulation and systematic design exploration.

AI.tldr: Extended Fourier neural operators (FNOs) with hypernetwork-based modulation for parameterized PDEs and systematic architectural exploration for coupled PDEs, achieving significantly lower errors than baselines.
AI.motivation: Parameterized and coupled PDEs are central to science and engineering applications, but existing neural operator methods that can handle both aspects simultaneously are limited. There's a need for methods that can effectively model both parameterized dynamics and coupled systems while maintaining efficiency.
AI.method: Two key extensions to Fourier neural operators: 1) Hypernetwork-based modulation that conditions the operator on physical parameters for parameterized dynamics, and 2) Systematic exploration of architectural choices for coupled systems, examining how to adapt operator components to balance shared structure with cross-variable interactions while retaining standard FNO efficiency.
AI.result: Evaluations on benchmark PDEs including 1D capacitively coupled plasma equations and Gray-Scott system show 55-72% lower errors than strong baselines, demonstrating effectiveness of the principled modulation and systematic design exploration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed extensions to FNOs with minimal architectural modifications effectively address both parameterized and coupled PDEs, offering significant performance improvements over existing methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Bayesian Repetition Penalty: A Principled Adjacent-Conditional Framework for Reversing Attention Collapse in Autoregressive Language Models
summary: Attention collapse in autoregressive language models -- manifested as repetitive token loops where the model becomes trapped in self-reinforcing attractors -- is a persistent pathology that existing decoding-time heuristics fail to address at its root cause. We present a principled framework that penalises or compensates anomalous confidence arising from collapsed generation patterns, by comparing a token's observed frequency against its corpus prior through an adjacent-conditional probability construction. The resulting self-normalising penalty ratio $R=f(m,n,p)/f(np,n,p)$ requires no ad hoc standardisation and admits a closed-form logit offset with zero approximation error. The correction is isolated from the loss gradient and accumulated into a frozen output-layer bias via exponential moving average, enabling deployment as a repair mechanism for models that have already collapsed without requiring intrusive modifications to standard training pipelines. Experimental validation on a 1.5B-parameter model demonstrates that the frozen-bias mechanism can rescue a model already trapped in a collapsed attractor, reducing 2-gram repetition from 0.073 to near 0 while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: A novel decoding-time method to fix attention collapse in autoregressive language models by applying self-normalizing penalty ratios based on token frequency analysis, implemented as a frozen output-layer bias that can rescue already collapsed models.
AI.motivation: Existing decoding-time heuristics fail to address attention collapse at its root cause. Attention collapse manifests as repetitive token loops where models become trapped in self-reinforcing attractors, a persistent pathology in autoregressive language models.
AI.method: Proposes a principled framework that penalizes anomalous confidence from collapsed generation patterns by comparing token frequency against corpus prior using adjacent-conditional probability. Uses self-normalizing penalty ratio R=f(m,n,p)/f(np,n,p) with closed-form logit offset. Correction is isolated from loss gradient and accumulated into frozen output-layer bias via exponential moving average.
AI.result: Experimental validation on 1.5B-parameter model shows frozen-bias mechanism can rescue models already trapped in collapsed attractors, reducing 2-gram repetition from 0.073 to near 0 while preserving generation quality.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a practical solution to attention collapse without requiring modifications to standard training pipelines, offering a repair mechanism for already collapsed models that addresses the root cause rather than superficial symptoms.

title: Learning to Optimize: Joint Routing and Flow Allocation on Sparse Non-Euclidean Networks
summary: We study an integrated pickup-and-delivery problem on sparse, non-Euclidean networks that jointly optimizes cyclic routing, cargo flow allocation, and cross-cycle service. The tight coupling of these operational constraints creates a complex discrete-continuous decision space with highly restricted feasible regions. To overcome these computational challenges, we propose Double-Channel Graph Attention (DCGA), an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework. DCGA isolates network reachability and demand-service logic into separate graph channels and constructs valid routes using a simulator-coupled, constraint-informed decoder. Experiments on LinerLib benchmarks demonstrate that DCGA achieves seconds-level inference and delivers state-of-the-art solution quality on instances beyond a specific scale, with its advantage over existing baselines widening significantly as problem size increases. Supported by extensive stability and ablation analyses, our results demonstrate that this structure-aware learning approach provides an effective, low-latency engine for realistic routing-and-flow optimization.

AI.tldr: DCGA (Double-Channel Graph Attention) is a reinforcement learning framework for integrated pickup-and-delivery problems that achieves state-of-the-art solution quality on large-scale sparse networks with seconds-level inference time.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the computational challenges of integrated pickup-and-delivery problems on sparse, non-Euclidean networks where cyclic routing, cargo flow allocation, and cross-cycle service constraints are tightly coupled, creating complex discrete-continuous decision spaces with highly restricted feasible regions.
AI.method: Proposes Double-Channel Graph Attention (DCGA), an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that isolates network reachability and demand-service logic into separate graph channels and constructs valid routes using a simulator-coupled, constraint-informed decoder.
AI.result: DCGA achieves seconds-level inference and delivers state-of-the-art solution quality on LinerLib benchmarks, with advantages over existing baselines widening significantly as problem size increases beyond a specific scale. Performance is supported by extensive stability and ablation analyses.
AI.conclusion: The structure-aware learning approach of DCGA provides an effective, low-latency engine for realistic routing-and-flow optimization problems, demonstrating the value of separating network reachability from demand-service logic in solving complex integrated logistics problems.

title: PANOPTICON: A PII-Based Assemblage of Naturalistic Output Tokens for Investigating Privacy Leakage Within LLM Context Window
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE CARS 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of generalizing human language for the completion of never-before-seen tasks, leading to widespread deployment. While this automation provides clear utility, completing these tasks often requires the insertion of Personally Identifiable Information (PII), strings of information that uniquely identify some individual, raising privacy concerns. However, ethics has prevented the curation of a public, authentic dataset of PII. Without an appropriate dataset, it is difficult to quantify privacy risks. Thus, we introduce the PANOPTICON pipeline and dataset. The dataset, generated by Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model, contains 67, 718 prompts, intended for the models context window, containing PII spans derived from 9,674 publicly available synthetic user profiles. We measure lexical diversity and S-BERT diversity of the created dataset to evaluate realism. Finally, we present a case study showcasing the utility of PANOPTICON data for understanding Prompt Inversion Attacks (PIAs). PANOPTICON thus emerges as the first benchmark dataset for studying PIAs over private corpora, providing a foundation for future LLM privacy research.

AI.tldr: PANOPTICON is a pipeline and dataset containing synthetic PII (Personally Identifiable Information) for studying privacy risks in LLMs, particularly Prompt Inversion Attacks.
AI.motivation: LLMs require PII insertion for many tasks, raising privacy concerns, but ethical constraints prevent creation of real PII datasets, making it difficult to quantify privacy risks.
AI.method: Created PANOPTICON pipeline generating synthetic PII dataset using Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model with 67,718 prompts containing PII from 9,674 synthetic user profiles; evaluated realism through lexical and S-BERT diversity metrics.
AI.result: Generated benchmark dataset for studying PIAs, with demonstrated utility through a case study on Prompt Inversion Attacks; first such dataset for PIA research over private corpora.
AI.conclusion: PANOPTICON establishes a foundation for LLM privacy research by providing the first benchmark dataset for studying Prompt Inversion Attacks, enabling future privacy risk quantification without using real PII.

title: Sparse Gaussian-Mixture-Model Q-Functions via Hadamard Overparametrization for Online Reinforcement Learning
comment: This work has been submitted to the Elsevier for possible publication
summary: This paper develops an online, off-policy policy-iteration framework for reinforcement learning (RL), based on sparse Gaussian-mixture-model Q-functions (S-GMM-QFs). The framework reconciles streaming, non-stationary data with the Riemannian structure of the parameter space while handling distributional mismatch through experience replay. S-GMM-QFs are introduced via Hadamard overparametrization, enabling interpretable sparsification through smooth regularization that facilitates Riemannian-based optimization. Overparametrization allows the framework to adaptively identify meaningful components from a large initial pool, yielding sparse models where interpretability emerges naturally from geometry: each component's parameters (means and covariances) explicitly encode its geometric role in the ambient state-action space. These geometric roles are learned through online gradient descent on a smooth objective over a (Cartesian-product) Riemannian manifold. Numerical tests demonstrate that S-GMM-QFs match or exceed deep RL methods while using substantially fewer parameters and achieving faster improvement per observed transition. Notably, parameter efficiency and interpretability combine to maintain strong generalization in low-parameter regimes where sparsified deep RL approaches degrade.

AI.tldr: Online off-policy RL framework using sparse Gaussian-mixture-model Q-functions with Hadamard overparametrization for interpretable sparsification and Riemannian optimization
AI.motivation: Reconcile streaming, non-stationary data with Riemannian structure of parameter space while handling distributional mismatch through experience replay; need interpretable and parameter-efficient RL methods that maintain generalization in low-parameter regimes
AI.method: Sparse Gaussian-mixture-model Q-functions (S-GMM-QFs) introduced via Hadamard overparametrization with smooth regularization; online gradient descent on Cartesian-product Riemannian manifold; adaptive component identification from large initial pool
AI.result: S-GMM-QFs match or exceed deep RL methods while using substantially fewer parameters and achieving faster improvement per observed transition; maintain strong generalization in low-parameter regimes where sparsified deep RL approaches degrade
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully combines parameter efficiency and interpretability through geometric modeling, with interpretability emerging naturally from Riemannian geometry and sparsification enabling better generalization in resource-constrained settings

title: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning
summary: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion.

AI.tldr: TTCov is a novel test-time data curation method that uses test-side information to select training data that better matches deployment distributions, particularly for autonomous driving, without requiring inference-time model updates.
AI.motivation: Standard data curation methods focus on training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing for deployment match. Deployed AI systems need to select training data from broad candidate pools to match deployment test distributions, but current methods don't use test-side information effectively before training.
AI.method: TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution components. It builds a task Atlas using LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs from unlabeled deployment samples. It then creates a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) by instantiating matched deployment APs with their frequencies, which operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. Finally, it selects a budgeted training set whose deployment AP distribution approximates this target.
AI.result: Applied to autonomous driving, TTCov selects data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than baseline data-curation methods. It also shows seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion while keeping adaptation off the inference path.
AI.conclusion: TTCov provides an effective test-time data curation approach that uses test-side information before training to improve deployment match, demonstrating significant advantages over traditional data curation methods in autonomous driving applications while maintaining inference efficiency.

title: A Multi-stage Constrained Optimization Framework for Data-driven Problems
summary: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) transform high-dimensional, often noisy data into a compact latent representation, making downstream optimization more tractable. Three challenges persist in VAE-based constrained optimization: (i) sampling effectively within the latent space, (ii) identifying the active decision variables that actually influence the objective and constraints, and (iii) enforcing constraints without destabilizing training. We propose a Multi-stage Constrained Optimization Framework (MCOF). First, an entropy-constrained VAE (EC-VAE) coupled with a feature selector embeds objective and constraint information into a designated subset of latent variables, so that optimization proceeds over a low-dimensional subspace while the remaining coordinates supply solution diversity. Second, a Uniform Transformation (UT) module applies a per-dimension probability integral transform, replacing the irregular aggregate posterior with a uniform distribution over a bounded box and mitigating posterior collapse and Gaussian mixture bias. Third, a constraint-priority filter method (CPFM) solves the resulting surrogate problem by alternating violation-reduction and objective-reduction steps under a filter acceptance test, returning solutions that are feasible for the learned surrogate to a specified tolerance without requiring multiplier estimation. Finally, unselected latent coordinates are resampled to generate diverse decodings of a single optimized solution. We validate MCOF on a synthetic problem, where we ablate each stage and recover the analytic optimum, and on a ZINC250k drug design task, where the generated molecules satisfy the imposed constraints and are entirely novel relative to the training set.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage VAE framework (MCOF) addresses sampling, variable selection, and constraint enforcement challenges in VAE-based constrained optimization using EC-VAE for embedding, uniform transformation for regularization, and constraint-priority filter for surrogate optimization.
AI.motivation: VAEs transform noisy data into compact representations for optimization, but face three key challenges: effective sampling in latent space, identifying active decision variables, and enforcing constraints without destabilizing training.
AI.method: MCOF uses: 1) Entropy-constrained VAE with feature selector to embed objective/constraint info into a subset of latent variables; 2) Uniform Transformation module to replace irregular posterior with uniform distribution; 3) Constraint-priority filter method to solve surrogate problem; 4) Resampling of unselected coordinates for diverse decodings.
AI.result: Validated on synthetic problem (recovers analytic optimum) and ZINC250k drug design (generates molecules satisfying constraints that are novel relative to training set). Ablation studies confirm each stage's contribution.
AI.conclusion: MCOF effectively addresses VAE-based constrained optimization challenges through a multi-stage framework combining dimensionality reduction, posterior regularization, constraint-aware optimization, and diversity generation.

title: Similarity All The Way Up: Multilingual Generalization in LLMs Relies on Language-Level Similarity Structures
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) grow more capable across diverse tasks, their (in)ability to generalize remains difficult to quantify and poorly understood beyond limited domains. In particular, LLMs are known to struggle generalizing multilingually, to languages outside of English, and that are poorly attested in their training data. To understand why this may be, and what enables some models to perform better than others, we turn to a long history of work across the cognitive sciences, arguing that successful generalization derives from appropriate representations in similarity space. We look at how well LLMs' representations capture the hierarchical similarity structure between distinct languages. Strikingly, we show LLMs' latent representations largely recover the hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree -- grouping languages that are members of the same subfamily closely together in representation space. Furthermore, we show that the degree to which models reflect the similarity structure of languages correlates with their performance on XNLI, a multilingual natural language inference benchmark. This extends classic work on similarity-driven generalization at scale, showing how models that represent similar languages similarly generalize better from one language to another.

AI.tldr: LLMs' multilingual generalization ability correlates with how well their latent representations capture hierarchical similarity structure between languages, particularly recovering the Indo-European language family tree.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with multilingual generalization, especially for languages poorly represented in training data, and it's unclear why some models perform better than others across different languages.
AI.method: The authors apply cognitive science principles about similarity-driven generalization, analyzing how well LLMs' representations capture hierarchical similarity structure between languages. They specifically examine whether LLM representations recover the Indo-European language family tree structure.
AI.result: LLMs' latent representations largely recover the hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree, grouping same-subfamily languages closely in representation space. Crucially, the degree to which models reflect this linguistic similarity structure correlates with their performance on the XNLI multilingual NLI benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Successful multilingual generalization in LLMs derives from appropriate representations in similarity space. Models that represent similar languages similarly generalize better across languages, extending classic similarity-driven generalization principles to large-scale language models.

title: Charging Phase Health Indicators for Battery State-of-Health Estimation: A Systematic Comparison of CC, CV, and Combined Approaches under Cross-Battery Validation
comment: This paper has been published in Eksploatacja i Niezawodnosc. Please cite the published version
summary: Accurate State-of-Health estimation is essential for safe battery operation and cost-effective maintenance. Although numerous health indicators have been derived from constant-current (CC) and constant-voltage (CV) charging phases, their effectiveness under realistic cross-battery validation remains insufficiently studied. This work addresses this gap through a systematic comparison of CC-only, CV-only, and combined indicator sets using rigorous Leave-One-Battery-Out (LOBO) validation on the NASA battery aging dataset. Four CV-phase indicators and CC phase duration are evaluated individually and in combination. Results show that the combined CC+CV approach achieves the best performance (R2 = 0.874), confirming that CC and CV phases capture complementary degradation information. Moreover, a 119% performance gap is observed between standard 5-fold cross-validation and LOBO validation, indicating that conventional evaluation overestimates practical accuracy. Based on these findings, practical guidelines are provided for indicator selection under data and computational constraints.

AI.tldr: Systematic comparison shows combined CC+CV charging indicators outperform CC-only or CV-only approaches for battery State-of-Health estimation, with rigorous cross-battery validation revealing significant overestimation in conventional evaluation methods.
AI.motivation: Current battery State-of-Health estimation methods using charging phase indicators lack systematic evaluation under realistic cross-battery validation scenarios, making it unclear which indicators work best in practical applications.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of CC-only, CV-only, and combined indicator sets using rigorous Leave-One-Battery-Out validation on NASA battery aging dataset, evaluating four CV-phase indicators and CC phase duration both individually and in combination.
AI.result: Combined CC+CV approach achieves best performance (R2 = 0.874), confirming CC and CV phases capture complementary degradation information. Standard 5-fold cross-validation shows 119% performance gap compared to LOBO validation, revealing conventional evaluation overestimates practical accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Practical guidelines are provided for indicator selection under data and computational constraints, emphasizing the importance of cross-battery validation for realistic battery State-of-Health estimation and the complementary value of combining CC and CV charging phase information.

title: RoleMix: Unifying Sequential and Non-Sequential Features via Semantic Tokenization for Post-Click Conversion Rate Prediction
summary: Post-click conversion rate (PCVR) prediction is central to industrial recommendation, but remains challenged by the structural mismatch between sparse, unordered multi-field features and long, domain-specific behavior histories. Existing models often process these signals through separate pathways and fuse them late, weakening semantic roles and limiting cross-signal refinement. We propose RoleMix, a unified interaction architecture that represents sequential and non-sequential evidence through a shared, role-preserving token interface. Non-sequential fields are converted into explicit semantic tokens that preserve user, item, pairwise, dense, contextual, and cross-feature roles, while long behavior domains are compressed into item- and context-aware sequence-query tokens through two-stage hierarchical window attention. The resulting global, semantic, and sequence-query tokens are jointly refined by stacked UniMixing-Lite blocks for PCVR prediction. On the large-scale KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, RoleMix achieves 83.648% online AUC, outperforming the official industrial baseline by 1.953%. Ablation studies show that semantic tokenization yields the largest isolated gain, highlighting a key principle for large-scale PCVR modeling: preserving field semantics at the token-interface level is as important as scaling the interaction backbone.

AI.tldr: RoleMix is a unified architecture for post-click conversion rate prediction that preserves semantic roles of features through tokenization and uses hierarchical attention for behavior sequences, achieving significant improvements over industrial baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing PCVR prediction models struggle with the structural mismatch between sparse, unordered multi-field features and long, domain-specific behavior histories. Current approaches process these signals separately and fuse them late, which weakens semantic roles and limits cross-signal refinement.
AI.method: RoleMix uses a shared, role-preserving token interface: non-sequential fields are converted into explicit semantic tokens preserving user, item, pairwise, dense, contextual, and cross-feature roles; long behavior domains are compressed into item- and context-aware sequence-query tokens via two-stage hierarchical window attention. All tokens are jointly refined by stacked UniMixing-Lite blocks.
AI.result: On the large-scale KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, RoleMix achieves 83.648% online AUC, outperforming the official industrial baseline by 1.953%. Ablation studies show semantic tokenization yields the largest isolated gain.
AI.conclusion: Preserving field semantics at the token-interface level is as important as scaling the interaction backbone for large-scale PCVR modeling. RoleMix demonstrates that explicit semantic role preservation enables better cross-signal refinement and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: An adaptive multi-fuzzy logic model for diagnosing transformer faults using dynamic weight optimization
comment: This paper has been published in e-Prime - Advances in Electrical Engineering, Electronics and Energy. Please cite the published version
summary: Dissolved gas analysis (DGA) is crucial for diagnosing early power transformer failures. Traditional DGA interpretation methods like Duval Triangle, IEC ratio, Roger ratio, Doernenburg ratio and Key Gas are inconsistent and vary in accuracy, especially for multiple fault conditions. We propose an Adaptive Multi-Fuzzy Logic (AMFL) model integrating multiple DGA methods with fuzzy logic and a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism. Unlike existing approaches with fixed weights, this system iteratively evaluates each method's diagnostic performance, identifies multiple fault types, and adjusts weights based on fault prediction accuracy. A feedback-based optimization recalibrates weights after each cycle to ensure optimal solution convergence. The model, implemented in MATLAB/Simulink, is validated against DGA datasets with known error conditions. Results show the AMFL model significantly improves diagnostic accuracy, especially in complex error scenarios, and enhances adaptability to new datasets. Comparative analysis demonstrates the proposed method outperforms traditional fixed weight multi-fuzzy systems in accuracy, consistency, and reliability of error detection. This work provides a robust, flexible diagnostic tool for transformer condition monitoring and supports more accurate asset management decisions.

AI.tldr: An Adaptive Multi-Fuzzy Logic (AMFL) model is proposed for transformer fault diagnosis using dissolved gas analysis, featuring dynamic weight adjustment of multiple DGA methods to improve accuracy over traditional fixed-weight approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional DGA interpretation methods (Duval Triangle, IEC ratio, etc.) are inconsistent and vary in accuracy, especially for multiple fault conditions. Existing multi-method approaches use fixed weights that don't adapt to diagnostic performance.
AI.method: Proposes an Adaptive Multi-Fuzzy Logic (AMFL) model that integrates multiple DGA methods with fuzzy logic and a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism. The system iteratively evaluates each method's diagnostic performance, identifies multiple fault types, and adjusts weights based on fault prediction accuracy using feedback-based optimization.
AI.result: The AMFL model, implemented in MATLAB/Simulink and validated against DGA datasets, shows significant improvement in diagnostic accuracy, especially in complex error scenarios. It enhances adaptability to new datasets and outperforms traditional fixed weight multi-fuzzy systems in accuracy, consistency, and reliability.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a robust, flexible diagnostic tool for transformer condition monitoring that supports more accurate asset management decisions through adaptive weight optimization of multiple DGA interpretation methods.

title: MPR-CiteG: Enhancing RAG with Multi-Portfolio Retrieval and Citation-Grounded Generation
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. The 1st International Workshop on Retrieval-Driven Generative AI & ScienceON AI Challenge 2025@CIKM
summary: This paper presents the MPR-CiteG framework, which achieved second place in the ScienceON AI Challenge by addressing two fundamental challenges in generative AI: inefficient retrieval and the absence of source verification. We propose a dual-component system, termed MPR-CiteG, in which the Multi-Portfolio Retriever (MPR) efficiently retrieves diverse and relevant information, while the Citation-Grounded Generation (CiteG) module ensures that every generated output remains factually consistent and explicitly attributed to its source. MPR-CiteG represents a significant step toward building more trustworthy and accurate LLMs that are not only capable of generating information but also of grounding their responses in reliable evidence, thereby mitigating common issues like model hallucination. Extensive experiments on the challenge dataset validate the effectiveness and reliability of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/2noweyh/MPR-citeG.

AI.tldr: MPR-CiteG is a framework that combines efficient retrieval with source-verified generation to create more trustworthy LLMs, achieving second place in the ScienceON AI Challenge.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses two key challenges in generative AI: inefficient information retrieval and lack of source verification, which lead to issues like model hallucination and factual inconsistencies in LLM outputs.
AI.method: Proposes a dual-component system: 1) Multi-Portfolio Retriever (MPR) for efficient retrieval of diverse relevant information, and 2) Citation-Grounded Generation (CiteG) module that ensures generated outputs remain factually consistent with explicit source attribution.
AI.result: The framework achieved second place in the ScienceON AI Challenge. Extensive experiments on the challenge dataset validated the effectiveness and reliability of the approach in creating more trustworthy and accurate LLMs.
AI.conclusion: MPR-CiteG represents a significant advancement toward building LLMs that can not only generate information but also ground responses in reliable evidence, mitigating common issues like model hallucination through explicit source attribution and verification.

title: Learning Sampling Parameters for Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models expose many inference-time sampling parameters, including prompts, negative prompts, classifier-free guidance scales, and noise schedules. These parameters are typically manually chosen once and then held fixed across prompts and denoising timesteps, even though different prompts and stages of generation can benefit from different parameter values. We introduce LeSAMP, a framework for learning prompt-conditioned, timestep-varying sampling parameters. We formulate parameter selection as a reinforcement learning problem: Given a user prompt, a large language model is trained to emit schedules for the chosen sampling parameters. We optimize our model using rewards from human preference models and VLM-as-a-judge. We evaluate our model on Flux.1 [dev] and Stable Diffusion 3.5, and find that compared to baselines, LeSAMP has a win rate of up to 68.12% using human preference scores and 73.37% using VLM-as-a-judge. These gains are validated in a user study where we achieve win rates of up to 59.46% over previous baselines. Our results suggest that learned sampling-parameter policies provide a complementary approach to existing post-training methods for improving diffusion model outputs.

AI.tldr: LeSAMP learns to automatically adjust diffusion model sampling parameters per-prompt and per-timestep using reinforcement learning, outperforming fixed-parameter baselines.
AI.motivation: Current text-to-image diffusion models use fixed sampling parameters across all prompts and denoising timesteps, even though different generation stages and prompts would benefit from adaptive parameter values.
AI.method: Formulates parameter selection as reinforcement learning problem. Uses large language model trained to emit schedules for sampling parameters conditioned on user prompts. Optimizes model using rewards from human preference models and VLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
AI.result: Evaluated on Flux.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5, achieving win rates up to 68.12% with human preference scores and 73.37% with VLM-as-a-judge. User study confirms win rates up to 59.46% over previous baselines.
AI.conclusion: Learned sampling-parameter policies provide complementary approach to existing post-training methods for improving diffusion model outputs, demonstrating benefits of adaptive parameter scheduling.

title: SEGRA: Structured Experience-Guided Graph Reasoning Agent for Gremlin Based Question Answering
summary: Enterprise IT support knowledge graphs capture rich relationships among cases, users, devices, symptoms, taxonomic categories, root causes, and historical resolutions. Yet querying them in Gremlin requires knowledge of graph schemas, traversal semantics, edge directionality, and property-graph-specific constraints, making them difficult for non-expert operators to use. We introduce SEGRA, an experience-guided agent for enterprise text-to-Gremlin question answering. SEGRA integrates intent routing, schema- and taxonomy-grounded query generation, multi-shot decomposition, execution-aware verification, and a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library that reuses verified query patterns. On an enterprise IT support benchmark, SEGRA achieves a $7.0\times$ higher mean judge score than backbone-only chain-of-thought prompting. Its skill library further reduces LLM calls by $20\%$ and dollar cost by $18\%$ relative to SEGRA without skills, while preserving answer quality. These results show that schema-grounded agent design and reusable execution experience improve both accuracy and efficiency for enterprise graph QA.

AI.tldr: SEGRA is an AI agent that converts natural language questions about enterprise IT support into Gremlin graph queries, using schema-grounded generation, experience-based skill libraries, and verification to improve accuracy and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Enterprise knowledge graphs contain valuable IT support information, but querying them requires technical Gremlin expertise that non-expert operators lack, creating accessibility barriers for utilizing this rich data.
AI.method: SEGRA combines intent routing, schema- and taxonomy-grounded query generation, multi-shot decomposition, execution-aware verification, and a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library that reuses verified query patterns.
AI.result: SEGRA achieves 7x higher mean judge score than backbone-only chain-of-thought prompting on enterprise IT support benchmark, with skill library reducing LLM calls by 20% and costs by 18% while preserving answer quality.
AI.conclusion: Schema-grounded agent design and reusable execution experience significantly improve both accuracy and efficiency for enterprise graph question answering, making knowledge graphs more accessible to non-expert users.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Discovering Periodic Orbits in the Gravitational Three-Body Problem
summary: Locating periodic solutions of chaotic dynamical systems normally requires an initial guess close enough to the target orbit for numerical continuation or gradient-based search to converge. We show that Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) trained on sparse, noisy observations \emph{without} initial conditions recover periodic orbits of the gravitational three-body problem, including orbit families absent from the training data. The method rests on a second-order ODE formulation, fixed-frequency Fourier features, percentile-based adaptive refinement, and a trainable scaling parameter, each validated on forward problems. Across two 100-seed ensembles, $23$--$25\%$ of runs converge to families not present in the training data. We then ask what determines which family emerges. Two $χ^2$ tests give a consistent answer: changing the training data source significantly shifts the distribution of recovered families ($p < 0.001$, Cramér's $V = 0.339$), whereas switching between the two initialization distributions tested does not ($p = 0.620$, $V = 0.094$). The random seed selects which family a given run recovers; the \emph{distribution} the weights are drawn from does not shift the aggregate frequencies, but the training data does. The evidence is empirical: we do not characterize the loss landscape analytically, and PINNs remain slower than conventional integrators on well-posed initial-value problems. What the experiments establish is that the recovered orbits are verifiable rather than merely plausible: the identified ones refine to genuine periodic solutions, a network trained on Lagrange data recovers the figure-eight choreography (Li--Liao class I.A.1, matched to seven significant digits in $T^*$), and one trained on figure-eight data recovers a Broucke--Hadjidemetriou--Hénon orbit closing to $δ_T < 10^{-9}$.

AI.tldr: PINNs trained on sparse, noisy data without initial conditions can discover periodic orbits in chaotic three-body systems, including orbit families not present in training data.
AI.motivation: Traditional methods for locating periodic solutions in chaotic systems require good initial guesses close to target orbits. The authors aim to show that PINNs can overcome this limitation and discover periodic orbits even from sparse, noisy observations without initial conditions.
AI.method: Use Physics-Informed Neural Networks with: 1) second-order ODE formulation, 2) fixed-frequency Fourier features, 3) percentile-based adaptive refinement, and 4) trainable scaling parameter. Validate on forward problems and test with 100-seed ensembles.
AI.result: 23-25% of runs converge to orbit families absent from training data. Training data source significantly determines which family emerges (p < 0.001), while initialization distribution does not (p = 0.620). The method recovers verifiable periodic solutions matched to high precision.
AI.conclusion: PINNs can discover periodic orbits in chaotic systems without initial guesses, with recovered orbits being verifiable rather than merely plausible. The training data distribution influences which orbit families emerge, while weight initialization distribution does not significantly affect aggregate frequencies.

title: Spatial Reasoning in LLM Game Agents: Impact of Causal Context and Multi-Step Planning
summary: LLM-based game agents often perform poorly on more complex tasks. This work examines whether these failures are linked to limited spatial reasoning and evaluates whether causal prompt augmentation and multi-step planning can improve win-rates while managing response latency. Using the open-source Qwen3 model family, we conduct experiments across varying model scales, reasoning modes, and planning horizons. We further introduce a focused GVGAI benchmark consisting of three custom games with five difficulty levels to isolate spatial navigation. The evaluation follows two paradigms: an initial ``positioning experiment'' to test an agent's ability to find its exact coordinates, and a study of game-play success. Our results show that while larger models with an enabled thinking mode identify their positions more accurately, overall performance in coordinate matching remains limited for smaller models. Win rates decrease as game levels and layout complexity increase, validating the benchmark's difficulty scaling. Integrating causal context into the prompts tends to improve the agents' success rates, particularly for bigger models. While enabling thinking mode and longer planning horizons significantly improve performance, multi-step planning further reduces mean per-step response times, offering a practical trade-off between reasoning depth and execution speed.

AI.tldr: LLM game agents struggle with complex tasks due to poor spatial reasoning. Using Qwen3 models, the study tests causal prompts and multi-step planning on custom GVGAI games, finding improvements with larger models and longer planning horizons.
AI.motivation: LLM-based game agents often fail on complex tasks, and the researchers want to determine if these failures are linked to limited spatial reasoning capabilities. They aim to evaluate whether causal prompt augmentation and multi-step planning can improve performance while managing response latency.
AI.method: Using the Qwen3 model family, experiments are conducted across varying model scales, reasoning modes, and planning horizons. A focused GVGAI benchmark is introduced with three custom games at five difficulty levels to isolate spatial navigation. Evaluation follows two paradigms: 1) "positioning experiment" to test coordinate identification, and 2) gameplay success analysis.
AI.result: Larger models with thinking mode identify positions more accurately, but coordinate matching remains limited for smaller models. Win rates decrease with increasing game difficulty and layout complexity. Causal context in prompts improves success rates, especially for bigger models. Thinking mode and longer planning horizons significantly improve performance, with multi-step planning reducing mean per-step response times.
AI.conclusion: Spatial reasoning limitations contribute to LLM game agent failures on complex tasks. Causal prompts and multi-step planning offer practical trade-offs between reasoning depth and execution speed, with larger models benefiting more from these enhancements.

title: Impute On-Demand: Adaptive Correlated Time Series Imputation for Changing Environments
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering (IEEE TKDE)
summary: Internet of Things (IoT) applications generate vast amounts of Correlated Time Series (CTS) data that often contain missing values and require imputation. Existing methods emphasize accuracy but often lack adaptability to changing IoT environments: they are vulnerable to sensor failures, cannot selectively impute only incomplete sensors, and use static architectures that do not adapt to resource availability. To address these limitations, we propose AdaCTSi, an adaptive CTS imputer for changing environments. AdaCTSi combines a One-shot Temporal Convolutional Network with a Learned Time-Sensor Index Table to extract and decouple complex spatio-temporal features into sensor-wise embeddings, enabling adaptation to varying sensor subsets. Sparse Spatial Attention efficiently extracts dynamic spatial correlations, while Correlation-Weighted Sensor Selection selects informative sensors to provide sufficient spatial context. Experiments with twelve baseline methods, three adaptability scenarios, and five benchmark datasets covering traffic, air quality, and trajectory data show that AdaCTSi reduces MAE by an average of 33.1% relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. A single trained model supports sensor-subset and resource-adaptive inference, and its modest memory footprint enables deployment on commodity computing devices, including MCUs.

AI.tldr: AdaCTSi: An adaptive Correlated Time Series imputation method for IoT that handles sensor failures, selectively imputes incomplete sensors, and adapts to changing resource constraints.
AI.motivation: IoT applications generate vast amounts of CTS data with missing values. Existing methods lack adaptability to changing IoT environments: they are vulnerable to sensor failures, cannot selectively impute only incomplete sensors, and use static architectures that don't adapt to resource availability.
AI.method: Proposes AdaCTSi combining One-shot Temporal Convolutional Network with Learned Time-Sensor Index Table to extract and decouple spatio-temporal features into sensor-wise embeddings. Uses Sparse Spatial Attention for dynamic spatial correlations and Correlation-Weighted Sensor Selection to choose informative sensors for spatial context.
AI.result: Experiments with 12 baseline methods, 3 adaptability scenarios, and 5 benchmark datasets show AdaCTSi reduces MAE by average 33.1% relative to strongest baseline. Single trained model supports sensor-subset and resource-adaptive inference with modest memory footprint for deployment on commodity devices including MCUs.
AI.conclusion: AdaCTSi effectively addresses adaptability limitations of existing CTS imputation methods for IoT environments, providing superior accuracy while supporting flexible deployment in resource-constrained scenarios.

title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts
summary: As AI agents operate with increasing autonomy in a multi-agent world, they will need to learn to cooperate with other agents and with humans to generate mutual benefits.
