We introduce SymStep: an LLM makes one atomic claim at a time (DEDUCE: Alice, pet, Cat), then a lightweight constraint propagator checks the claim for consistency with prior accepted deductions, rejects contradictions, and cascades implied facts automatically. SymStep+G additionally provides MRV guidance after each accepted step, directing the LLM toward the most constrained unresolved variable. On a 35-puzzle retained subset of ZebraLogicBench, a benchmark of 1,000 Einstein-style logic puzzles, Direct and CoT both achieve 0%, while SymStep+G reaches 97%. On AR-LSAT analytical reasoning problems, SymStep achieves 100% vs. CoT's 87%. On LGP-14, SymStep+G achieves 100% vs. 0% for CoT and Logic-LM, the strongest prior symbolic+LLM baseline we compare against. Ablation studies reveal that MRV guidance is a key mechanism for reducing directionless cycling, while consistency checking provides a safety net against explicit contradictions. Across six benchmarks spanning five task domains, SymStep variants match or exceed every baseline on constraint-dense and arithmetic tasks. Experiments on AQUA-RAT algebra confirm the advantage is constraint-density-specific.

AI.tldr: SymStep introduces a novel reasoning approach where LLMs make atomic claims followed by constraint propagation, achieving near-perfect results on constraint-dense logical reasoning tasks where CoT fails.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting often fails on constraint-dense logical reasoning tasks because unverified errors accumulate silently across steps, leading to incorrect conclusions. There's a need for more reliable reasoning methods for complex logical puzzles.
AI.method: SymStep breaks reasoning into atomic steps: 1) LLM makes one atomic claim at a time, 2) lightweight constraint propagator checks consistency with prior deductions and rejects contradictions, 3) automatically cascades implied facts. SymStep+G adds MRV (Minimum Remaining Values) guidance to direct the LLM toward most constrained unresolved variables after each accepted step.
AI.result: On ZebraLogicBench puzzles: Direct/CoT 0% vs SymStep+G 97%. On AR-LSAT: SymStep 100% vs CoT 87%. On LGP-14: SymStep+G 100% vs CoT/Logic-LM 0%. Ablation shows MRV reduces directionless cycling and consistency checking prevents contradictions. SymStep variants outperform all baselines across six benchmarks spanning five domains.
AI.conclusion: SymStep's hybrid approach combining LLMs with lightweight symbolic constraint propagation and MRV guidance effectively solves constraint-dense logical reasoning tasks where pure neural methods fail, demonstrating the importance of integrating symbolic reasoning with neural models for complex reasoning problems.

title: Source-Free Controlled Adaptation of Teachers for Continual Test-Time Adaptation
summary: In many real-world scenarios, encountering continual shifts in domain during inference is very common. Consequently, continual test-time adaptation (CTTA) techniques leveraging a teacher-student framework have gained prominence, allowing models to adapt continuously even after deployment. In such a framework, a weight-averaged mean teacher is used to produce pseudo-labels from test data for self-training. The mean teacher gets updated as an exponential moving average of the student parameters using a high value of momentum that is kept fixed even if different distributions of test data are encountered. To combat the resulting drift of the model, we propose a novel controlled teacher adaptation methodology that dynamically sets a proper momentum value depending on the quality of the incoming data. Additionally, we estimate class prototypes from the source pretrained model to help align the target data as they come in. Importantly, our method does not require access to source data or its statistics at any stage of the pipeline, making it truly source-free. We perform extensive experiments on benchmark datasets to demonstrate that our approach outperforms different state-of-the-art adaptation frameworks, many of which require access to source data.

AI.tldr: A novel controlled teacher adaptation method for continual test-time adaptation that dynamically adjusts momentum based on incoming data quality and uses class prototypes from the source model, achieving state-of-the-art performance without requiring source data access.
AI.motivation: Real-world scenarios often involve continual domain shifts during inference, requiring models to adapt continuously after deployment. Existing teacher-student frameworks for continual test-time adaptation use fixed momentum values for mean teacher updates, which can lead to model drift when encountering different test data distributions.
AI.method: Proposes a controlled teacher adaptation methodology that: 1) Dynamically sets proper momentum values based on the quality of incoming test data, 2) Estimates class prototypes from the source pretrained model to help align target data, 3) Operates in a completely source-free manner without needing source data or statistics.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that the proposed approach outperforms different state-of-the-art adaptation frameworks, including many that require access to source data, despite being completely source-free.
AI.conclusion: The proposed controlled teacher adaptation method effectively addresses model drift in continual test-time adaptation scenarios by dynamically adjusting momentum and using source model prototypes, achieving superior performance without the need for source data access, making it practical for real-world deployment.

title: Structure over Depth: A Single-Block Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Multi-Entity Reasoning
summary: Modeling multi-entity temporal data requires capturing dependencies across entities, time, and their interactions. Transformer-based approaches perform well but often rely on deep stacks of layers to learn these heterogeneous dependencies implicitly, increasing computational cost. We revisit this problem from a structural perspective and decompose multi-entity temporal dynamics into three interaction types: spatial interactions among entities, temporal interactions across time, and cross interactions coupling the two domains. We propose a structured spatio-temporal transformer block that explicitly models all three within a single stage. It uses parallel spatial and temporal self-attention, followed by bidirectional cross-attention, and combines the outputs through learnable gated fusion. By directly encoding these complementary views, the model reduces the need for deep stacking. We evaluate the approach on video-based group activity recognition, skeleton-based human interaction analysis, and wearable sensor-based activity recognition. Despite its simplicity, the single structured Transformer block matches or outperforms deeper architectures with only 1.76M parameters. The results suggest that depth in prior models partly compensates for implicit and entangled interaction modeling, whereas explicit factorization offers a more efficient and transparent alternative. More broadly, this work supports a structure-first design principle: expressive multi-entity temporal reasoning can emerge by exposing interaction structure rather than relying on depth.

AI.tldr: A single-structured Transformer block with explicit modeling of spatial, temporal, and cross interactions matches or outperforms deeper architectures in multi-entity temporal tasks while using far fewer parameters (1.76M).
AI.motivation: Transformer-based approaches for multi-entity temporal data often rely on deep stacks of layers to implicitly learn heterogeneous dependencies across entities and time, which increases computational cost. The paper seeks to address this inefficiency by taking a structural perspective.
AI.method: The paper proposes a structured spatio-temporal Transformer block that explicitly decomposes multi-entity temporal dynamics into three interaction types: spatial interactions among entities, temporal interactions across time, and cross interactions coupling the two domains. The model uses parallel spatial and temporal self-attention, followed by bidirectional cross-attention, with learnable gated fusion to combine outputs.
AI.result: Despite its simplicity, the single structured Transformer block matches or outperforms deeper architectures across three tasks (video-based group activity recognition, skeleton-based human interaction analysis, wearable sensor-based activity recognition) while using only 1.76M parameters. This demonstrates that explicit factorization can replace deep stacking.
AI.conclusion: Depth in prior models compensates for implicit and entangled interaction modeling, while explicit factorization offers a more efficient and transparent alternative. The work supports a "structure-first" design principle where expressive multi-entity temporal reasoning emerges from exposing interaction structure rather than relying on depth.

title: Soft-Constrained Optimization of Latent Space in Variational Autoencoders
summary: The usefulness of a variational autoencoder (VAE) depends on two properties of its latent space that are hard to obtain together: high encoding capacity in the individual latent variables, and a low-dimensional, disentangled organization of those variables. Weakening the Kullback-Leibler regularization raises capacity but degrades disentanglement, while strengthening it prunes latent variables away entirely. We formulate VAE training as a soft-constrained optimization problem that addresses both. First, we impose an entropy-based constraint (EC) on individual latent variables, showing that the entropy of a latent code upper-bounds the mutual information it carries about the generative factors of the data. Second, we propose a weight-filter method that exploits the slack of the soft constraint to prune low-entropy dimensions during downstream training. On dSprites, the EC raises the aggregate latent-variable activation score by 43-62% over a vanilla VAE, attains the highest FactorVAE score among the \b{eta} \b{eta}-VAE variants (0.891 vs 0.847), and lowers reconstruction error by up to 38%. On MNIST, the weight filter reduces the latent dimensionality supplied to a downstream classifier from ten to two while holding accuracy above 90%, converging in 37% fewer epochs than the same procedure without the EC. We also find that low-entropy discrete factors tend to merge into a single latent variable, whereas high-entropy continuous factors are distributed across several.

AI.tldr: A novel VAE training approach using entropy constraints improves both latent variable capacity and disentanglement while enabling automatic dimensionality reduction for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: VAEs face a fundamental trade-off between high encoding capacity in individual latent variables (needed for rich representations) and low-dimensional, disentangled organization (needed for interpretability). Standard KL regularization either limits capacity or prunes variables entirely.
AI.method: 1. Formulate VAE training as soft-constrained optimization with entropy-based constraints (EC) on individual latent variables, showing entropy upper-bounds mutual information about generative factors. 2. Propose weight-filter method that exploits constraint slack to prune low-entropy dimensions during downstream training.
AI.result: On dSprites: EC raises aggregate latent-variable activation by 43-62%, achieves highest FactorVAE score among β-VAE variants (0.891 vs 0.847), and reduces reconstruction error by up to 38%. On MNIST: Weight filter reduces latent dimensionality from 10 to 2 while maintaining >90% accuracy, converging 37% faster than baseline. Discovered that low-entropy discrete factors merge into single variables, while high-entropy continuous factors distribute across multiple variables.
AI.conclusion: The proposed entropy-constrained VAE framework successfully addresses the capacity-disentanglement trade-off, providing both improved representation quality and automatic dimensionality reduction, with insights into how different factor types organize in latent space.

title: Compiler-Grounded Hierarchical Diagnosis for LLM-Based Triton Kernel Optimization
summary:
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated kernel generation and optimization, but most existing approaches rely on surface signals such as compilation feedback and profiling metrics. These signals reveal that a kernel is slow, but not why the backend compiler fails to realize a profitable optimization, especially on emerging accelerators such as NPUs. We therefore formulate kernel optimization as a progressive cross-layer diagnosis problem that links runtime symptoms to IR structure and compiler behavior before rewriting source. Based on this insight, we present our system, a compiler-grounded and hierarchical optimization framework for Triton kernels. the system escalates from lightweight pattern triage and profiling diagnosis to IR attribution and compiler-grounded analysis only when deeper evidence is needed, then proposes evidence-backed source-level rewrites.
  We implement the system on Triton for Ascend NPUs and evaluate it on 37 successfully converted entries from a standardized NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950 benchmark. Across these entries, the system attains a geometric-mean speedup of 4.35$\times$ and a median speedup of 2.73$\times$ from the initial to optimized Triton kernel; 22/37 exceed 2$\times$ and 13/37 exceed 5$\times$. The complete distribution ranges from near-baseline entries to large wins, motivating transparent reporting of the current system's scope and limitations.

AI.tldr: A compiler-grounded hierarchical framework for optimizing Triton kernels on NPUs that links runtime symptoms to IR structure and compiler behavior before proposing evidence-backed source rewrites.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based kernel optimization approaches rely on surface signals like compilation feedback and profiling metrics, which reveal that a kernel is slow but not why the backend compiler fails to realize profitable optimizations, especially on emerging NPU accelerators.
AI.method: Formulates kernel optimization as a progressive cross-layer diagnosis problem, escalating from lightweight pattern triage and profiling diagnosis to IR attribution and compiler-grounded analysis only when deeper evidence is needed, then proposes evidence-backed source-level rewrites.
AI.result: Implemented on Triton for Ascend NPUs and evaluated on 37 successfully converted entries from a standardized NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950 benchmark. Achieved geometric-mean speedup of 4.35× and median speedup of 2.73×; 22/37 exceed 2× and 13/37 exceed 5×.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates significant performance improvements for Triton kernels on NPUs through a hierarchical, evidence-based approach, though transparent reporting of scope and limitations is needed due to variable speedups across different kernels.

title: On the post-hoc Evaluation of PDE Discovery: A Multifaceted Challenge of Scientific Advancement
summary: Partial differential equation (PDE) discovery aims to identify from data the governing law of a physical system. Constituting a cornerstone of scientific advancement, it has become during the past decade a major line of research in the rapidly evolving field of Physics-informed Machine Learning (PiML). Among the remaining open problems to address in this domain, the post-hoc evaluation of discovered PDEs raises the particular difficulty of being multifaceted. Indeed, it requires jointly considering predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization capacity. Given that some of these properties are conflicting, it is worth noting that the wide range of existing evaluation metrics only partially address the overall problem, potentially leading to overly interpreted conclusions about the validity of a presumed new physical theory. From an abundant literature spanning machine learning, numerical analysis, information theory or symbolic regression, we propose, to our knowledge, the first taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics, and discuss their advantages and limitations in depth. Based on the observation that evaluation is often achieved on a case-by-case basis and that a universally accepted methodology remains elusive, we further provide recommendations with the aim of promoting standardized and reliable practices, before sketching promising future lines of research in this field. We argue that this paper is intended both for ML experts who design new PDE discovery algorithms and for users of these methods aiming, in real applications, to discover and validate well-founded scientific laws.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first comprehensive taxonomy of evaluation metrics for PDE discovery methods, analyzing their limitations and proposing standardized practices for reliable validation of discovered physical laws.
AI.motivation: Current PDE discovery evaluation lacks standardized methodology, with existing metrics only partially addressing multifaceted requirements like predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and generalization. This leads to potentially over-interpreted conclusions about new physical theories.
AI.method: Conducts systematic literature review spanning machine learning, numerical analysis, information theory, and symbolic regression to create the first comprehensive taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics, analyzing their advantages and limitations.
AI.result: Develops a comprehensive taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics, identifies their limitations in addressing conflicting evaluation dimensions, and provides recommendations for standardized practices to promote reliable PDE discovery validation.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes foundational framework for PDE discovery evaluation, arguing that both ML algorithm designers and users need standardized methodologies to validate discovered scientific laws reliably, and outlines promising future research directions.

title: SQBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Task Delivery by Language-Model Agents in Production-Oriented Workflows
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures. Code and aggregate results: https://github.com/shaqiu-ai/SQBench
summary: Existing evaluations of large language models cover knowledge, reasoning, coding, and tool use, but they rarely treat a verifiable deliverable produced within a constrained workflow as the unit of evaluation. We introduce SQBench, a benchmark for evaluating production-oriented task delivery by language-model agents. SQBench v1.0 contains 220 standardized tasks organized into L1 atomic capabilities, L2 composite skills, and L3 business scenarios. Each task requires an agent to process input assets, use available tools, and produce an explicitly specified deliverable. The evaluation first computes functional Completion and then derives Risk Penalty and Performance from independently evidenced triggers in a 10D Risk Matrix. A Strict Pass requires Completion = 1 and Risk Penalty = 0. We evaluate 27 model configurations under a common protocol, with one run per configuration-task pair. The highest prespecified Weighted Pass@1 is 60.5%. Mean Strict Pass@1 on L3 is 18.5%, and every configuration performs worse on L3 than on both L1 and L2, indicating that delivery under domain constraints is a shared weakness within the current task set. Of 2,348 results with Completion = 1, 113 (4.8%) fail the Strict Pass criterion because of risks such as unverifiable citations, inappropriate resource use, or format violations. These results show that functional completion alone does not fully characterize delivery quality and that risk determinations should be reported separately.

AI.tldr: SQBench is a benchmark for evaluating language model agents on production-oriented task delivery with risk assessment, showing current models struggle with domain-constrained business scenarios despite functional completion.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluations focus on knowledge, reasoning, coding, and tool use but rarely evaluate verifiable deliverables produced within constrained workflows, which is crucial for production deployment.
AI.method: Introduces SQBench v1.0 with 220 standardized tasks organized in 3 levels (atomic capabilities, composite skills, business scenarios), each requiring asset processing, tool use, and specific deliverables. Evaluation uses Completion score plus Risk Matrix (10D) to calculate Risk Penalty, with Strict Pass requiring Completion=1 and Risk Penalty=0.
AI.result: Evaluated 27 model configurations: highest Weighted Pass@1 is 60.5%, mean Strict Pass@1 on L3 business scenarios is only 18.5%. All models perform worse on L3 than L1/L2. 4.8% of completed tasks failed Strict Pass due to risks like unverifiable citations, inappropriate resource use, or format violations.
AI.conclusion: Functional completion alone doesn't characterize delivery quality; risk assessment is essential for production readiness. Current LLM agents have significant weaknesses in domain-constrained business scenarios, indicating room for improvement in practical deployment.

title: WISERouter: LLM Routing with Workload Budget Constraint
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve impressive performance across multiple domains, but using the most capable model for every query is prohibitive at scale. LLM routing exploits diversity in model capability and cost by assigning each query to a suitable model to balance utility and budget. Current methods have two limitations: (i) they either use heuristics that do not always enforce the budget constraint or impose a fixed per-query budget that cannot adapt across the workload and leads to suboptimal performance; (ii) they require supervised learning on a dense dataset with statistics for every query-model pair, which is expensive to collect. To address these challenges, we formulate LLM routing as a constrained contextual multi-armed bandit problem and introduce WISERouter (WR for short), a framework that supports offline learning from historical interactions as well as online learning with exploration. We further prove that WR-Online achieves a sublinear regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T})$ over a time horizon $T$. Empirical results on RouterBench and SWE-Bench demonstrate that (i) WR-Offline surpasses existing baselines in performance under a fixed budget and adheres more closely to budget constraints, and (ii) WR-Online achieves comparable performance to the baselines, while using substantially less exploration data.

AI.tldr: WISERouter: A bandit-based framework for optimal LLM routing that balances performance and cost through both offline and online learning approaches with proven theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Current LLM routing methods have two main limitations: 1) They either use heuristics that don't enforce budget constraints or impose fixed per-query budgets that lead to suboptimal performance, and 2) They require expensive supervised learning on dense query-model datasets that are costly to collect.
AI.method: Formulates LLM routing as a constrained contextual multi-armed bandit problem and introduces WISERouter (WR), a framework supporting both offline learning from historical interactions and online learning with exploration. The paper proves WR-Online achieves sublinear regret bound of O(√T).
AI.result: Empirical results on RouterBench and SWE-Bench show: (i) WR-Offline outperforms existing baselines in performance under fixed budget and adheres better to budget constraints, (ii) WR-Online achieves comparable performance to baselines while using substantially less exploration data.
AI.conclusion: WISERouter effectively addresses limitations of current LLM routing methods by providing a theoretically-grounded bandit-based framework that achieves better performance-cost tradeoffs with less data, enabling practical deployment at scale.

title: AgentOmnia: Scaling Agentic Models for Full-Scenario Applications
summary: Large language model agents have advanced rapidly, yet progress remains fragmented across domains, capabilities, task difficulty, and interaction settings. We frame this as full-scenario agentic scaling and present AgentOmnia, a framework coordinating task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and improvement across To-Consumer (ToC), To-Business (ToB), and To-Employee (ToE) applications. An extensible Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy aligns these stages and enables fine-grained diagnosis with OmniaBench. AgentOmnia combines bidirectional environment-task synthesis with tool-dependency, program-structured, and solver-based pipelines, constructing 5,018 stateful environments with 255,375 tools and 52,361 tasks. Programs, solvers, and verifiers provide correctness signals, while supervised fine-tuning, online agentic reinforcement learning, and a rollback curriculum support post-training. Evaluation failures translate into Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) for targeted self-evolution. Starting from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, AgentOmnia raises the pass rate on the OmniaBench challenging subset from 9.16% to 37.11% and the macro-average across OmniaBench, $τ^2$-Bench, DeepPlanning, and VitaBench from 22.86% to 41.69%. Under a unified protocol,it leads the evaluated agentic post-trained baselines on OmniaBench and retains the highest four-benchmark macro-average. It also surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on all four benchmarks and exceeds Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the macro-average. Gains span three application splits, ten capability dimensions, eight atomic-difficulty factors, and 76 of 90 level-1 domains, indicating broad rather than category-specific improvement. A one-round study provides initial evidence for PRD-guided self-evolution, motivating validation at larger scales and in industrial settings.

AI.tldr: AgentOmnia is a unified framework for scaling AI agents across all scenarios, using a comprehensive taxonomy and multi-stage pipeline to improve agent performance across diverse domains and applications.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent development is fragmented across domains, capabilities, task difficulty, and interaction settings, lacking a unified approach for full-scenario agentic scaling.
AI.method: AgentOmnia coordinates task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and improvement using a Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy. It employs bidirectional environment-task synthesis with tool-dependency, program-structured, and solver-based pipelines, constructing 5,018 stateful environments with 255,375 tools and 52,361 tasks. Uses supervised fine-tuning, online agentic reinforcement learning, and rollback curriculum for post-training.
AI.result: Raised pass rate on OmniaBench challenging subset from 9.16% to 37.11% and macro-average across four benchmarks from 22.86% to 41.69%. Outperformed evaluated agentic post-trained baselines on OmniaBench and achieved highest four-benchmark macro-average. Surpassed larger models (Qwen3-235B) and showed broad improvement across application splits, capabilities, difficulty factors, and domains.
AI.conclusion: AgentOmnia provides a comprehensive framework for scaling agents across diverse scenarios with demonstrated effectiveness, and the PRD-guided self-evolution approach shows promise for continuous improvement.

title: A Comparison of Data Augmentation Methods for Training Deep Neural Networks on Synthetic Aperture Sonar
comment: This paper was originally published in the proceedings of the International Conference on Underwater Acoustics 2026
summary: In this work we study Automatic Target Recognition (ATR) for Synthetic Aperture Sonar (SAS) data with a focus on deep neural networks (DNNs). The main challenge in training DNNs for SAS ATR arises from the limited quantity of labeled target examples, which arises due to the significant costs and time required to collect real-world SAS data. One successful general strategy for mitigating the problem of limited training data is augmentation, which generates additional synthetic training data by introducing realistic variations to available real-world data. Prior research has investigated a variety of augmentation strategies for SAS ATR, including conventional image augmentations (e.g., contrast changes, cropping) as well as physics-based augmentations, which are motivated the specific physics of SAS data. Building on prior work, we systematically compare many of these existing augmentation strategies for training DNNs for SAS ATR. We also investigate the impact of augmentation when combined with modern DNN architectures such as transformers. The results indicate that augmentation can improve target recognition accuracy, although benefits vary, and not all augmentations are beneficial.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares various data augmentation strategies (including conventional image augmentations and physics-based methods) for training deep neural networks on Synthetic Aperture Sonar data for Automatic Target Recognition, particularly when dealing with limited labeled training data.
AI.motivation: The primary motivation is addressing the challenge of limited labeled target examples in SAS ATR due to the high costs and time required for real-world data collection. There's a need to effectively train DNNs with scarce data, and data augmentation offers a promising solution to mitigate this data scarcity problem.
AI.method: The researchers systematically compare existing augmentation strategies for SAS ATR, including conventional image augmentations (contrast changes, cropping) and physics-based augmentations motivated by SAS data physics. They also investigate the impact of these augmentations when combined with modern DNN architectures like transformers.
AI.result: Results show that augmentation can improve target recognition accuracy, but the benefits vary significantly across different augmentation strategies. Importantly, not all augmentations are beneficial - some may not provide performance improvements.
AI.conclusion: Data augmentation is a valuable strategy for improving SAS ATR performance with limited training data, but careful selection of augmentation methods is crucial since not all augmentations provide benefits. The combination of augmentation with modern architectures like transformers shows promise for further improvements.

title: CachedSearch: Training-Free Cached Exploration for Test-Time Search in Video Diffusion
summary: Test-time search lets small video diffusion models rival larger ones, but costs 2-10x more. All candidates are fully denoised, although most are discarded. Training-free caching makes each rollout 2-3x faster at near-lossless quality. Composition is safe only if lossy caching preserves verifier rankings. We present the first study of whether caching corrupts candidate ranking in video test-time search. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with an adaptive caching wrapper (~2x per-candidate speedup), ImageReward scores seed-matched cached and full rollouts. Median per-prompt Spearman rank correlation is 0.905, with 72% top-1 agreement on the VBench suite. VBench-2.0 replicates this result on a harder suite. Recomputing the cached winner at full compute retains 90-94% of the full-search gain. Errors cluster among near-tied candidates, making corruption self-limiting. This finding leads to CachedSearch. It explores every candidate with aggressive caching, then re-generates only the winner at full compute. At N=8, it captures 94.7% of best-of-N's gain at 63% of the cost. Capture rises with width. At matched budget, it searches twice as wide for 38% more gain. The result holds from 1.3B-14B across six models and four families: Wan, LTX, CogVideoX, and Hunyuan. Wan2.1-14B matches the 1.3B model's fidelity. Mid-trajectory pruning multiplies the exploration saving to 3.11x at 88.6% capture. Ports to other model families require recalibrating a single parameter, showing that fidelity tracks architecture rather than parameter count. CachedSearch is training-free, verifier-agnostic, and orthogonal to the search algorithm, making it a plug-in multiplier for test-time scaling.

AI.tldr: CachedSearch is a training-free caching method that speeds up video test-time search by 2-3x while preserving 90-94% of quality gains, allowing smaller models to explore wider candidate spaces efficiently.
AI.motivation: Test-time search improves video diffusion model quality but is computationally expensive (2-10x cost), requiring full denoising of all candidates even though most are discarded. There's a need to reduce this computational burden while maintaining quality.
AI.method: Proposes CachedSearch with aggressive caching during candidate exploration, then re-generates only the winner at full compute. Key innovation: caching only corrupts rankings among near-tied candidates (self-limiting property), making it safe. Validated with adaptive caching wrapper on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and other models.
AI.result: At N=8, captures 94.7% of best-of-N's quality gain at 63% cost. With matched budget, searches twice as wide for 38% more gain. Median Spearman correlation 0.905 between cached/full rollouts, 72% top-1 agreement. Works across 1.3B-14B models from four families (Wan, LTX, CogVideoX, Hunyuan).
AI.conclusion: CachedSearch enables efficient test-time search scaling as a plug-in multiplier: training-free, verifier-agnostic, and orthogonal to search algorithm. Shows fidelity tracks architecture rather than parameter count, with Wan2.1-14B matching 1.3B model's fidelity.

title: Scale Weight Decay and Train Better
summary: The discovery of scaling laws has motivated training neural networks on ever increasing quantities of data. This is typically done with a constant decoupled weight decay which causes the network weights to shrink steadily over the course of training. Taking inspiration from the Robbins--Monro conditions, we propose to scale weight decay by the fraction of the peak learning rate $η/η_{\max}$. We prove that this scaled weight decay preserves the asymptotic stationarity guarantees of the corresponding unregularized methods for both stochastic gradient descent and the non-Euclidean spectral optimizer Muon, thereby avoiding the additional asymptotic bias introduced by constant decoupled weight decay. This retains the stability benefits of weight decay without changing the asymptotic optimization target. Using a steady-state analysis, we explain why under standard weight decay the weight norm shrinks steadily as training proceeds, whereas under scaled weight decay it settles to a roughly constant value. When applied to the training of mixture-of-experts models, Muon with scaled weight decay (Muon-SW) consistently outpaces Muon with identical hyperparameters, reaching the same validation loss $\mathbf{30\%}$ faster at our largest scale across models from $72 - 930$ million parameters trained at $\sim 600$ tokens per active parameter. If this trend continues to hold, the method promises to substantially accelerate the pre-training of frontier models while requiring only a few lines of code to implement.

AI.tldr: Proposing scaled weight decay that preserves asymptotic stationarity guarantees while maintaining stability benefits, showing consistent performance improvements in large-scale mixture-of-experts models.
AI.motivation: Constant decoupled weight decay causes network weights to shrink steadily during training, introducing asymptotic bias and potentially suboptimal performance as models scale.
AI.method: Scale weight decay by the fraction of peak learning rate (η/η_max), preserving asymptotic stationarity guarantees for both SGD and non-Euclidean spectral optimizer Muon.
AI.result: Muon with scaled weight decay (Muon-SW) consistently outperforms Muon with standard weight decay, reaching same validation loss 30% faster at largest scale across models from 72-930M parameters.
AI.conclusion: Scaled weight decay retains stability benefits without changing asymptotic optimization target, promising substantial acceleration of frontier model pre-training with minimal implementation overhead.

title: An Ontology for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate quantum-mechanical energies and forces---conventionally computed by density functional theory (DFT) or wave-function methods---at a fraction of the cost. The field encompasses a growing ecosystem of algorithms, training datasets, hyperparameters, and target materials, yet the metadata needed to systematically compare, reproduce, and build upon MLIP studies remains scattered across papers, scripts, and ad-hoc file formats. We present the MLIPs ontology, an OWL 2 DL ontology that captures the concepts needed to describe MLIP methods, their hyperparameters, training datasets with DFT provenance, and published benchmarks. The ontology is organized into three modules---Method, Training Data, and Benchmark---and connects existing ontologies in materials science (MDO, CMSO/ASMO) and machine learning (ML-Schema), complementing dataset-side schemas such as Croissant. It declares 27 formal axioms enforcing data completeness and consistency, including property chains that link trained models to their methods and training data. We demonstrate the ontology through a running example based on Moment Tensor Potentials and evaluate it through competency-question execution on a 20-paper seeded knowledge graph, OWL reasoning, and comparison with existing ontologies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MLIPs ontology - an OWL 2 DL ontology for standardizing metadata about machine learning interatomic potentials, addressing the fragmentation of MLIP research data.
AI.motivation: The metadata needed to systematically compare, reproduce, and build upon MLIP studies remains scattered across papers, scripts, and ad-hoc file formats, creating reproducibility and comparability issues in the field.
AI.method: Developed MLIPs ontology as an OWL 2 DL ontology with three modules (Method, Training Data, and Benchmark), integrated with existing ontologies (MDO, CMSO/ASMO, ML-Schema), and included 27 formal axioms for data consistency and completeness.
AI.result: Created a functional ontology that successfully connects trained models to their methods and training data through property chains, demonstrated through a running example with Moment Tensor Potentials and evaluated via competency-question execution, OWL reasoning, and comparison with existing ontologies on a 20-paper knowledge graph.
AI.conclusion: The MLIPs ontology provides a formal, structured framework for organizing and sharing MLIP research metadata, enabling systematic comparison, reproducibility, and knowledge building across the field while complementing existing standardization efforts.

title: SCTA: An Agentic Framework for Stable and Interpretable Target Gene Discovery from Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. To appear in the ACM SIGKDD Workshop on Data Mining in Bioinformatics (BioKDD 2026)
summary: Identifying therapeutic target genes from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data remains a fundamental challenge in translational biology. Unlike bulk assays, scRNA-seq captures heterogeneous cellular states and rare subpopulations, but this same heterogeneity makes target discovery highly sensitive to analytical choices throughout the pipeline, including preprocessing, cell population selection, differential expression analysis, and downstream biological interpretation. As a result, existing workflows and general-purpose analysis agents often produce unstable or difficult-to-interpret target hypotheses, limiting their reliability for disease-focused discovery. We present SCTA (Single-Cell Target Agent), a decision-centric agentic framework for stable and interpretable target gene discovery from scRNA-seq data. Rather than treating analysis as a single general-purpose reasoning task, SCTA decomposes target discovery into specialized agents aligned with key decision points in the single-cell pipeline and constrains downstream reasoning with structured biological evidence. In a representative ablation study on hereditary chronic pancreatitis, we demonstrate that SCTA's full evidence integration yields the most stable target selection across independent runs among the tested configurations, while recovering biologically coherent, disease-relevant mechanisms validated in prior studies. These results suggest that decision-aware agent orchestration tailored to the structure of single-cell analysis can improve the robustness, interpretability, and practical utility of target discovery in precision medicine.

AI.tldr: SCTA is a decision-centric agentic framework for stable and interpretable therapeutic target gene discovery from single-cell RNA-seq data, decomposing analysis into specialized agents to improve robustness over existing unstable workflows.
AI.motivation: Current scRNA-seq target discovery is highly sensitive to analytical choices, producing unstable or difficult-to-interpret results that limit reliability for disease-focused discovery, despite capturing cellular heterogeneity better than bulk assays.
AI.method: SCTA decomposes target discovery into specialized agents aligned with key decision points in the single-cell pipeline (preprocessing, cell population selection, differential expression analysis, etc.) and constrains downstream reasoning with structured biological evidence.
AI.result: In an ablation study on hereditary chronic pancreatitis, SCTA's full evidence integration yielded the most stable target selection across independent runs among tested configurations while recovering biologically coherent, disease-relevant mechanisms validated in prior studies.
AI.conclusion: Decision-aware agent orchestration tailored to single-cell analysis structure can improve robustness, interpretability, and practical utility of target discovery in precision medicine.

title: Characterisation of Density-based FM generation methods in the context of Information Fusion
summary: Fuzzy Integral (FI) based aggregation provides a powerful mechanism for nuanced aggregation, for example, in ensemble approaches or decision-level fusion more generally. The main challenge of this approach is the appropriate parametrization of the Fuzzy Measure (FM), which captures the worths of the individual components--and their combinations--which are being fused. Here, widely used approaches including the Sugeno-$λ$ and Decomposable FMs, parametrize the FM by extrapolating from the densities, i.e. the weights associated with individual sources, while respecting the FM's monotonicity constraint. This paper articulates that this information is, in general, insufficient to uniquely identify a discrete FM; but shows how an interval-valued FM can indeed be determined uniquely. We proceed to show how the incorporation of additional information beyond the above, such as the choice of a specific FI and a dataset, then allows for obtaining even more specific interval-valued FMs. In practice, establishing the quality of an empirically determined FM is not trivial. To help address this, we show how the likelihood with which a resulting interval FM encompasses the `ideal', i.e. the commonly intangible, best, or ground-truth numeric FM, can be determined, producing a confidence interval at a given confidence level. Finally, based on a series of experiments, we demonstrate empirically that the Choquet FI output based on this FM can also be regarded as the confidence interval for the `ideal' information fusion result, providing a novel means to characterize FI fusion outcomes a priori and charting a pathway for future research.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the parameterization challenge of Fuzzy Measures (FMs) for Fuzzy Integral aggregation by showing how interval-valued FMs can be uniquely determined from limited information, providing confidence intervals for ideal fusion results.
AI.motivation: Fuzzy Integral aggregation is powerful for ensemble methods and decision fusion, but the main challenge is appropriately parameterizing the Fuzzy Measure. Traditional approaches using only density information (individual source weights) are insufficient to uniquely determine a discrete FM.
AI.method: Proposes using interval-valued FMs that can be uniquely determined from density information alone. Further incorporates additional information like specific FI choice and datasets to obtain more specific interval-valued FMs. Develops methods to calculate confidence intervals for how well determined interval FMs encompass the ideal FM.
AI.result: Shows that interval-valued FMs can be uniquely determined where traditional numeric FMs cannot. Demonstrates empirically that Choquet FI outputs based on these FMs can be regarded as confidence intervals for ideal fusion results. Provides a novel means to characterize FI fusion outcomes with confidence intervals.
AI.conclusion: The approach of using interval-valued FMs with confidence intervals provides a robust framework for handling uncertainty in Fuzzy Measure parameterization, offering a priori characterization of fusion outcomes and establishing a foundation for future research in confidence-aware fuzzy information fusion.

title: DriveDNA: A Large-Scale Multimodal Naturalistic Driving Dataset and Benchmark for Driving Style Identification
summary: Driving style captures stable, driver-specific patterns in how a vehicle is driven. In naturalistic data, however, this signal is hard to isolate because drivers are observed in different vehicles, on different roads, and under different conditions, so models may mistake vehicle- or situation-specific regularities for driver-specific style. We introduce DriveDNA, a large-scale naturalistic dataset and benchmark for personalized driving-style modeling, comprising 4,121 drives from 465 drivers across 115 vehicle models and totaling 975 hours of human-controlled driving at 10 Hz with forward video, collected from community drivers in everyday use. DriveDNA defines driving style as a consistent, driver-specific behavioral pattern in how a vehicle moves under similar conditions. The benchmark evaluates this signal through three core tasks: few-shot driver re-identification, personalized behavior prediction, and condition-matched comparison, and provides behavioral annotations plus 276,248 rule-generated maneuver events across six classes with large-scale human auditing. We evaluate baselines spanning classical descriptors, supervised and self-supervised time-series encoders, multimodal fusion, probabilistic prediction, and zero-shot foundation models under a fixed multi-seed protocol. Learned representations substantially outperform classical descriptors on unseen drivers (AUROC .935 vs. .707) and retain driver-specific information under matched driving conditions, while descriptor performance approaches chance. Video-only models achieve comparable re-identification accuracy but exhibit severe route leakage, showing that strong recognition may arise from contextual shortcuts rather than driving behavior. These findings show that reliable driving-style evaluation must assess both the behavioral value of learned representations and their robustness to vehicle, drive, and condition confounds.

AI.tldr: DriveDNA introduces a large-scale naturalistic dataset and benchmark for personalized driving-style modeling, enabling evaluation of driver-specific behavioral patterns while controlling for vehicle and situational confounds.
AI.motivation: Current driving style models struggle to isolate driver-specific patterns from vehicle- and situation-specific regularities in naturalistic data, as drivers are observed in different vehicles, roads, and conditions.
AI.method: Collected 4,121 drives from 465 drivers across 115 vehicle models (975 hours at 10Hz with video). Defined driving style as consistent driver-specific behavioral patterns under similar conditions. Created benchmark with three tasks: few-shot driver re-identification, personalized behavior prediction, and condition-matched comparison. Includes behavioral annotations and 276,248 rule-generated maneuver events with human auditing.
AI.result: Learned representations substantially outperform classical descriptors on unseen drivers (AUROC .935 vs. .707) and retain driver-specific information under matched conditions, while descriptor performance approaches chance. Video-only models achieve comparable re-identification but suffer from severe route leakage, showing contextual shortcuts rather than genuine driving behavior learning.
AI.conclusion: Reliable driving-style evaluation must assess both behavioral value of learned representations and their robustness to vehicle, drive, and condition confounds. The DriveDNA benchmark provides necessary controls to properly isolate driver-specific signals from contextual shortcuts.

title: CAPT: A Multi-task Continuous Autoregressive Transformer enabling Cross-dataset and Cross-species Transfer for Calcium Population Dynamics
summary: Large-scale calcium imaging has created an opportunity to build foundation-style models for neural population dynamics, but a central question remains unresolved: \textbf{whether a model pretrained on one collection of recordings can generalize to new datasets, experimental paradigms, and even species.} Existing approaches are often designed for specific tasks and evaluated on a single dataset, making it unclear whether their learned representations are reusable for new calcium trace datasets. To tackle this gap, we present \textbf{CAPT}, a \textbf{C}ontinuous \textbf{A}utoregressive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{T}ransformer for calcium population dynamics. CAPT models continuous calcium traces directly through a continuous patch tokenization strategy and is trained autoregressively, enabling end-to-end pretraining and adaptation to diverse downstream tasks. We first pretrain CAPT on a large-scale mouse calcium imaging dataset and evaluate its transferability across independent mouse, larval zebrafish, and \textit{C. elegans} datasets collected by different laboratories. In these transfer settings, the pretrained backbone is frozen and only adaptation modules are updated. Across neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks, CAPT consistently outperforms specialized and general-purpose baselines. Alongside predictive performance, multimodal analyses using NeuroPAL annotations in \textit{C. elegans} datasets show that CAPT embeddings form a shared functional space across datasets and capture anatomical cell-identity-related structure. These results suggest that the continuous autoregressive modeling opens up possibilities for a simple route towards general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging, which can generalize across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species.

AI.tldr: CAPT is a continuous autoregressive transformer for calcium population dynamics that demonstrates cross-dataset, cross-paradigm, and cross-species transferability in neural foundation models.
AI.motivation: Existing models for calcium imaging data are often task-specific and evaluated on single datasets, lacking generalizability across different datasets, experimental paradigms, and species. There's an unresolved question about whether foundation-style models can be pretrained on one collection of recordings and successfully transferred to new contexts.
AI.method: CAPT (Continuous Autoregressive Population Transformer) models continuous calcium traces directly using a continuous patch tokenization strategy with autoregressive training. The model is pretrained on large-scale mouse calcium imaging data, then evaluated in transfer settings where only adaptation modules are updated while the pretrained backbone remains frozen.
AI.result: CAPT outperforms specialized and general-purpose baselines across neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks. It demonstrates successful transfer across mouse, larval zebrafish, and C. elegans datasets from different labs. Multimodal analyses show that CAPT embeddings form a shared functional space across datasets and capture anatomical cell-identity-related structure.
AI.conclusion: Continuous autoregressive modeling provides a simple route toward general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging that can generalize across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species, addressing the critical transferability question in neural population dynamics modeling.

title: Latent-LoRA: Compact Latent-Space Adapters with Gradient-Free Routing for Continual Learning
summary: Large language models generalize well to individual tasks but lack an inherent mechanism for learning them sequentially, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To mitigate this, LoRA-based continual learning methods allocate a separate low-rank adapter per task, yet existing approaches either require task identity at inference or sum all adapters indiscriminately, letting irrelevant branches distort the output. Recent gating-based solutions route inputs to the correct adapter but introduce trainable parameters that themselves need protection against forgetting. In this work, we observe that pooled token embeddings from a frozen LLM embedding layer already separate task distributions throughout the learning sequence. A Gaussian mixture model fitted on these embeddings, without any gradient-based training, is sufficient for task-agnostic adapter selection at test time. This eliminates the need for a learned gating module. On the adapter side, constraining each task's parameters to the principal subspace of the pretrained weights via SVD yields a compact latent-space parameterization. Within this subspace, orthogonal regularization directly controls inter-task interference. The resulting system, Latent-LoRA, is replay-free, requires no trainable routing component, and uses substantially fewer parameters per task. Experiments across five model scales and two established continual learning benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance with near-zero forgetting.

AI.tldr: Latent-LoRA is a novel continual learning method for LLMs that uses token embeddings to identify tasks without training a gating module, and constrains adapter parameters to the principal subspace of pretrained weights to prevent forgetting.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. Existing LoRA-based continual learning methods either require task identity at inference or indiscriminately sum adapters, while gating-based solutions introduce trainable parameters that themselves need protection against forgetting.
AI.method: 1) Uses pooled token embeddings from a frozen LLM embedding layer to separate task distributions, fitting a Gaussian mixture model without gradient training for task-agnostic adapter selection. 2) Constrains each task's parameters to the principal subspace of pretrained weights via SVD for compact parameterization. 3) Applies orthogonal regularization within this subspace to control inter-task interference.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance across five model scales and two established continual learning benchmarks with near-zero forgetting. It's replay-free, requires no trainable routing component, and uses substantially fewer parameters per task.
AI.conclusion: Latent-LoRA effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting in LLMs by leveraging inherent task separation in token embeddings and principal subspace constraints, eliminating the need for complex gating mechanisms while maintaining performance with minimal parameter overhead.

title: SeekJudge: A Practical Reward Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Computer-Use Agents
summary: Deciding whether a trajectory actually fulfills its instruction governs how we measure computer-use agents on long-horizon graphical-user-interface tasks and how we train them with reinforcement learning. This judgment has long relied on rule-based evaluation, which struggles to align with human intention and goes stale when an app updates or its online content drifts. Existing model-based judges attempt to address these problems but still leave a performance gap to the rule-based evaluation. We propose the \textbf{SeekJudge} framework, in which four role-specialized agents, a Condense, a Ground, a Seek and an Analyze agent, reach a verdict through a Seek--Analyze loop over the trajectory. A seed-calibrated distillation pipeline trains one specialized $9$B model to serve as the shared backbone for all four agents. Measured by downstream success rate on held-out RL test goals, SeekJudge is the first practical model-based reward to match or surpass native rule-based supervision in online RL. Beyond accuracy, SeekJudge provides step-level judgments, runs far cheaper than a closed-source large model, and keeps a small per-call context that scales to much longer trajectories. We further contribute a general architectural improvement to the reward server that speeds up judging in RL. Together these make model-based reward a practical drop-in for rule-based supervision in CUA reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: SeekJudge is a framework using four specialized agents to judge computer-use agent trajectories, trained via distilled 9B model backbone, matching or surpassing rule-based evaluation for RL training while being cheaper and scalable.
AI.motivation: Rule-based trajectory evaluation for computer-use agents struggles with human intention alignment, becomes outdated with app updates/content drift, and existing model-based judges have performance gaps.
AI.method: Four role-specialized agents (Condense, Ground, Seek, Analyze) work in a Seek-Analyze loop; trained via seed-calibrated distillation pipeline using a shared 9B model backbone; includes architectural improvements for reward server.
AI.result: First practical model-based reward matching/surpassing native rule-based supervision on RL test goals; provides step-level judgments, runs cheaper than closed-source large models, maintains small context that scales to long trajectories.
AI.conclusion: SeekJudge makes model-based reward a practical drop-in replacement for rule-based supervision in computer-use agent reinforcement learning, with better accuracy, scalability, and cost-effectiveness.

title: Covariance Last-Layer Ensembles: Function-Space Diversity for Efficient Uncertainty Quantification
summary: A Last-Layer Ensemble (LLE), $K$ linear units on one shared frozen feature map, is an efficient single-pass approach to the disagreement-based epistemic uncertainty for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Its weakness is that members share the backbone gradient and can converge toward the same function, collapsing the inter-member diversity the signal depends on. Whether last-layer diversity can be restored, and what mitigates the collapse, is an open question. The weight-orthonormality defining Orthonormal Certificates (OC), the weight-orthonormal special case of the LLE, is only an indirect correction; it decorrelates the weights of the members, not their predictions. Here, we instead target the collapse directly in function space, with a Covariance Last-Layer Ensemble (cov-LLE) that places a direct covariance penalty on member activations. Cov-LLE restores the function-space diversity that weight-orthonormality cannot, and at matched $K$ recovers much of the diversity and calibration of a deep ensemble at $1\times$ backbone cost (in-distribution prediction variance $0.05\!\to\!9.3$ vs.\ $22.1$ ($\times10^{-3}$), and ECE $0.135\!\to\!0.090$ vs.\ $0.035$, for a $K\times$-cost deep ensemble), at no cost to accuracy. Viewing OC as a last-layer ensemble also organizes detectors into a two-axis taxonomy (by how their units are trained and how their outputs are scored) and exposes the OC score as a magnitude, motivating a scale-invariant, label-free direction score that repairs its near-OOD failure, adding $+0.16$ to $+0.18$ ROC AUC on every backbone.

AI.tldr: Covariance Last-Layer Ensemble (cov-LLE) adds direct covariance penalty on member activations to restore function-space diversity for better OOD detection, matching deep ensemble performance at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Last-Layer Ensembles (LLE) are efficient for epistemic uncertainty estimation but suffer from diversity collapse as members share backbone gradients and converge to similar functions, limiting OOD detection effectiveness.
AI.method: Introduces Covariance Last-Layer Ensemble (cov-LLE) that places direct covariance penalty on member activations in function space (not just weight orthonormality), and proposes scale-invariant direction score to improve OC detection.
AI.result: Cov-LLE restores function-space diversity that weight-orthonormality cannot, recovering deep ensemble diversity and calibration at 1× backbone cost (vs K× cost), with no accuracy loss. Direction score improves OC near-OOD detection by +0.16 to +0.18 ROC AUC.
AI.conclusion: Targeting collapse directly in function space via covariance penalty is effective for maintaining ensemble diversity, and reorganizing detectors reveals improvements to OC scoring for better near-OOD detection.

title: TopoFE: topology-aware LLM-guided Automated Feature Engineering
summary: Automatic feature engineering (AutoFE) for tabular learning can be naturally formulated as a program synthesis problem, where the objective is to discover predictive feature transformations from an exponentially large search space. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the expressiveness of AutoFE by enabling feature program generation beyond predefined operator libraries. However, existing LLM-based approaches remain fundamentally limited by stateless generation and homogeneous search: feature proposals are produced from static prompts without accumulating search experience, while single-population exploration quickly converges to dominant transformation patterns and rarely discovers complementary feature compositions across transformation families. We propose TOPOFE, a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework for LLM-guided feature engineering. TOPOFE combines family-specialized exploration, adaptive prompt memory, and topology-guided knowledge transfer to efficiently discover diverse and compositional feature programs. Experiments on 29 public tabular datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art AutoFE methods across classification and regression tasks. Beyond predictive performance, TOPOFE discovers more diverse and transferable feature programs that generalize across multiple downstream predictors and LLM backbones.

AI.tldr: TOPOFE is a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework that uses LLMs for automatic feature engineering, enabling more diverse and complementary feature program discovery compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based AutoFE approaches are limited by stateless generation (no accumulation of search experience) and homogeneous search (single-population exploration leading to convergence to dominant patterns, missing complementary feature compositions across different transformation families).
AI.method: TOPOFE combines family-specialized exploration, adaptive prompt memory, and topology-guided knowledge transfer in a multi-island evolutionary framework to efficiently discover diverse and compositional feature programs.
AI.result: Experiments on 29 public tabular datasets show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art AutoFE methods across classification and regression tasks. The method discovers more diverse and transferable feature programs that generalize across multiple downstream predictors and LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: TOPOFE addresses fundamental limitations in existing LLM-based AutoFE approaches by introducing an evolutionary framework with topology awareness and specialized exploration, enabling discovery of more diverse and complementary feature transformations.

title: Controllable Diversity in Normalization-Based Implicit Ensembles via Softmax-Temperature Modulation
summary: Deep ensembles provide the most reliable uncertainty estimates in deep learning, but their cost grows linearly with the number of members. Implicit ensembles lower this cost by sharing a single backbone across members. Member diversity is a primary determinant of ensemble quality, yet no implicit ensemble can shape it during training; existing methods fix it at initialisation or build it into the architecture. We introduce $σ$N-Ens, a normalisation-based implicit ensemble that treats each member as a task in a multi-task architecture and modulates the shared backbone through sigmoid-bounded scalers. We also introduce a softmax-temperature regulariser, which shapes the equilibrium level of sharing between members and traces the accuracy-calibration frontier. Because only normalisation layers are replicated, the mechanism can wrap convolutional and transformer backbones alike, also allowing pretrained models to be adapted through a short fine-tune. We frame the epistemic uncertainty such an ensemble expresses as modulation uncertainty, and explain why its calibration holds under input corruption, and why its out-of-distribution detection is weaker. Our method is evaluated across ResNets and transformers on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet and SST-2. $σ$N-Ens matches or outperforms deep ensembles at a fraction of their parameter cost, scales with ensemble size where partitioning methods collapse, and maintains calibration under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: σN-Ens is a normalization-based implicit ensemble method that treats each member as a task in multi-task architecture, using sigmoid-bounded scalers to modulate shared backbone, achieving deep ensemble performance at fraction of cost with better scaling and calibration under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Deep ensembles provide reliable uncertainty estimates but have linear cost growth with number of members. Implicit ensembles reduce cost by sharing backbone but cannot shape member diversity during training - existing methods either fix diversity at initialization or build it into architecture.
AI.method: Introduces σN-Ens, a normalization-based implicit ensemble where each member is treated as a task in multi-task architecture. Uses sigmoid-bounded scalers to modulate shared backbone through normalization layers. Only normalization layers are replicated, allowing method to wrap convolutional and transformer backbones. Includes softmax-temperature regularizer to shape equilibrium level of sharing between members and trace accuracy-calibration frontier.
AI.result: Evaluated across ResNets and transformers on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet and SST-2. σN-Ens matches or outperforms deep ensembles at fraction of parameter cost. Scales with ensemble size where partitioning methods collapse. Maintains calibration under distribution shift and holds calibration under input corruption (though OOD detection is weaker).
AI.conclusion: σN-Ens provides an effective implicit ensemble approach that addresses cost limitations of deep ensembles while maintaining performance and calibration. The method enables member diversity shaping during training through task-based architecture and can work with various backbones including pretrained models through fine-tuning.

title: RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning
summary: Rare diseases collectively affect an estimated 3.5% to 5.9% of the population, yet more than 70% of patients are misdiagnosed and many endure years of evaluation before a diagnosis is reached, because early presentations are nonspecific and relevant expertise is scarce and unevenly distributed. Artificial intelligence could provide support, but existing systems address isolated stages of care, overwhelmingly diagnosis. They typically depend on the results of downstream investigations, and they treat the variability between models as noise to be eliminated. Here we present RareLens, a system that supports clinical decision-making across the entire rare disease trajectory by exploiting this variability. When heterogeneous large language models evaluate the same case, they generate divergent but complementary reasoning, which RareLens aligns and calibrates into a single convergent, actionable decision at each stage. Four coordinated modules perform primary-visit risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis. Developed and evaluated on RareBench, a real-world dataset of 157,525 cases spanning all 33 Orphanet categories and more than 7,000 conditions, RareLens outperformed every frontier model tested, including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro, at each stage. It achieved an area under the curve of 0.917 for screening and top-1 accuracies of 65.5% and 89.8% for diagnosis and treatment. In an external study spanning 1,287 cases and 23 physicians, autonomous RareLens and physicians assisted by RareLens both substantially outperformed unaided physicians. These findings indicate that aligning divergent model reasoning, rather than scaling a single model, offers a generalizable strategy for high-uncertainty clinical decision-making.

AI.tldr: RareLens is an AI system that coordinates multiple LLMs to support rare disease decision-making across screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis, outperforming state-of-the-art models and unaided physicians.
AI.motivation: Rare diseases affect 3.5-5.9% of the population but face high misdiagnosis rates (70%) due to nonspecific early symptoms and scarce expertise. Existing AI systems focus only on diagnosis, treat model variability as noise, and depend on downstream investigations.
AI.method: RareLens exploits variability between heterogeneous LLMs by aligning and calibrating their divergent but complementary reasoning into convergent decisions. It uses four coordinated modules for risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis.
AI.result: On RareBench dataset (157,525 cases, 7,000+ conditions), RareLens outperformed GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro: AUC 0.917 for screening, top-1 accuracies 65.5% for diagnosis and 89.8% for treatment. In external study with 1,287 cases and 23 physicians, both autonomous RareLens and physician-assisted RareLens substantially outperformed unaided physicians.
AI.conclusion: Aligning divergent model reasoning rather than scaling a single model offers a generalizable strategy for high-uncertainty clinical decision-making, supporting the entire rare disease trajectory effectively.

title: XMix: Combating Extremely Noisy Labels via Local Smoothness in Self-Supervised Feature Space
summary: Supervised deep learning models rely on large, accurately labeled datasets, yet noisy annotations are often unavoidable and can severely degrade performance under high noise levels. Recent state-of-the-art methods tackle this by using sample selection strategies that exploit the memorization effect to filter out clean data for semi-supervised learning. However, these methods struggle with extreme noise, class imbalance, and require careful tuning or prior noise knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose XMix, a novel framework that leverages local smoothness in the self-supervised feature space to systematically enhance all stages of the sample selection process, without dependence on potentially corrupted labels. First, XMix estimates the noise rate using maximum likelihood among self-supervised feature neighbors. Second, these neighbors then help identify additional clean samples and ensure balanced selection across classes during sample selection. Finally, in the semi-supervised learning phase, XMix uses neighboring samples to generate more reliable pseudo-labels. Our empirical results show that XMix substantially outperforms existing methods in extremely noisy environments and maintains superior performance in standard LNL benchmarks.

AI.tldr: XMix is a novel framework that uses self-supervised feature space local smoothness to improve sample selection for learning with noisy labels, outperforming existing methods especially in extreme noise conditions.
AI.motivation: Supervised deep learning models require large accurately labeled datasets, but noisy annotations are common and degrade performance, especially at high noise levels. Existing sample selection methods struggle with extreme noise, class imbalance, and require careful tuning or prior noise knowledge.
AI.method: XMix leverages local smoothness in self-supervised feature space to enhance all stages of sample selection: 1) estimates noise rate using maximum likelihood among feature neighbors, 2) uses neighbors to identify additional clean samples and ensure balanced class selection, 3) generates more reliable pseudo-labels using neighboring samples in semi-supervised learning phase.
AI.result: XMix substantially outperforms existing methods in extremely noisy environments and maintains superior performance in standard Learning with Noisy Labels (LNL) benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The XMix framework effectively addresses limitations of existing sample selection methods by using self-supervised feature space information to improve noise rate estimation, sample selection balance, and pseudo-label reliability, making it robust to extreme noise without dependence on corrupted labels.

title: Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving
summary: Investigating how affective states such as confusion and frustration persist and transition during co-situated collaborative problem solving (CPS) is important for understanding the dynamics of epistemic emotions. However, the accurate identification of affective states remain challenging as there is no gold-standard truth in this space. Here, we analyze affective states collected through retrospective cued-recall during an in-person CPS task. Using ordered network analysis (ONA), we examine (1) the overall ordered structure of affective states and how this structure differs across self-caught and probe-caught reporting methods, and (2) what aspects of this ordered structure are emphasized differently in slower and faster groups. We find that ONA reveals differences in persistence and transition patterns that are not apparent from descriptive summaries alone. In particular, we observe a stable epistemic core linking curiosity, optimism, and confusion, with different reporting methods emphasizing different connections among states. An analysis between faster and slower groups show that roles of confusion and disengagement also shift significantly during collaboration, particularly in their relationship to conflict. We interpret our findings in the context of collaboration and discuss their implications in developing AI systems that support CPS.

AI.tldr: ONA reveals affective state dynamics in collaborative problem solving - shows stable epistemic core of curiosity, optimism, confusion, with reporting methods and group speed revealing different patterns.
AI.motivation: Understanding how affective states like confusion and frustration persist and transition during collaborative problem solving is important for understanding epistemic emotions dynamics, but accurate identification is challenging due to lack of gold-standard truth.
AI.method: Ordered network analysis (ONA) applied to affective states collected through retrospective cued-recall during in-person CPS tasks, comparing self-caught vs probe-caught reporting methods and faster vs slower groups.
AI.result: ONA reveals differences in persistence and transition patterns not apparent from descriptive summaries; stable epistemic core linking curiosity, optimism, confusion; different reporting methods emphasize different connections; confusion and disengagement roles shift significantly between faster/slower groups, particularly in relation to conflict.
AI.conclusion: Findings provide insights into affective dynamics in collaboration, with implications for developing AI systems that support collaborative problem solving.

title: A Coulomb Particle Model for Learning Kernel Attention in Transformers
comment: Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics (HiLD), ICML 2026
summary: Randomized features provide a scalable approximation to kernel machines, but their performance depends strongly on the choice of feature distribution. We propose a particle-based method that learns this distribution by optimizing kernel-target alignment while regularizing particles with a Riesz/Coulomb repulsive potential. The resulting Hamiltonian yields diverse, task-adaptive random features and admits a mean-field description through a McKean--Vlasov equation. We instantiate the method in linearized Transformer attention by learning positive random-feature maps in a first alignment phase, then freezing the kernel and training the remaining network parameters with cross-entropy. Experiments on synthetic classification and sentence-level benchmarks show that learned kernelized attention can improve accuracy, calibration, and robustness for several feature maps while preserving linear-attention inference complexity.

AI.tldr: A particle-based method learns task-adaptive random feature distributions by optimizing kernel-target alignment with repulsive regularization, applied to linearized Transformer attention for improved performance while maintaining linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Randomized features provide scalable kernel approximations, but their performance depends heavily on feature distribution selection. Current methods lack adaptive, task-specific feature distributions.
AI.method: Propose particle-based optimization of feature distributions using kernel-target alignment with Riesz/Coulomb repulsive regularization. Use Hamiltonian dynamics yielding a McKean-Vlasov mean-field description. Apply to linearized Transformers: first learn positive random-feature maps via alignment, then freeze kernel and train remaining parameters with cross-entropy.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic classification and sentence-level benchmarks show improved accuracy, calibration, and robustness across feature maps while preserving linear-attention inference complexity.
AI.conclusion: The method enables learning diverse, task-adaptive random features that enhance linearized Transformer attention performance without increasing computational complexity.

title: ESF-Bench: Benchmarking Challenging Slot-Filling Scenarios for Real-World Enterprise Applications
summary: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has driven transformative adoption across enterprises. However, deploying these models in real-world settings presents unique challenges due to complex system constraints and unexpected user behaviors. Among these applications, slot filling is essential for converting unstructured input into structured, actionable data. In this work, we introduce ESF-Bench, a challenging Enterprise Slot Filling benchmark consisting of 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots over 8 unique domains. Curated using a taxonomy of the 57 most challenging slot-filling scenarios observed during real-world enterprise deployments, ESF-Bench exposes notable limitations in current state-of-the-art LLMs, with GPT-OSS-120b low successfully extracting slots for only 20.7% of benchmark samples. To support continued research in this area, we publicly release the benchmark dataset, taxonomy, and accompanying evaluation code on GitHub.
