AI.tldr: ESF-Bench is a challenging enterprise slot filling benchmark with 810 multi-turn samples across 8 domains, revealing current LLMs only successfully extract slots for 20.7% of samples.
AI.motivation: While large language models are widely adopted in enterprises, deploying them for slot filling (converting unstructured input to structured data) faces challenges due to complex system constraints and unexpected user behaviors in real-world settings.
AI.method: Created ESF-Bench, a benchmark consisting of 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots over 8 unique domains, curated using a taxonomy of 57 most challenging slot-filling scenarios observed during real-world enterprise deployments.
AI.result: ESF-Bench exposes notable limitations in current state-of-the-art LLMs, with GPT-4-120b successfully extracting slots for only 20.7% of benchmark samples, showing significant room for improvement.
AI.conclusion: The research highlights the gap between current LLM capabilities and enterprise slot filling requirements, and the authors publicly release the benchmark dataset, taxonomy, and evaluation code to support continued research in this area.

title: Flash-CNNCap: Capacitance Extraction via Image Mapping
summary: We present Flash-CNNCap, a CNN-based capacitance extractor that reformulates full-matrix capacitance prediction as image-to-image regression over spatial contribution maps. Prior scalar CNN-based extractors require $O(n^2)$ forward passes to recover all pairwise capacitances in a window with $n$ conductors. Flash-CNNCap replaces the scalar target with dense contribution maps: a total-capacitance model and a master-conditioned coupling model each predict a spatial map that is reduced to conductor-level values through mask aggregation, cutting full-matrix reconstruction to $O(n)$ passes. The resulting totals and symmetrized pairwise couplings define the corresponding Maxwell-style capacitance matrix under the standard off-diagonal sign convention. The maps are learned from conductor-level labels without per-pixel supervision. An ablation study over 13 model configurations selects a U-Net that matches ResNet baselines on total capacitance (1.5-3.1% MARE) and achieves the strongest coupling accuracy (3.0-4.6% MARE) across all evaluated CapBench subsets, with a $17.5\times$ full-matrix speedup on windows containing 134 conductors on average. A deployed pipeline reads Design Exchange Format (DEF) geometry and writes Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) output, processing 1,024 windows in 51.23 seconds with a $4.4\times$ speedup over OpenRCX on the same benchmark. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/THU-numbda/flash-cnncap.

AI.tldr: Flash-CNNCap: A CNN-based capacitance extractor that predicts full capacitance matrices in O(n) passes instead of O(n²) by reformulating prediction as image-to-image regression over spatial contribution maps.
AI.motivation: Previous CNN-based capacitance extractors require O(n²) forward passes to compute all pairwise capacitances for n conductors, which is computationally expensive. There's a need for faster full-matrix capacitance extraction to accelerate circuit parasitic analysis in chip design.
AI.method: Reformulates full-matrix capacitance prediction as image-to-image regression using spatial contribution maps. Uses two models: a total-capacitance model and a master-conditioned coupling model that predict spatial maps, which are then reduced to conductor-level values through mask aggregation. Employs a U-Net architecture learned from conductor-level labels without per-pixel supervision.
AI.result: Achieves 1.5-3.1% MARE on total capacitance (matching ResNet baselines) and 3.0-4.6% MARE on coupling capacitance. Provides 17.5× speedup on full-matrix extraction for windows with ~134 conductors, and 4.4× speedup over OpenRCX processing 1,024 windows in 51.23 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Flash-CNNCap demonstrates efficient full-matrix capacitance extraction with significant speed improvements over previous methods while maintaining accuracy. The approach enables practical deployment for parasitic extraction in chip design with available code and models.

title: Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation
comment: 43 pages, 9 figures. Working paper v3.13.0. Benchmark data, rule encodings and per-case result artefacts: https://github.com/Aethis-ai/confidently-wrong-benchmark
summary: We document a failure class in frontier large language models -- exception chain collapse -- observed in eligibility evaluation under nested conditional rules of the form "A is required UNLESS B applies, UNLESS C overrides B". The failure reproduces at first observation, but its empirical surface is unstable: between March and April 2026 several failure cells closed silently under the same model alias, with no version bump (GPT-5.4 on construction insurance moved from 96.6% to 100%, same prompt and harness). For regulated workflows, frontier-model accuracy is a moving compliance boundary that shifts without notice. We present the Aethis Eligibility Module, a neuro-symbolic architecture in which LLMs author rules from authoritative sources and an SMT-based layer executes them deterministically, consistent with the authored specification regardless of model drift, reasoning-effort defaults, or prompt format. Three evidence bases: (i) a controlled benchmark of 225 scenarios across four regulatory domains documents the pattern and, in replication, the drift that partially closed it; (ii) a 20-scenario adversarial extension on construction insurance, where the engine scores 20/20, as does one of four frontier configurations (GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort), while the other three, including Anthropic's strongest model at evaluation time, fail the same coverage-gap edge case; (iii) external validation on nine peer-reviewed LegalBench tasks, 949 held-out cases, where the engine is significantly more accurate than all three frontier models (combined McNemar's p <= 0.003), with margins up to +41 points on the curated multi-prong tasks against the Anthropic models. The contribution is to relocate uncertainty from the inference boundary, where it is silent, to the specification boundary, where it is deliberate and audited. All scenarios, rule encodings, and results are public and reproducible.

AI.tldr: Exception chain collapse is a failure class in frontier LLMs where models incorrectly evaluate eligibility under nested conditional rules (A unless B, unless C). The paper introduces a neuro-symbolic system that separates rule authoring (by LLMs) from deterministic execution (by SMT solver) to provide stable, auditable compliance boundaries.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs exhibit unstable accuracy in regulatory compliance scenarios, with silent performance changes that create moving compliance boundaries. For regulated workflows, this unpredictability is unacceptable as it shifts compliance standards without notice.
AI.method: Propose Aethis Eligibility Module: a neuro-symbolic architecture where LLMs author rules from authoritative sources, and an SMT-based layer executes them deterministically. This separates specification from inference, ensuring consistent execution regardless of model drift or prompt variations.
AI.result: 1) Benchmark of 225 scenarios shows pattern and silent drift; 2) 20-scenario adversarial extension shows engine perfect (20/20) vs variable LLM performance; 3) LegalBench validation on 949 cases shows engine significantly outperforms frontier models (p≤0.003), up to +41 points on multi-prong tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully relocates uncertainty from the inference boundary (where it's silent and unstable) to the specification boundary (where it's deliberate and audited), providing deterministic compliance for regulated workflows. All materials are public for reproducibility.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Predicting Nitrous Oxide Flux
summary: Nitrous oxide (N$_2$O) is the dominant ozone-depleting substance emitted in the 21st century, and the third largest contributor to anthropogenic greenhouse gases due to its high potency and long atmospheric lifetime, with more than 70% of N$_2$O emissions occurring as a result of agricultural processes. Current approaches to predicting N$_2$O flux emissions include process-based models such as DayCent and Cycles, as well as classical AI models, but the application of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to predicting N$_2$O flux emissions is largely underexplored. Our paper draws upon the mechanistic equations that underlie the DayCent family of process-based models to construct a rigorously derived, literature-traceable physics residual. We then build and train an MLP-based PINN on a multi-site agricultural dataset spanning four geographically distinct US agricultural sites. Across all tested values of the physics loss weighting hyperparameter $λ$, our PINN consistently and substantially outperformed uncalibrated Cycles simulation (R$^2=0.01$), with our MLP baseline achieving mean R$^2=0.411$ across ten random seeds. Physics constraints consistently degrade model performance in holdout validation, with marginal degradation at low $λ$ and significant degradation at high $λ$, but consistently improve model performance and reduce performance variability in leave-one-site-out validation. This suggests that physics constraints sacrifice in-distribution accuracy for out-of-distribution robustness, anchoring the model toward biogeochemically plausible behavior on unfamiliar soil conditions --- though cross-site generalization remains challenging, with negative R$^2$ across all seeds and $λ$ values on our geographically distinct held-out site.

AI.tldr: Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) for N2O flux prediction using agricultural data shows physics constraints degrade in-distribution accuracy but improve out-of-distribution robustness, though cross-site generalization remains challenging.
AI.motivation: N2O is a major ozone-depleting substance and greenhouse gas, mostly from agriculture. Current prediction methods (process-based models, classical AI) have limitations, and PINNs are underexplored for N2O flux prediction.
AI.method: Used mechanistic equations from DayCent models to create physics residual, built MLP-based PINN trained on multi-site US agricultural dataset with varying physics loss weighting hyperparameter λ, compared to baseline MLP and uncalibrated Cycles simulation.
AI.result: PINNs consistently outperformed uncalibrated Cycles (R²=0.01). MLP baseline achieved mean R²=0.411. Physics constraints degraded in-distribution performance but improved out-of-distribution robustness in leave-one-site-out validation. Cross-site generalization remained poor with negative R².
AI.conclusion: Physics constraints sacrifice in-distribution accuracy for out-of-distribution robustness, anchoring models toward biogeochemically plausible behavior on unfamiliar conditions, but significant challenges remain for cross-site generalization of N2O flux predictions.

title: Key-Interval A*: Accelerating Grid Pathfinding via Structural Abstraction
summary: Existing exact methods for 4-connected grid pathfinding reduce online search, but often either retain fine-grained search states or require substantial preprocessing. This paper presents Key-Interval A* (KIA*), an optimal pathfinding algorithm that uses lightweight preprocessing to construct and search over a compact interval-level abstraction of free space. KIA* represents free space using intervals: maximal contiguous runs of traversable cells. It extracts key intervals that capture structural boundary changes and connects them through contiguous non-key regions. KIA* then performs A*-style search on the resulting key-interval graph and constructively reconstructs grid paths from interval chains, without cell-level local search. We prove the completeness and optimality of KIA* on 4-connected grids. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that KIA* preserves exact shortest-path lengths and achieves the fastest runtime on seven of eight benchmark groups, with the largest gains on structured and game maps.

AI.tldr: KIA* (Key-Interval A*) is an optimal 4-connected grid pathfinding algorithm that uses lightweight preprocessing to create an interval-level abstraction of free space, enabling faster search while preserving exact shortest-path lengths.
AI.motivation: Existing exact methods for 4-connected grid pathfinding either retain fine-grained search states (inefficient online) or require substantial preprocessing (burdensome). There's a need for a method that balances preprocessing overhead with efficient online search performance.
AI.method: KIA* represents traversable space using intervals (maximal contiguous runs of traversable cells). It extracts key intervals that capture structural boundary changes, connects them through contiguous non-key regions to create a key-interval graph, then performs A*-style search on this compact abstraction and reconstructs grid paths from interval chains without cell-level local search.
AI.result: KIA* preserves exact shortest-path lengths (proven completeness and optimality) and achieves fastest runtime on 7 out of 8 benchmark groups, with largest performance gains on structured and game maps.
AI.conclusion: KIA* successfully bridges the gap between fine-grained search and heavy preprocessing approaches, providing an optimal pathfinding solution that is both theoretically sound (proven complete and optimal) and practically efficient (fastest on most benchmarks), particularly effective for structured environments.

title: ADVERSARIAL: And-Inverter Graph-Assisted Hardware Trojan Detection At Scale
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication at the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: Modern System-on-Chip (SoCs) often contain hundreds of millions to tens of billions of gates, making existing Hardware Trojan (HT) detection methods impractical due to their immense scale. The proposed approach incorporates symbolically enabled learning by modeling flattened gate-level netlists as Boolean networks represented as And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs), where all internal nodes are 2-input AND gates and inversions reside on the edges. Each directed connection is expressed as a triple within a Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) framework, producing compact, constant-size per-node representations that retain multi-hop structural context. The AIG's bounded fan-in and uniform semantics ensure training and inference complexity scale linearly with edge count, addressing major scalability bottlenecks in HT detection. Symbolically enabled learning across deep datapaths enables the model to differentiate circuit structures from rare and functionally inconsistent connections that signify potential Trojan triggers and payloads. Experiments on large-scale SoC benchmarks demonstrate clear geometric separation between Trojan and benign nodes and practical scalability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable Hardware Trojan detection method using Knowledge Graph Embeddings on And-Inverter Graphs, achieving linear complexity and effective separation of Trojan nodes in large SoCs.
AI.motivation: Modern SoCs contain hundreds of millions to billions of gates, making existing Hardware Trojan detection methods impractical due to scalability issues. Current approaches struggle with the immense scale of modern circuits.
AI.method: The method models flattened gate-level netlists as Boolean networks using And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs). It represents each directed connection as a triple within a Knowledge Graph Embedding framework, producing compact, constant-size per-node representations. Symbolically enabled learning across deep datapaths allows differentiation between circuit structures and suspicious connections.
AI.result: Experiments show clear geometric separation between Trojan and benign nodes in large-scale SoC benchmarks. The method achieves practical scalability with training and inference complexity that scales linearly with edge count, addressing previous scalability bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a scalable solution for Hardware Trojan detection in large-scale SoCs by leveraging Knowledge Graph Embeddings on AIGs, enabling effective identification of Trojan triggers and payloads while maintaining linear complexity.

title: Inference-Time Consensus for Mitigating Hidden Behaviors from LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent work shows that fine-tuning language models on even a small amount of poisoned data can install targeted misbehavior, and ostensibly benign data can transmit hidden preferences that generalize broadly. Standard defenses, such as data filtering, mixing in harmless data, and regularization, attenuate these effects but do not eliminate them. We instead pursue robustness through redundancy: collecting multiple datasets from different sources and only learning what is common between them. Thus, if only a subset of sources are malicious, the misbehavior will be blocked. In order to implement this defense strategy, we fine-tune a separate reference model on each source's dataset and aggregate their next-token distributions at decoding time. We introduce two consensus decoders: a token-wise minimum, which caps each token at the lowest probability any source assigns, and a base-relative variant, which reverts to the base probability on any token the sources move in opposing directions. We further relax exact agreement to tolerate partial support across sources and different surface expressions of the same intention. Across controlled poisoning tasks, subliminal learning, and emergent misalignment, consensus decoding suppresses source-specific misbehavior while preserving shared desirable behavior, including cases where union training and weight averaging retain the unwanted behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes consensus decoding as a defense against data poisoning in language model fine-tuning, using redundancy across multiple datasets to block malicious behavior while preserving desirable shared behavior.
AI.motivation: Recent research shows that even small amounts of poisoned data during fine-tuning can install targeted misbehavior in language models, and hidden preferences can transmit through ostensibly benign data. Standard defenses like data filtering, mixing in harmless data, and regularization only attenuate but don't eliminate these effects.
AI.method: The authors propose robustness through redundancy: collecting multiple datasets from different sources and learning only what's common between them. They fine-tune separate reference models on each source's dataset and aggregate their next-token distributions at decoding time. They introduce two consensus decoders: 1) token-wise minimum (caps each token at the lowest probability any source assigns), and 2) base-relative variant (reverts to base probability on any token the sources move in opposing directions). They further relax exact agreement to tolerate partial support across sources and different surface expressions of the same intention.
AI.result: Across controlled poisoning tasks, subliminal learning, and emergent misalignment, consensus decoding suppresses source-specific misbehavior while preserving shared desirable behavior. This approach works in cases where union training and weight averaging retain the unwanted behavior.
AI.conclusion: Consensus decoding provides an effective defense strategy against data poisoning by leveraging redundancy across multiple data sources. It successfully blocks malicious behavior when only a subset of sources are compromised, while maintaining the shared desirable behaviors that all clean sources agree upon.

title: WorldDiT: A Unified Diffusion Architecture for World and Action Modeling
summary: Many recent robot policies pursue stronger control by using large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as the action backbone. We introduce WorldDiT, a unified diffusion transformer architecture that couples action generation with visual world modeling and achieves strong performance without a large pretrained VLM action backbone. During training, a single diffusion transformer generates continuous action chunks and predicts normalized RGB patch targets from future camera frames. Across four LIBERO simulation suites, WorldDiT lies on the reported Pareto frontier for total model parameters and mean success among methods reporting all four suites. These results provide a strong sub-billion-parameter baseline for future scaling studies.

AI.tldr: WorldDiT is a unified diffusion transformer that generates robot actions while predicting future visual patches, achieving strong performance without large pretrained vision-language models, providing an efficient baseline for future scaling.
AI.motivation: Recent robot policies rely heavily on large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as action backbones, which can be computationally expensive. The authors aim to create a more efficient approach that doesn't depend on these large VLMs while maintaining strong performance.
AI.method: WorldDiT uses a single diffusion transformer architecture that couples action generation with visual world modeling. It generates continuous action chunks while simultaneously predicting normalized RGB patch targets from future camera frames, enabling joint learning of action and visual prediction.
AI.result: WorldDiT achieves strong performance across four LIBERO simulation suites and lies on the reported Pareto frontier for both total model parameters and mean success rate. It provides a sub-billion-parameter baseline that competes with methods using larger pretrained VLMs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed WorldDiT demonstrates that strong robot control performance can be achieved without reliance on large pretrained VLMs, offering a computationally efficient alternative that maintains competitive performance and serves as a solid baseline for future scaling studies.

title: NeurGO: Learning to Generate Elite Candidates for Meta-Black-Box Expensive Optimization
summary: Expensive black-box optimization is ubiquitous in science and engineering, where function evaluations are costly and the evaluation budget is limited. Traditional evolutionary algorithms and Meta-BlackBox Optimization (MetaBBO) approaches typically consume most evaluations on candidate selection, often wasting precious budget on inferior solutions. Although surrogate-assisted evolution and Bayesian optimization aim to reduce evaluations through surrogate models, constructing an accurate global model from limited data remains challenging, and model bias can easily trap the search in local optima. To overcome these limitations, we propose NeurGO, a generative MetaBBO framework that directly synthesizes elite candidates from historical population states. Specifically, we employ an attention-based encoder to capture the population-level search trend and condition a decoder on this representation to generate high-quality candidates, avoiding the expensive evaluation of large offspring pools. We then design a quality-diversity loss to maintain solution quality and population diversity throughout the search. Through extensive benchmarking on CEC 2008 and the COCO BBOB test suites, our method achieves better optimization performance under the same evaluation budget and exhibits faster convergence.

AI.tldr: NeurGO is a generative meta-black-box optimization framework that uses attention-based neural networks to directly synthesize elite candidates from historical population states, avoiding expensive evaluations of large candidate pools and achieving better optimization with limited evaluation budgets.
AI.motivation: Traditional evolutionary algorithms and MetaBBO approaches waste precious evaluation budgets on inferior solutions during candidate selection. While surrogate-assisted methods and Bayesian optimization aim to reduce evaluations, constructing accurate global models from limited data is challenging and model bias can trap searches in local optima.
AI.method: Proposes NeurGO, a generative MetaBBO framework with attention-based encoder to capture population-level search trends, conditions a decoder on this representation to generate high-quality candidates directly, and employs quality-diversity loss to maintain both solution quality and population diversity.
AI.result: Extensive benchmarking on CEC 2008 and COCO BBOB test suites shows NeurGO achieves better optimization performance under the same evaluation budget and exhibits faster convergence compared to other methods.
AI.conclusion: NeurGO successfully overcomes limitations of traditional evolutionary algorithms and surrogate methods by directly generating elite candidates from population states, effectively reducing wasted evaluations and achieving superior optimization performance with limited budgets in expensive black-box optimization problems.

title: Greedy dynamical meta-learning
summary: Gradient descent scales well to large models, but becomes unstable over long time horizons. Gradient-free optimizers can scale to arbitrary timespans, but are hobbled by high dimensions. Since learning occurs in large models over long timescales, neither of these approaches is likely to produce traits which can accelerate the learning process. Instead, we propose a meta-learning algorithm in which the agent learns to modify its own weights and biases. Our algorithm consists of an inner loop, wherein the agent performs some high-dimensional optimization upon itself, and an outer loop, wherein we perform some low-dimensional optimization upon the inner loop. Since the outer loop handles very few parameters, standard zeroth-order methods may be used.

AI.tldr: A meta-learning algorithm where agents learn to modify their own weights and biases through a two-loop optimization process to accelerate learning in large models over long timescales.
AI.motivation: Existing optimization methods have limitations: gradient descent becomes unstable over long time horizons, while gradient-free optimizers struggle with high dimensions. Neither approach is effective for learning in large models over extended timescales.
AI.method: The proposed algorithm uses a two-loop optimization process: an inner loop where the agent performs high-dimensional optimization on itself (modifying its own weights and biases), and an outer loop where low-dimensional optimization is performed on the inner loop parameters.
AI.result: The approach enables stable optimization over long timescales while handling high-dimensional parameter spaces, as the outer loop has few parameters that can be optimized using standard zeroth-order methods.
AI.conclusion: This meta-learning framework addresses the limitations of both gradient descent and gradient-free optimization by combining high-dimensional self-modification with low-dimensional meta-optimization, potentially accelerating learning in large-scale models.

title: DECAF: De-Clustering for Adaptive Representational Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning, which aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model, is a key requirement for privacy, accountability, and adaptive deployment. We argue that many unlearning methods are vulnerable to a simple clustering attack, which can recover class structure in an unsupervised manner, limiting their suitability for continual deployment where removal requests must be handled reliably on demand. To address this, we propose DECAF (DE-Clustering for Adaptive Forgetting), a post-hoc method that operates only on the forget set and is designed to break the cluster. DECAF combines input noise, confidence suppression, and entropy-based output diversification to disrupt the residual feature-space structure associated with forgotten data. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, DECAF attains 0.10% forget-class accuracy, 79.4% retain accuracy, and an AUS of 0.88, surpassing all other baselines. In cluster-based analysis, it attains performance comparable to that of unlearning methods that use the full training set, while being significantly more efficient. Code: https://github.com/ale256/representation_unlearning.

AI.tldr: DECAF is a post-hoc machine unlearning method that breaks residual feature clusters of forgotten data using input noise, confidence suppression, and entropy-based diversification to prevent clustering attacks, achieving state-of-the-art forgetting performance with high efficiency.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning methods need to reliably remove specific training data influences for privacy and accountability. Existing methods are vulnerable to clustering attacks that can recover class structure, limiting their suitability for continual deployment where removal requests must be handled reliably on demand.
AI.method: DECAF is a post-hoc unlearning method that operates only on the forget set. It combines three techniques: (1) input noise to disrupt features, (2) confidence suppression to reduce prediction certainty, and (3) entropy-based output diversification to break residual feature-space clusters associated with forgotten data.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, DECAF achieves 0.10% forget-class accuracy, 79.4% retain accuracy, and an AUS (Area Under the Curve) of 0.88, surpassing all other baselines. It achieves performance comparable to full training set methods while being significantly more efficient in cluster-based analysis.
AI.conclusion: DECAF effectively addresses clustering attack vulnerabilities in machine unlearning, providing reliable forgetting through targeted disruption of residual feature-space structures, making it suitable for continual deployment scenarios requiring on-demand data removal.

title: Do LLMs Know Their Vulnerable Scenarios?
summary: Safety-aligned large language models are trained to refuse harmful requests, yet embedding the same requests in particular scenarios can bypass their safeguards. Existing red-teaming methods empirically identify effective scenarios through observed attack outcomes, but why particular scenarios weaken refusal remains mechanistically unclear. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability studies have characterized both refusal directions and jailbreak-associated features, without explaining the relationship between the two representations. In this work, we show that scenario-wrapped prompts activate internal scenario directions whose causal steering consistently reduces refusal scores. Building on this finding, we propose \textsc{Concept2Scenario}, a concept-based attribution framework for vulnerable scenario discovery. It instantiates a broad concept space with a sparse autoencoder, attributes refusal suppression to individual concepts, translates the identified concepts into interpretable natural-language scenarios, and identifies synergistic scenario combinations through interaction attribution. Across three open-source models, two safety benchmarks, and six black-box jailbreak methods, the discovered scenarios serve as reusable priors that improve average attack success rates by up to $18.2$ percentage points. They also transfer to GPT-5, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash, suggesting that some scenario-level refusal vulnerabilities are shared across model families. Moreover, the identified combinations outperform their individual constituents and enable iterative attacks to succeed in fewer turns.

AI.tldr: A new framework called Concept2Scenario identifies vulnerable scenarios that bypass LLM safety filters by attributing refusal suppression to individual concepts, translating them to natural-language scenarios, and discovering synergistic combinations to improve jailbreak success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing red-teaming methods empirically identify effective scenarios for jailbreaking LLM safety filters but don't explain why particular scenarios weaken refusal mechanisms mechanistically. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability studies have characterized refusal directions without explaining their relationship to jailbreak-associated features.
AI.method: The Concept2Scenario framework: 1) Shows scenario-wrapped prompts activate internal scenario directions that reduce refusal scores, 2) Instantiates a broad concept space with sparse autoencoder, 3) Attributes refusal suppression to individual concepts, 4) Translates concepts to interpretable natural-language scenarios, 5) Identifies synergistic scenario combinations through interaction attribution.
AI.result: The discovered scenarios improve average attack success rates by up to 18.2 percentage points across three open-source models, two safety benchmarks, and six black-box jailbreak methods. They transfer to GPT-5, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash, suggesting shared scenario-level vulnerabilities across model families. The identified combinations outperform individual constituents and enable iterative attacks with fewer turns.
AI.conclusion: The Concept2Scenario framework provides a mechanistic understanding of how scenarios bypass LLM safety filters by linking internal concept representations to refusal vulnerabilities, offering reusable priors for more effective jailbreaking that transfer across different model architectures.

title: Variational Boosting for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve differential equations by minimizing the residual of a nonlinear operator over a neural parameterization of the solution. However, monolithic PINNs often suffer from ill-conditioning, spectral bias, and optimization instability.
  We introduce a variational boosting framework in which solutions are constructed additively in function space. Each stage trains a weak learner whose converged correction satisfies a local orthogonality condition, equivalent to a projected functional gradient descent step onto the tangent space of the network's function manifold. Because each correction network is deliberately small, the restricted minimization admits full Newton or conjugate gradient updates, which are typically infeasible in large PINNs. The resulting method separates global nonlinear refinement into a sequence of well-conditioned subproblems while preserving the full variational structure of the operator.
  This framework provides a geometric interpretation of multi-stage PINNs as projected functional gradient descent and enables stable second-order optimization for nonlinear differential equations.

AI.tldr: A variational boosting framework for Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) that addresses ill-conditioning and optimization issues by constructing solutions additively using small correction networks with second-order optimization methods.
AI.motivation: Monolithic PINNs suffer from ill-conditioning, spectral bias, and optimization instability, which hinders their effectiveness in solving differential equations.
AI.method: Introduces a variational boosting framework where solutions are constructed additively in function space. Each stage trains a small "weak learner" correction network using projected functional gradient descent onto the tangent space, enabling full Newton or conjugate gradient updates that are typically infeasible in large PINNs.
AI.result: The method separates global nonlinear refinement into a sequence of well-conditioned subproblems while preserving the full variational structure of the operator, enabling stable second-order optimization for nonlinear differential equations.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a geometric interpretation of multi-stage PINNs as projected functional gradient descent and enables more stable and efficient optimization for solving differential equations compared to monolithic PINNs.

title: Delegation Intelligence in Deep Search: A Controllable Framework for Disentangled Capability Diagnosis
summary: Deep search is becoming a core capability of modern agent systems, yet it is typically evaluated solely based on end-to-end answer accuracy. This coupled evaluation paradigm entangles retrieval quality, long-context comprehension, evidence verification, and tool-use decisions, making it difficult to determine whether a model truly knows when and how to delegate information seeking to search. To this end: (1) We formalize this meta-capability as Delegation Intelligence in deep search and decompose it into complementary dimensions-Search Decision-Making (recognizing information insufficiency and deciding whether, when, and how to search) and Information Synthesis and Verification (aggregating evidence from multiple sources, judging source reliability, and synthesizing information under noisy, potentially adversarial conditions). (2) To enable disentangled and reproducible measurement, we develop a controllable synthesis pipeline built on document-grounded reverse engineering. This yields a general recipe for constructing controlled deep-search evaluations rather than a single fixed dataset. (3) As a concrete instantiation, we construct DelegSearchBench, together with a disentangled evaluation protocol that isolates each capability dimension by varying document composition and tool access. (4) Across representative models, we demonstrate that deep-search competence cannot be adequately characterized by final-answer accuracy alone...

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Delegation Intelligence for deep search, decomposes it into search decision-making and information synthesis dimensions, develops a controlled synthesis pipeline, creates DelegSearchBench for disentangled evaluation, and shows that end-to-end accuracy alone is insufficient to assess deep-search capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current deep search evaluations rely solely on end-to-end answer accuracy, which entangles multiple capabilities (retrieval quality, long-context comprehension, evidence verification, tool-use decisions). This makes it difficult to determine if models truly understand when and how to delegate information seeking to search.
AI.method: 1) Formalizes Delegation Intelligence and decomposes it into Search Decision-Making and Information Synthesis/Verification dimensions. 2) Develops a controllable synthesis pipeline using document-grounded reverse engineering for constructing controlled deep-search evaluations. 3) Instantiates this as DelegSearchBench with a disentangled evaluation protocol that isolates each capability dimension by varying document composition and tool access.
AI.result: Demonstrates across representative models that deep-search competence cannot be adequately characterized by final-answer accuracy alone. The proposed framework enables disentangled and reproducible measurement of search delegation capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a formal framework for evaluating Delegation Intelligence in deep search, providing a recipe for controlled evaluation rather than just a fixed dataset. This enables better assessment of whether models truly know when and how to delegate information seeking to search tools.

title: Joint Flow Matching for Generator-Consistent Classification
summary: We introduce Joint Flow Matching (JFM), a training framework for continuous normalising flows over multiple variables. Standard flow matching transports variables from noise to data simultaneously, offering no natural mechanism for forward and reverse conditional inference from a shared joint model. JFM resolves this by assigning opposite roles to each variable at the temporal endpoints. We prove that JFM produces a consistent joint distribution where that forward or reverse integration are conditionals of the same joint. We explore this consistency in the context of joint classification and generation as the basis for interpretability in discriminative-generative models. We validate JFM on conditional datasets producing competitive accuracy with inherently well-calibrated confidence scores without post-hoc calibration, and classifier-consistent image generation.

AI.tldr: Joint Flow Matching (JFM) is a new framework for training continuous normalizing flows that enables both forward and reverse conditional inference from a shared joint model by assigning opposite roles to variables at temporal endpoints.
AI.motivation: Standard flow matching transports variables from noise to data simultaneously but lacks a natural mechanism for forward and reverse conditional inference from a shared joint model. The authors want to create a framework that enables both discriminative (classification) and generative tasks from the same model, supporting interpretability in discriminative-generative models.
AI.method: JFM assigns opposite roles to each variable at the temporal endpoints during training. Instead of transporting all variables from noise to data simultaneously, it creates a framework where variables have different roles at the start and end points, enabling both forward and reverse conditional inference from the same joint model.
AI.result: The authors prove that JFM produces a consistent joint distribution where forward or reverse integration are conditionals of the same joint. Experiments show competitive accuracy on conditional datasets with inherently well-calibrated confidence scores without post-hoc calibration, and classifier-consistent image generation.
AI.conclusion: Joint Flow Matching provides a principled framework for training continuous normalizing flows that enables both discriminative and generative tasks from a single model, offering well-calibrated confidence scores and classifier-consistent generation without additional calibration steps.

title: ObsDriveBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Understanding under Adverse Weather with Observability Awareness
summary: Autonomous driving under adverse weather remains a critical challenge, yet existing vision-language benchmarks mainly evaluate under standard conditions, synthetic corruptions, or single modality. As a result, it remains unclear how vision-language models behave under real-world adverse weather with multi-modal inputs. We argue that a key difficulty lies in degraded environmental observability: under fog, rain, snow, and low illumination, multi-modal observations become unreliable and cross-modally inconsistent, posing challenges to scene understanding, and subsequent decision-making. To study this, we introduce \textbf{ObsDriveBench}, a real-world multi-modal benchmark for adverse-weather autonomous driving. Our benchmark is designed with three capability dimensions: \textbf{observability awareness}, \textbf{spatial reliability}, and \textbf{risk-aware decision-making}, enabling fine-grained diagnosis of model behavior under degraded observations. We construct the benchmark through observability meta-annotation, scene description, and capability oriented multiple-choice tasks over synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs, forming a benchmark with over 14k training and 13k test questions. Experiments reveal consistent performance degradation of existing vision-language models. We further introduce \textbf{ObsDrive} model with normal-weather supervised fine-tuning and adverse-weather reinforcement learning, improving robustness across all three capabilities. The dataset and evaluation code will be released at \href{https://github.com/russellyq/ObsDriveBench}{\texttt{ObsDriveBench}}.

AI.tldr: A benchmark and model called ObsDriveBench/ObsDrive for evaluating vision-language models in autonomous driving under real-world adverse weather conditions, focusing on degraded environmental observability across multi-modal inputs.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language benchmarks mainly evaluate under standard conditions, synthetic corruptions, or single modalities, failing to capture how models behave under real-world adverse weather with multi-modal inputs. A key challenge is degraded environmental observability where multi-modal observations become unreliable and cross-modally inconsistent under fog, rain, snow, and low illumination.
AI.method: Introduces ObsDriveBench benchmark with three capability dimensions: observability awareness, spatial reliability, and risk-aware decision-making. Constructed through observability meta-annotation, scene description, and capability-oriented multiple-choice tasks over synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs. Also proposes ObsDrive model with normal-weather supervised fine-tuning and adverse-weather reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Created benchmark with over 14k training and 13k test questions. Experiments show consistent performance degradation of existing vision-language models under adverse conditions. ObsDrive model demonstrates improved robustness across all three capabilities compared to existing models.
AI.conclusion: ObsDriveBench provides a valuable real-world benchmark for evaluating vision-language models in adverse weather driving scenarios, revealing limitations of current approaches. The proposed ObsDrive model with specialized training shows promise in addressing degraded observability challenges. The work advances multi-modal evaluation for autonomous driving under real-world adverse conditions.

title: Understanding Machine Unlearning Through the Lens of Mode Connectivity
summary: Machine Unlearning aims to remove undesired information from trained models without full retraining from scratch. Despite recent progress, the loss landscape and optimization geometry of unlearning are poorly understood. In this paper, we study machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity--the phenomenon that independently trained models can often be connected by smooth low-loss paths in parameter space. We introduce {\em mode connectivity in unlearning} (MCU) and evaluate it across a range of settings, including curriculum learning, second-order optimization, and connectivity across different unlearning methods. We find that many unlearned models lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior, while changes in training dynamics can move solutions into different basins. MCU also reveals that models within the same basin can differ substantially on privacy metrics, and that unlearning progresses nonlinearly from the original model to the unlearned model. In addition, linear connectivity suggests that most approximate unlearning methods are mechanistically distinct from retraining. Finally, MCU-based ensembling can improve generalization and robustness to relearning attacks, and MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty. To our knowledge, this is the first study of machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "mode connectivity in unlearning" (MCU) as a new lens to study machine unlearning, revealing that many unlearned models lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior, and that unlearning progresses nonlinearly from original to unlearned models.
AI.motivation: Despite recent progress in machine unlearning, the loss landscape and optimization geometry of unlearning are poorly understood. The paper aims to study machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity to better understand how models behave during unlearning processes.
AI.method: The paper introduces mode connectivity in unlearning (MCU) and evaluates it across various settings including curriculum learning, second-order optimization, and connectivity across different unlearning methods. They analyze smooth paths between models and examine retain/forget behavior along these paths.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Many unlearned models lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior; (2) Training dynamics changes can move solutions into different basins; (3) Models within same basin differ substantially on privacy metrics; (4) Unlearning progresses nonlinearly; (5) Linear connectivity suggests approximate unlearning methods are distinct from retraining; (6) MCU-based ensembling improves generalization and robustness; (7) MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study of machine unlearning through mode connectivity, providing new insights into optimization geometry, revealing mechanistic differences between approximate methods and retraining, and showing practical benefits through MCU-based ensembling for improved generalization and robustness.

title: Verification-Notebook Learning for Source-Aware Multimodal Misinformation Detection
summary: Multimodal misinformation verification is challenging because misleading signals may come from different parts of a post and require different forms of evidence. LVLMs are well suited to this task, but their verification performance often depends on the inference procedure applied to each instance. Existing methods improve this procedure through stronger prompting, retrieval, or deliberation, but rarely retain the verification patterns learned from previous examples. We propose Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that learns an external verification procedure for a frozen LVLM before inference. VNL builds a compact notebook of decision principles, evidence cues, and recurring pitfalls from prior verification experience. The notebook remains fixed during inference and guides the verification of new examples. Rather than updating model parameters or storing demonstrations, VNL records learned knowledge in an artifact that can be inspected directly. Experiments show that VNL consistently outperforms a range of competitive baselines. Further analyses show that the Verification Notebook improves fine-grained source attribution while remaining compact and interpretable, providing an effective way to accumulate verification knowledge without model training.

AI.tldr: VNL is a non-parametric framework that learns an external verification procedure for frozen LVLMs by building a compact notebook of decision principles, evidence cues, and pitfalls from prior verification experience to guide new examples.
AI.motivation: Multimodal misinformation verification is challenging because misleading signals come from different parts of posts requiring different evidence forms. LVLMs are suited but their performance depends on inference procedures, and existing methods rarely retain verification patterns learned from previous examples.
AI.method: Proposes Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that learns an external verification procedure for frozen LVLMs by building a compact notebook of decision principles, evidence cues, and recurring pitfalls from prior verification experience. The notebook remains fixed during inference and guides verification of new examples without updating model parameters or storing demonstrations.
AI.result: Experiments show VNL consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Further analyses show the Verification Notebook improves fine-grained source attribution while remaining compact and interpretable.
AI.conclusion: VNL provides an effective way to accumulate verification knowledge without model training through an inspectable artifact that guides multimodal misinformation verification.

title: Adaptive Data Admission and Retention for Streaming Federated Learning
summary: We study streaming federated learning with limited client memory, where newly generated training data incur time-varying sampling costs and must be selectively admitted and retained over time. We consider a joint server-side admission and client-side memory-management framework with the objective of minimizing the cumulative excess population risk under a sampling-cost budget and buffer constraints. We first derive a learning-error bound that explicitly captures the effects of instantaneous training sample size, distinct-sample growth, and reuse imbalance through a characterization of the effective sample size. Through a surrogate penalty obtained from this bound, we develop an Active-Constraint Drift-Plus-Penalty (ACDPP) policy that combines a structured client-side $K$-step retention rule with a server-side online admission rule and a time-varying rectangular admission region. We further present a sequence of comparison arguments, via an auxiliary constant-admission policy, that connects the ACDPP learning bound to a costless oracle benchmark. This yields explicit guarantees in terms of sublinear regret and sampling-cost violation, while the buffer-occupancy violation is controlled through offline selection of the retention horizon. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed policy remains close to the oracle benchmark while satisfying the sampling-cost and buffer constraints.

AI.tldr: A streaming federated learning framework with active constraints for managing client memory and sampling costs, achieving near-oracle performance with controlled constraint violations.
AI.motivation: Addresses the challenge of streaming federated learning where clients have limited memory, new training data incur time-varying sampling costs, and data must be selectively admitted and retained over time under resource constraints.
AI.method: Proposes an Active-Constraint Drift-Plus-Penalty (ACDPP) policy combining structured client-side K-step retention rules with server-side online admission rules and time-varying rectangular admission regions, based on a derived learning-error bound that captures training sample size, distinct-sample growth, and reuse imbalance.
AI.result: The policy achieves sublinear regret and sampling-cost violation guarantees compared to a costless oracle benchmark, with buffer-occupancy violation controlled through retention horizon selection, demonstrating close-to-oracle performance on multiple datasets while satisfying constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ACDPP framework effectively manages streaming federated learning with limited client memory and sampling costs, providing theoretical guarantees and practical performance that bridges online learning with resource-constrained federated systems.

title: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents
summary:
Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change.
  We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses authorization challenges in long-lived AI agents that evolve after deployment, proposing a "state-bound" model with transition envelopes and immutable effect ceilings to ensure authorization continuity as agents mutate.
AI.motivation: Long-lived AI agents evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring new skills/tools, revising workflows, and delegating work, which creates authorization problems. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions, and when evolution occurs under a live authorization grant, the subject exercising authority or the context may no longer match what the user originally evaluated.
AI.method: The paper formulates "authorization continuity" to determine when existing grants remain valid. It proposes a state-bound model with a transition envelope and immutable effect ceiling fixed at grant time. The envelope determines whether a grant survives mutation, while below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. The approach distinguishes requested from realized effects and relies on complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity.
AI.result: The paper proves that under the specified conditions (complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, monitor integrity), mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. The research also maps six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.
AI.conclusion: The state-bound model with transition envelopes and immutable effect ceilings provides a framework for maintaining authorization continuity in evolving AI agents, ensuring that agents cannot exceed their granted authority bounds even as they mutate and evolve over time.

title: When Should Active RAG Retrieve? A Budget-Aware Evaluation of Utility, Calibration, and Cost
comment: Accepted at the ACM SIGKDD KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI; 7 pages, 1 figure, and 4 tables
summary: Active RAG systems decide when to retrieve external knowledge during generation, making them a budget-sensitive case of agentic RAG and self-adaptive retrieval. Yet evaluations often leave the operating point underspecified: two systems may both claim a 50% evidence-usage budget while realizing different held-out usage rates, so higher accuracy can reflect a looser budget rather than a better retrieval policy. We study budget-aware evaluation for Active RAG by recasting active retrieval as utility estimation, where retrieval is valuable only through its marginal correctness change over a no-retrieval answer. This view separates three questions that single-point evaluations conflate: whether trigger scores rank useful retrieval decisions, whether thresholds calibrated on past data meet future budgets, and how trigger-side computation changes deployment cost. We operationalize these questions with exact top-k utility frontiers, deployable threshold frontiers, conservative budget frontiers, harm audits, and cost decompositions. Across knowledge-intensive multi-hop QA datasets and open instruction models, retrieval harm is non-negligible, router rankings change across datasets and budgets, nominal thresholds can miss target usage, and simple uncertainty or retrieval-score baselines often rival learned utility routers. Budget-aware Active RAG evaluations should therefore report frontiers, realized usage, threshold-transfer error, harm rates, and cost decompositions alongside accuracy.

AI.tldr: Active RAG systems need budget-aware evaluation frameworks because current evaluations conflate retrieval policy quality with budget adherence, leading to misleading comparisons.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of Active RAG systems underspecify operating points, allowing systems claiming the same evidence-usage budget to actually use different amounts of retrieval. This means higher accuracy might reflect looser budget adherence rather than better retrieval policies.
AI.method: Recast active retrieval as utility estimation where retrieval's value depends on marginal correctness improvement over no-retrieval. Introduce budget-aware evaluation metrics: exact top-k utility frontiers, deployable threshold frontiers, conservative budget frontiers, harm audits, and cost decompositions.
AI.result: Across knowledge-intensive multi-hop QA datasets and open instruction models: retrieval harm is non-negligible, router rankings change across datasets/budgets, nominal thresholds often miss target usage, and simple uncertainty or retrieval-score baselines compete with learned utility routers.
AI.conclusion: Active RAG evaluations should report frontiers, realized usage, threshold-transfer error, harm rates, and cost decompositions alongside accuracy for proper budget-aware assessment.

title: Hybrid Advantage Estimation with Unified Critic for VLM Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) now act as agents in interactive environments, where success requires coherent reasoning and decision-making across turns. Although end-to-end training in agentic environments can improve such multi-turn decision-making abilities, current methods mainly rely on either token-wise optimization over concatenated token trajectories or turn-wise optimization with uniform within-turn credit. In this work, we establish theoretical formulations for the two levels of optimization and derive a hybrid advantage that serves both objectives. Furthermore, with an appropriate choice of discount factor and learning target, we prove that a unified critic model can estimate values for both turn-wise and token-wise. As such, we propose HyGAE, an actor-critic framework that jointly optimizes token- and turn-level objectives with the hybrid advantage and unified critic. We conduct extensive evaluations of HyGAE across five multi-turn decision-making environments, where it achieves an average success rate of 91% and a significant improvement of 10% over other methods. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis showing that the exact analytic form of the hybrid advantage and return is crucial for optimization. Project Page: https://wx-zhang.github.io/hygae-web/.

AI.tldr: HyGAE: A hybrid actor-critic framework that jointly optimizes token-level and turn-level objectives with unified critic model for improved multi-turn decision-making in vision-language agents.
AI.motivation: Current methods for training VLMs in agentic environments rely on either token-wise optimization over concatenated token trajectories or turn-wise optimization with uniform within-turn credit, which are suboptimal for multi-turn decision-making requiring coherent reasoning across turns.
AI.method: Proposes HyGAE framework with: 1) Theoretical formulations for both optimization levels, 2) Derived hybrid advantage serving both objectives, 3) Unified critic model estimating values for both turn-wise and token-wise with appropriate discount factor, 4) Actor-critic architecture jointly optimizing token- and turn-level objectives.
AI.result: Achieves 91% average success rate across five multi-turn decision-making environments, with 10% improvement over other methods. Analysis shows the exact analytic form of hybrid advantage and return is crucial for optimization.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid advantage formulation and unified critic enable effective joint optimization of token- and turn-level objectives, significantly improving multi-turn decision-making capabilities of vision-language agents in interactive environments.

title: Capacity-Aware Deep Learning for Generalizable Traffic Volume Estimation Across Links and Cities
summary: Network-wide traffic volume estimation typically relies on propagating measurements from fixed sensors, making performance highly dependent on sensor density and limiting deployment in sparsely instrumented networks. We propose a link-level learning framework that estimates hourly traffic volumes from widely available territorial data only, including probe speed profiles, road and topological descriptors, along with weather observations. A supervised local mapping is learned from sparse sensor measurements and evaluated under two generalization settings: intra-network (unseen links within the training network) and inter-network (unseen city). This formulation frames traffic volume estimation as a spatial out-of-distribution generalization problem under sparse supervision. To enhance spatial robustness, we introduce a capacity-aware formulation that models volume as the product of a link-specific structural capacity and an hourly regime-aware utilization ratio, embedding traffic-theoretic constraints directly into the learning process. Extensive experiments in both generalization settings demonstrate that the proposed structural constraints consistently outperform a state-of-the-art baseline under spatial distribution shift.

AI.tldr: A traffic volume estimation framework that uses widely available territorial data (probe speeds, road descriptors, weather) instead of dense sensor networks, with capacity-aware modeling for spatial robustness and strong performance under spatial distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Current traffic volume estimation relies on propagating measurements from fixed sensors, which limits deployment in sparsely instrumented networks and makes performance highly dependent on sensor density. There's a need for methods that can work with widely available data sources rather than dense sensor networks.
AI.method: A link-level learning framework that estimates hourly traffic volumes from territorial data (probe speed profiles, road/topological descriptors, weather observations). Uses supervised local mapping from sparse sensor measurements. Introduces capacity-aware formulation modeling volume as product of link-specific structural capacity and hourly regime-aware utilization ratio, embedding traffic-theoretic constraints into learning. Evaluates under intra-network (unseen links within same network) and inter-network (unseen city) generalization settings.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the proposed structural constraints consistently outperform a state-of-the-art baseline under spatial distribution shift. The framework demonstrates strong performance in both intra-network and inter-network generalization settings.
AI.conclusion: The capacity-aware formulation effectively frames traffic volume estimation as a spatial out-of-distribution generalization problem under sparse supervision, providing a robust solution that works with widely available data and performs well even when generalizing to unseen networks/cities.

title: SpecAHD: Localize to Specialize for Automated Heuristic Design in Large-Scale Routing Problems
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, and 3 tables. Supplementary material included
summary: LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) typically scores executable programs on complete instances or within fixed solver components. In large-scale routing problems, localized reconstruction reduces the size of each optimization task, but repair regions within the same incumbent can exhibit substantially different structures. One construction rule must therefore compromise across them. In this paper, we propose SpecAHD, a coupled bilevel framework for within-instance specialization. An upper-level search learns where to expose bounded repair regions, while a lower-level search evolves a complementary repertoire of executable heuristics for the induced repair tasks. The upper-level program determines the repair tasks seen by the lower level, while checked repair outcomes determine how upper-level programs are evaluated. The lower-level objective favors heuristics that perform well on average or solve tasks that the current repertoire handles poorly. For the repair tasks induced by a fixed upper-level program and a fixed lower-level candidate pool, this objective is monotone submodular, allowing greedy repertoire selection with a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee. Across four routing problems and multiple LLM backbones, SpecAHD reduces held-out objective cost by up to 57.7% against the strongest competing AHD baseline and outperforms the per-instance baseline envelope on most public instances.

AI.tldr: SpecAHD is a bilevel framework for automated heuristic design that specializes heuristics to different repair regions within routing instances, using LLM-based program generation with a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) methods use general heuristic programs that must compromise across diverse local repair regions within routing problems, even though these regions can have substantially different structures.
AI.method: SpecAHD uses a coupled bilevel framework: upper-level search learns where to expose bounded repair regions, while lower-level search evolves a complementary repertoire of executable heuristics for these repair tasks. The lower-level objective optimizes for heuristics that perform well on average or handle tasks poorly addressed by the current repertoire.
AI.result: SpecAHD reduces held-out objective cost by up to 57.7% against the strongest competing AHD baseline and outperforms per-instance baselines on most public instances across four routing problems and multiple LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Within-instance specialization through SpecAHD's bilevel framework significantly improves LLM-based heuristic design for routing problems by adapting heuristics to local repair regions rather than using generalized compromises.

title: Constrained Reinforcement Learning Using Successor Representations
comment: published in Transactions for Machine Learning Research 2026
summary: Real-world Reinforcement Learning depends on the ability to formulate safety constraints into a policy. A common way to model such constraints is to introduce an additional cost signal in the Markov Decision Process, which notifies the agent of unwanted behavior independently of the reward signal. Unfortunately, current methods are hard to adapt to changes in the cost function introduced by, e.g., domain shift or obstacles moving over time. The lack of adaptability means that policies are too unflexible to deal with complex real-world conditions. We propose the Safe Deep Successor Representation (SafeDSR), a novel method that allows quick retraining of policies towards new cost structures. SafeDSR extends the Deep Successor Representation (Kulkarni et al., 2016) to Constrained Reinforcement Learning by introducing a single learnable weight matrix to decouple the learned value function across dynamics, rewards, and costs. This matrix can be updated in a supervised manner instead of having to adapt the whole network if the cost structure of the environment changes. We demonstrate this ability in a freely configurable two-dimensional navigation environment and show that our method is competitive on a simple navigation task while being considerably more flexible

AI.tldr: SafeDSR enables fast policy retraining for new safety constraints using a learnable weight matrix with the Deep Successor Representation, allowing adaptation to changing cost functions without retraining entire networks.
AI.motivation: Real-world RL requires safety constraints, but current methods lack adaptability to changing cost functions caused by domain shifts or moving obstacles, making policies inflexible for complex real-world conditions.
AI.method: Extends Deep Successor Representation to Constrained RL by introducing a single learnable weight matrix that decouples the learned value function across dynamics, rewards, and costs. The matrix can be updated supervised when cost structure changes instead of retraining the whole network.
AI.result: Demonstrated in a configurable 2D navigation environment, showing competitiveness on simple navigation tasks while being considerably more flexible than existing methods.
AI.conclusion: SafeDSR provides a flexible approach for adapting RL policies to changing safety constraints, enabling quick retraining without complete network adaptation, making it suitable for dynamic real-world environments.

title: Focus Is All You Need: Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration for Multi-Agent Graph Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) enable autonomous agents for reasoning, planning, and tool use. Recent systems increasingly organize these agents as graphs of specialized, interconnected nodes. Although graph-based orchestration supports flexible decomposition and coordination, it creates a key challenge: \textbf{attention allocation}. As workflows grow, existing approaches often execute graph components uniformly, wasting resources on irrelevant or low-impact tasks. We introduce \textbf{Attention Orchestration}, a paradigm that extends Transformer-style attention from token representations to workflow-level agent coordination. Our framework, \textbf{Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration (AGAO)}, dynamically estimates agent importance based on user objectives, graph dependencies, and computational constraints. AGAO combines three components: (1) goal-aware attention, measuring semantic relevance between user goals and agent capabilities; (2) topology-aware attention, modeling structural dependencies in agent graphs; and (3) resource-aware attention, allocating budgets and execution priorities across heterogeneous agents. Together, these mechanisms transform static agent graphs into adaptive systems that focus computation on goal-critical reasoning paths. Experiments across diverse multi-agent workloads show that AGAO improves task effectiveness while reducing unnecessary computation, latency, and token consumption compared with existing graph-based execution strategies. Our work establishes \textbf{Attention Engineering} as a direction for scalable, intelligent multi-agent systems. Code: https://github.com/MingzhouFan97/AGAO.

AI.tldr: AGAO introduces an attention-based orchestration framework for multi-agent LLM systems that dynamically allocates computational resources to goal-relevant agents rather than executing all agents uniformly, improving efficiency and effectiveness.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agent systems increasingly use graph-based orchestration with specialized, interconnected nodes, they face attention allocation challenges - existing approaches execute graph components uniformly, wasting resources on irrelevant or low-impact tasks.
AI.method: The AGAO framework extends Transformer-style attention to workflow-level coordination, combining three components: goal-aware attention (semantic relevance between user goals and agent capabilities), topology-aware attention (structural dependencies in agent graphs), and resource-aware attention (budget allocation across heterogeneous agents).
AI.result: Experiments across diverse multi-agent workloads show that AGAO improves task effectiveness while reducing unnecessary computation, latency, and token consumption compared to existing graph-based execution strategies.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes "Attention Engineering" as a direction for scalable, intelligent multi-agent systems, transforming static agent graphs into adaptive systems that focus computation on goal-critical reasoning paths.

title: ACRL: Adaptive Control of Training-Inference Discrepancy for Stable Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) training for Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffers from instability due to the discrepancy between training and inference. This training-inference discrepancy stems from two primary factors: an architectural separation between training and inference engines, and the use of low-precision quantization in inference versus higher-precision computation in training. To address training instability issues caused by high training-inference discrepancy, we present the principles and methods for its adaptive control. We propose Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning (ACRL), which adaptively maintains the training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range to ensure stable RL training. Beyond stabilization, ACRL inherently increases policy entropy, thereby enhancing exploration and improving accuracy. The experimental results show that when the inference engine utilizes FP8 quantization, ACRL consistently maintains the training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range and stabilizes RL training. Furthermore, ACRL not only matches the accuracy of the BF16 baseline but also outperforms importance sampling (IS) fixes.

AI.tldr: ACRL (Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning) adaptively controls training-inference discrepancy in LLM RL training to stabilize training and improve exploration.
AI.motivation: RL training for LLMs suffers from instability due to training-inference discrepancy caused by architectural separation between training/inference engines and precision differences (training uses higher precision vs inference uses lower quantization).
AI.method: Propose Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning (ACRL) that adaptively maintains training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range through adaptive control principles and methods.
AI.result: With FP8 inference quantization, ACRL maintains discrepancy in reasonable range and stabilizes RL training. ACRL matches BF16 baseline accuracy and outperforms importance sampling fixes.
AI.conclusion: ACRL effectively addresses RL training instability by adaptive control of training-inference discrepancy, achieving stable training while enhancing exploration through increased policy entropy.

title: Compute Globally, Materialize Locally: The Memory Contract of Sparse Event-KV
summary: Long-horizon agents increasingly reuse their KV cache as memory: a serving system keeps a subset of cached entries and drops the rest. Eviction and episodic-memory schemes therefore rest on a premise rarely tested directly, that a retained event is still informative once the observations that produced it are gone. We test it by omitting one earlier observation from what is served, across otherwise identical agent histories. Among items sensitive to that observation, the answer overwhelmingly follows the omitted value, though no served span says which value is correct. We call this semantic materialization: a downstream event's cached rows act as an independently servable view of computation whose inputs are gone. It can also be written on purpose. A deliberately phrased, answer-free event raises donor-aligned recovery from 6% to 51% on Qwen3-8B without ever naming the value, whereas passively harvesting natural mentions from long-term dialog yields no detected advantage. What such a row carries is specific and bounded. Compact state survives, larger payloads decay toward chance, and whether a construction writes at all turns on phrasing rather than on meaning alone, so two phrasings the model comprehends equally well can diverge sharply. The result is a memory contract for sparse event-KV serving: what to write, where it lands, and what survives once the source is gone. For anyone who evicts the corollary is that dropping a source event and observing no accuracy loss does not show the source was unnecessary.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that in LLM inference with KV caching, even after removing source observations, downstream cached entries can still independently carry specific semantic information that influences model outputs - a phenomenon called "semantic materialization."
AI.motivation: Current long-horizon agents use KV cache eviction policies that assume retained events remain informative even after original observations are dropped. However, this fundamental premise has rarely been tested directly.
AI.method: The authors test the premise by omitting one earlier observation from otherwise identical agent histories and examining how downstream events respond.
