By synthesizing existing methods and insights from the perspective of semantic intelligence, this survey aims to support the continued development of AI toward HLSI.

AI.tldr: This survey paper examines AI's transition from Basic-Level Semantic Intelligence (BLSI) to High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI), reviewing tasks like humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, and persuasion across text, speech, vision, and multimodal scenarios to advance AI toward genuinely human-like intelligence.
AI.motivation: The development of AI shows a clear trajectory from simple to complex semantic processing, similar to human cognitive development. However, the systematic transition from Basic-Level Semantic Intelligence (BLSI) to High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI) has not been comprehensively examined in prior work, creating a gap that needs addressing to advance AI toward genuinely human-like intelligence.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic survey of existing research on HLS tasks across text, speech, vision, and multimodal scenarios. They summarize data construction methods, modeling and optimization strategies, and evaluation methodologies for both understanding and generation of High-Level Semantics.
AI.result: The survey provides a comprehensive examination of HLS tasks including humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, persuasion, narrative, and other HLS phenomena. It synthesizes existing methods and insights from the perspective of semantic intelligence development.
AI.conclusion: High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI) is essential for advancing AI toward genuinely human-like intelligence. By systematically examining the transition from BLSI to HLSI and synthesizing existing approaches, this survey supports continued AI development toward sophisticated semantic reasoning capabilities.

title: FlowCTS: On-policy Continuous Trajectory Supervision of Flow Models
summary: While on-policy distillation (OPD) effectively addresses sparse rewards and exposure bias in large language model post-training, its extension to flow models remains underexplored. To this end, we propose Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which matches subsequent student and reference trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. Using the integral relation between trajectories and velocity fields, we derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound and discretize it into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps. Under a multi-reference setup, single-state FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD with faster convergence. FlowCTS-OPD improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, while outperforming a mixed-reward RL baseline across all target metrics. Further analysis reveals a clear temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD arising from its auxiliary SDE transition kernels. Beyond on-policy setting,FlowCTS also consistently outperforms vanilla SFT , particularly on OCR, while increasing supervision steps exhibit a trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty.

AI.tldr: Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS) is proposed for flow models, improving on-policy distillation by matching student and reference trajectories from the same state, outperforming both KL-based distillation and reinforcement learning baselines.
AI.motivation: While on-policy distillation (OPD) works well for language models, its extension to flow models remains underexplored. The paper aims to address this gap and improve distillation for flow models, where vanilla KL-based OPD suffers from temporal supervision mismatch due to auxiliary SDE transition kernels.
AI.method: Proposes Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which matches subsequent student and reference trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. Uses the integral relation between trajectories and velocity fields to derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound, discretized into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps. Evaluated under multi-reference setup.
AI.result: Single-state FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD with faster convergence. Improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06. Outperforms mixed-reward RL baseline across all target metrics. Also consistently outperforms vanilla SFT, particularly on OCR. Analysis shows increasing supervision steps involves trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty.
AI.conclusion: FlowCTS is an effective method for extending on-policy distillation to flow models, addressing limitations of KL-based approaches through trajectory matching. It demonstrates superior performance across multiple metrics and reveals important insights about temporal supervision in flow model distillation.

title: MemChain: Learning Interpretable Memory Traces for Memory-Augmented LLM Agents
summary: Memory-augmented LLM agents typically answer queries by retrieving relevant memories and feeding them directly to an answer model. This retrieval-as-evidence paradigm assumes retrieved memories are already suitable for reasoning, leaving the answer model to resolve redundancy, conflicts, and weak relevance while incurring substantial context overhead in long-term memory tasks. We propose MemChain, a trainable post-retrieval memory policy that transforms retrieved candidates into answer-facing active memory, represented as a compact and grounded evidence context. Given a user query and retrieved candidates, MemChain first generates a question-conditioned evidence plan, then constructs an ordered grounded evidence trace that organizes retrieved memories according to their semantic roles and dependencies, and finally executes explicit memory actions to produce a concise evidence context for answer generation. To train the mediator, we introduce a two-stage learning framework. Supervised trace learning first teaches the policy to generate structurally valid plans, traces, actions, and evidence contexts. We then propose Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO), a reinforcement learning objective that optimizes the memory policy using downstream answer quality while jointly encouraging trace grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and answer stability across multiple rollouts. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that MemChain consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models while substantially reducing the memory context passed to the answer model.

AI.tldr: MemChain is a trainable post-retrieval memory policy that transforms retrieved memories into a compact, organized evidence context for LLM agents, reducing context overhead while improving answer quality through structured evidence planning and optimization.
AI.motivation: Current memory-augmented LLM agents use a "retrieval-as-evidence" paradigm that directly feeds retrieved memories to answer models, which assumes memories are already suitable for reasoning. This approach forces answer models to handle redundancy, conflicts, and weak relevance while incurring substantial context overhead in long-term memory tasks.
AI.method: MemChain transforms retrieved candidates into answer-facing active memory through a three-step process: (1) generates question-conditioned evidence plan, (2) constructs ordered grounded evidence trace organizing memories by semantic roles and dependencies, and (3) executes explicit memory actions to produce concise evidence context. Training uses a two-stage framework: supervised trace learning for structural validity, followed by Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO) - a reinforcement learning objective optimizing answer quality while encouraging trace grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and answer stability.
AI.result: Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks show MemChain consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models while substantially reducing the memory context passed to answer models.
AI.conclusion: MemChain provides an effective trainable approach for post-retrieval memory processing that transforms raw retrieved memories into structured, concise evidence contexts, overcoming limitations of direct retrieval-as-evidence paradigms and improving both performance and efficiency in memory-augmented LLM systems.

title: From Machine Learning to Large-Scale EO Products: Best Practices for Making Maps
comment: ECCV 2026 TerraBytes II Workshop paper, non-archival
summary: Recent years have seen a rapid expansion in the production of large-scale geospatial maps derived from Earth observation (EO) data, driven largely by advances in machine learning (ML) and large computing infrastructure. Although the barrier to generating such maps has dropped substantially, established best practices have yet to emerge, and design decisions made early in the pipeline can quietly propagate errors into the final product. Producing a technically sound and scientifically credible product remains challenging. Choices made at every stage are tightly coupled: preprocessing decisions shape the training signal, dataset design governs what the model can learn and how reliably its performance can be assessed, and global-scale inference introduces engineering challenges in compute and data access at scale, as well as artifact mitigation. Furthermore, uncertainty quantification and independent map validation each require dedicated methodological attention that is often underestimated. This paper presents a concise, end-to-end account of the recommended practices spanning the pipeline from satellite data to an operational map product. We organize the discussion around six interconnected themes: the EO data infrastructure landscape, data selection and preprocessing, ML dataset construction and model training, uncertainty quantification, map production and distribution, and validation. This paper is a condensed version of a longer guide that provides greater depth across all stages, accessible online at ghjuliasialelli.github.io/MLEO-Maps/.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an end-to-end guide on best practices for creating large-scale geospatial maps from Earth observation data using machine learning, covering six key themes from data infrastructure to validation.
AI.motivation: The rapid expansion of large-scale geospatial mapping from Earth observation data has occurred without established best practices. Early design decisions in the pipeline can quietly propagate errors, making it challenging to produce technically sound and scientifically credible map products despite advances in ML and computing infrastructure.
AI.method: The paper presents a concise, end-to-end account of recommended practices organized around six interconnected themes: EO data infrastructure landscape, data selection/preprocessing, ML dataset construction/model training, uncertainty quantification, map production/distribution, and validation.
AI.result: The paper delivers a comprehensive framework for addressing the tightly coupled choices throughout the mapping pipeline, providing guidance on preprocessing decisions, dataset design, global-scale inference challenges, and methodological attention needed for uncertainty quantification and validation.
AI.conclusion: Producing reliable geospatial maps requires careful consideration of interconnected decisions across the entire pipeline. This condensed guide (with a longer version available online) serves as a resource for establishing best practices in the emerging field of ML-driven Earth observation mapping.

title: Scaling GUI Agents with Visual State Transitions
summary: We introduce State Transition Pretraining (STP) as a new scaling axis for GUI agents. During the STP stage, we continually pretrain a unified multimodal model on visual state transitions by jointly optimizing inverse dynamics (predicting actions from state changes) and forward dynamics (predicting next states from current states and actions). This optimization equips the model with better action-grounded visual representations and an internal world model of GUI dynamics. When subsequently fine-tuned on trajectories with task instructions, our STP-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained solely via direct trajectory fine-tuning across agent benchmarks in both desktop and mobile GUI scenarios (AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey). Further empirical studies show that joint dynamics optimization yields stable improvements over single-objective training, and downstream performance scales steadily with the volume of transition data.

AI.tldr: State Transition Pretraining (STP) improves GUI agents by pretraining on visual state transitions (inverse+forward dynamics) before task fine-tuning, consistently outperforming direct fine-tuning across desktop/mobile benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agents are typically trained via direct trajectory fine-tuning on task instructions, but may lack robust visual representations and internal models of GUI dynamics. The authors propose that pretraining on state transitions could provide better action-grounded visual understanding and world modeling capabilities.
AI.method: Introduces State Transition Pretraining (STP) as a new scaling axis. Continually pretrains a unified multimodal model on visual state transitions by jointly optimizing: 1) Inverse dynamics (predicting actions from state changes), and 2) Forward dynamics (predicting next states from current states and actions). This is followed by fine-tuning on trajectories with task instructions.
AI.result: STP-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained solely via direct trajectory fine-tuning across AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey benchmarks for both desktop and mobile GUI scenarios. Joint dynamics optimization outperforms single-objective training, and performance scales steadily with transition data volume.
AI.conclusion: State Transition Pretraining is an effective scaling axis for GUI agents that provides better action-grounded visual representations and internal world models through joint optimization of inverse and forward dynamics, leading to superior performance across diverse GUI environments.

title: The K-SCAN Clustering Algorithm
summary: In the Big Data era, the scalability of clustering algorithms constitutes a key challenge. Traditional density-based methods (e.g., DBSCAN) offer robustness to noise and the ability to detect non-linear clusters, yet their quadratic time complexity $O(N^2)$ drastically limits their applicability. Conversely, partitional algorithms (e.g., K-Means), with their linear complexity $O(N)$, impose sphericity on the resulting groups and fail in the presence of outliers. This paper presents K-SCAN -- a novel hybrid algorithm that optimizes this trade-off. The method integrates preliminary vector quantization (stochastic Mini-Batch K-Means) to extract a reduced set of weighted micro-clusters, followed by a subsequent density-based structural analysis. Empirical evaluation on datasets of up to $10^6$ samples confirms the linear computational complexity of the proposed solution. K-SCAN achieves more than a 3-fold speed-up over the hierarchical BIRCH algorithm, avoiding the costly management of tree-based structures. The method precisely identifies non-linear manifolds while maintaining structural stability (Adjusted Rand Index > 0.99), even with noise levels reaching 55\% of the data volume. The main limitation of the proposed algorithm, which could not be fully eliminated in the present study, remains its susceptibility to over-smoothing and its difficulty in separating clusters with highly heterogeneous local density. In complex visual spaces, this can lead to the loss of the finest topological details.

AI.tldr: K-SCAN is a novel hybrid clustering algorithm that combines vector quantization (Mini-Batch K-Means) with density-based analysis to achieve linear time complexity while maintaining ability to detect non-linear clusters and handle noise.
AI.motivation: In the Big Data era, there's a fundamental trade-off between traditional density-based methods like DBSCAN (which handle noise and non-linear clusters but have O(N²) complexity) and partitional methods like K-Means (which have O(N) complexity but impose spherical clusters and fail with outliers). The motivation is to create a scalable clustering algorithm that can handle large datasets while preserving the advantages of density-based methods.
AI.method: K-SCAN uses a two-stage hybrid approach: 1) Preliminary vector quantization using stochastic Mini-Batch K-Means to extract a reduced set of weighted micro-clusters, and 2) Subsequent density-based structural analysis on these micro-clusters. This reduces computational complexity while maintaining the ability to detect non-linear structures.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on datasets up to 10⁶ samples confirms linear computational complexity. K-SCAN achieves >3× speed-up over hierarchical BIRCH algorithm, maintains structural stability (Adjusted Rand Index > 0.99) even with 55% noise levels, and accurately identifies non-linear manifolds while avoiding costly tree-based structures.
AI.conclusion: K-SCAN successfully addresses the scalability challenge of density-based clustering while maintaining robustness to noise and ability to detect non-linear clusters. However, limitations include susceptibility to over-smoothing and difficulty separating clusters with highly heterogeneous local density, which can lead to loss of fine topological details in complex visual spaces.

title: EchoBridge: Long-Tail-Aware ECG-Echocardiography Text Alignment for Echocardiography-Derived Cardiac Findings
summary: Standardized echocardiography conclusions provide meaningful supervision for learning ECG representations of echocardiography-derived cardiac findings. Global ECG--text alignment may entangle modality-specific factors, while long-tailed finding distributions provide sparse positive supervision for low-prevalence conditions. We propose EchoBridge with Complementary Shared--Private Projection (CSPP) and Adaptive Prototype Boundary Calibration (APBC). CSPP maps each modality into shared and auxiliary private projections, reduces directional redundancy via within-modality orthogonality, and bidirectionally aligns normalized shared projections. APBC organizes the shared hypersphere with class-specific prototypes, training-frequency-adaptive angular margins, and spherical Riesz repulsion. We evaluate EchoBridge on EchoNext-Mini and independent PKUPH and SHTMU cohorts under four protocols: prompt-based inference without downstream classifier training, in-domain frozen linear probing, target-domain cross-center frozen linear probing, and source-only cross-center transfer, supplemented by finding-specific analyses. EchoBridge improves classifier-free AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 over the strongest baselines by 7.88, 5.61, and 4.54 points, respectively, and achieves the highest point estimates across all in-domain and target-domain probing budgets and both source-only transfer cohorts. Finding-specific analyses show gains for most conditions, including several low-prevalence valvular findings.

AI.tldr: EchoBridge improves ECG representation learning for echocardiography findings using complementary projections and adaptive prototype calibration, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple clinical cohorts.
AI.motivation: Standardized echocardiography conclusions can supervise ECG representation learning, but global ECG-text alignment may entangle modality-specific factors, and long-tailed finding distributions provide sparse supervision for low-prevalence conditions.
AI.method: Proposed EchoBridge with two main components: 1) Complementary Shared–Private Projection (CSPP) that maps each modality into shared/private projections with within-modality orthogonality and bidirectional alignment, and 2) Adaptive Prototype Boundary Calibration (APBC) that organizes shared hypersphere with class prototypes, adaptive angular margins, and spherical Riesz repulsion.
AI.result: Evaluation on EchoNext-Mini and independent PKUPH/SHTMU cohorts shows EchoBridge improves classifier-free AUROC/AUPRC/F1 by 7.88/5.61/4.54 points over baselines. Achieves highest performance across all in-domain/target-domain probing budgets and both source-only transfer cohorts, with gains for most conditions including low-prevalence valvular findings.
AI.conclusion: EchoBridge effectively learns ECG representations for echocardiography findings by addressing modality entanglement and long-tailed distribution issues through complementary projections and adaptive prototype calibration, demonstrating strong generalization across clinical cohorts.

title: A Motion-Aware Vector Quantization Framework with Centroid Reuse for Efficient VLA Inference
summary:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong potential for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency on GPUs limits real-time deployment. Existing accelerators, such as Dadu-Corki, improve efficiency but treat VLA models as full-precision workloads, leaving substantial redundancy in both memory and computation underexploited.
  In this paper, we propose VQVLA, an algorithm-hardware co-design framework that accelerates VLA inference by exploiting weight similarity and execution dynamics. We first introduce MotionVQ, a motion-aware vector quantization scheme that dynamically adjusts quantization precision based on the robot's execution state, reducing memory access while preserving task success rate. We then propose a merged-centroid vectorized GEMM paradigm that operates on the codebook-index representation, eliminating redundant multiplications through spatial aggregation and temporal reuse of centroids. To realize these optimizations, we design an accelerator that efficiently supports dynamic precision selection and centroid-reuse computation. Experimental results show that VQVLA achieves 6.5x, 2.8x, 1.9x, 3.3x, and 4.3x speedup over the A100 GPU, Dadu-Corki, LUT-DLA, CodeGEMM, and ShiftAddLLM, respectively, with negligible accuracy degradation.

AI.tldr: VQVLA is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework that accelerates Vision-Language-Action models using motion-aware vector quantization and centroid-reuse computation, achieving significant speedup over existing solutions.
AI.motivation: VLA models have high inference latency on GPUs that limits real-time deployment, and existing accelerators treat them as full-precision workloads without exploiting substantial redundancy in memory and computation.
AI.method: Proposes VQVLA with two main innovations: 1) MotionVQ - motion-aware vector quantization that dynamically adjusts precision based on robot execution state, 2) merged-centroid vectorized GEMM paradigm that operates on codebook-index representation to eliminate redundant multiplications through spatial aggregation and temporal centroid reuse, supported by a custom accelerator.
AI.result: VQVLA achieves 6.5x speedup over A100 GPU, 2.8x over Dadu-Corki, 1.9x over LUT-DLA, 3.3x over CodeGEMM, and 4.3x over ShiftAddLLM with negligible accuracy degradation.
AI.conclusion: The VQVLA framework successfully exploits weight similarity and execution dynamics through algorithm-hardware co-design to significantly accelerate VLA inference while maintaining accuracy, making it suitable for real-time embodied AI applications.

title: LOCKS: Page-Local Compact Key Summaries for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
summary: Serving large language models at long context is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which is read in full at every decode step. Attention keys are locally low-rank though globally high-rank: shared low-rank bases discard page-specific directions that a page's own compact basis retains. LOCKS gives every page its own spectral summary (resident, about a tenth the cache's size), reconstructs within-page logits, estimates each page's attention mass by log-sum-exp, and attends only the top pages; selection itself reads no candidate keys or values. Selecting on this summary alone stays within about a point of the full cache on long-document QA (LongBench-v1), tracks the read-every-key oracle on retrieval-dense RULER down to the smallest budgets, and shows its largest margins on long-form reasoning (AIME26, MATH-500), where baseline selectors collapse. At its shipped $2048$-token budget LOCKS matches FullKV aggregate quality at $100$K$+$ context while attending about $2\%$ of the tokens, and halves per-token decode latency ($2.0\times$ at $1$M tokens) against dense attention. LOCKS ships as a drop-in plugin for unmodified vLLM, with batched decode running in full CUDA graphs.

AI.tldr: LOCKS is a memory-efficient KV cache management system that uses per-page spectral summaries to select top pages for attention, reducing computation to ~2% of tokens while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Serving large language models at long context is bottlenecked by the KV cache, which is read in full at every decode step, creating computational inefficiency. Traditional approaches require accessing the entire KV cache even though attention patterns are sparse in long contexts.
AI.method: LOCKS gives every page its own spectral summary (resident, about a tenth the cache's size), reconstructs within-page logits, estimates each page's attention mass by log-sum-exp, and attends only the top pages. Selection reads no candidate keys or values, operating only on compact summaries.
AI.result: LOCKS stays within about a point of the full cache on LongBench-v1, tracks the read-every-key oracle on RULER down to smallest budgets, and shows largest margins on long-form reasoning (AIME26, MATH-500). At 2048-token budget, it matches FullKV quality at 100K+ context while attending ~2% of tokens, and halves per-token decode latency (2.0× speedup at 1M tokens) against dense attention.
AI.conclusion: LOCKS provides an effective drop-in solution for efficient long-context LLM serving by exploiting the locally low-rank nature of attention keys, enabling significant computational savings while maintaining accuracy, with practical implementation in vLLM using CUDA graphs.

title: Agent-UCT: Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees for Agentic Workflow Optimization with Cost-Awareness
summary: Optimizing agentic workflows, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, requires navigating a combinatorial space of discrete component choices under tight evaluation budgets. Existing approaches - heuristic search, black-box optimization, and standard tree search methods - do not explicitly exploit the compositional structure of these workflows, leading to redundant computation and inefficient budget allocation. We introduce Agent-UCT (Agent-based Cost-Aware Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees), a tree search algorithm that extends UCT with a reuse-aware regularization term derived from a bipartite prefix reuse graph. Agent-UCT biases selection toward branches that leverage previously materialized configuration prefixes, reducing redundant execution while maintaining effective exploration. Our framework, RAGSpace, unifies heterogeneous RAG components from LongRAG, LightRAG, and Self-RAG into a five-dimensional configuration space, enabling systematic cross-framework recombination. WTB (Workflow Test Bench) provides deterministic replay, content-addressable caching, and transactional consistency, ensuring that intermediate states are materialized once and reused across the search. Experiments on HotpotQA and UltraDomain demonstrate that Agent-UCT identifies configurations with the highest out-of-sample performance among the evaluated fixed framework presets. Under full-pool evaluation, bipartite prefix reuse reduces logical search cost by 73.6% relative to the no-prefix-sharing cost upper bound. Compared with full-pool evaluation, sampling-based evaluation further achieves a 4.2x wall-clock speedup. Agent-UCT, RAGSpace, and WTB together provide a unified framework for cost-aware, reproducible, and compositionally efficient agentic workflow optimization.

AI.tldr: Agent-UCT is a novel tree search algorithm that optimizes RAG workflows by reusing component prefixes, reducing redundant computations by 73.6% while achieving better performance than existing fixed frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for optimizing agentic workflows like RAG pipelines suffer from redundant computation and inefficient budget allocation because they don't exploit the compositional structure of these workflows. Current approaches (heuristic search, black-box optimization, standard tree search) fail to leverage the fact that many workflow configurations share common component prefixes.
AI.method: The paper introduces Agent-UCT, a tree search algorithm extending UCT with a reuse-aware regularization term derived from a bipartite prefix reuse graph. This biases selection toward branches that leverage previously materialized configuration prefixes. The framework includes RAGSpace (unifying heterogeneous RAG components from LongRAG, LightRAG, and Self-RAG into a five-dimensional configuration space) and WTB (Workflow Test Bench) which provides deterministic replay, content-addressable caching, and transactional consistency.
AI.result: On HotpotQA and UltraDomain benchmarks, Agent-UCT identifies configurations with the highest out-of-sample performance among evaluated fixed framework presets. Bipartite prefix reuse reduces logical search cost by 73.6% relative to no-prefix-sharing upper bound. Sampling-based evaluation achieves 4.2x wall-clock speedup compared to full-pool evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Agent-UCT combined with RAGSpace and WTB provides a unified framework for cost-aware, reproducible, and compositionally efficient agentic workflow optimization. The approach successfully leverages workflow compositionality to dramatically reduce redundant computation while maintaining or improving performance.

title: BettiSplit: Topology-Guided Privacy-Aware Split Learning Against Feature Inversion and Gradient Leakage
summary: Split learning enables collaborative model training by partitioning neural networks across clients and servers. However, improper split placement can lead to severe privacy leakage through intermediate representations. In this work, we propose a topology-guided framework for privacy-aware split learning based on the persistent Betti complexity of smashed activations. Through comprehensive layer-wise analysis, we show that privacy risk in split learning is highly non-uniform across layers and exhibits sharp transition regions that are not captured by architectural depth alone. In particular, feature inversion fidelity increases from negligible reconstruction to as high as 0.98 SSIM at deeper, privacy-critical split points. We further demonstrate that Betti complexity consistently identifies representation regimes associated with elevated feature-space privacy leakage across architectures and datasets. Leveraging this observation, we introduce BettiSafe, a topology-guided split selection strategy that identifies privacy-sensitive layers without requiring explicit attack execution. BettiSafe improves resistance to feature inversion by 2 to 5 times compared to depth-based heuristics while preserving classification accuracy. In addition, Betti-based regularisation increases inversion difficulty by nearly 5 x without degrading model utility, enabling a favourable privacy utility tradeoff. Overall, our results highlight topological complexity as a promising structural descriptor for secure, adaptive, and representation-aware split learning in real-world collaborative systems

AI.tldr: Topology-guided split learning framework using persistent Betti complexity to identify privacy-critical layers and improve resistance to feature inversion attacks.
AI.motivation: Split learning enables collaborative model training but improper split placement can cause severe privacy leakage through intermediate representations. Current methods don't adequately capture non-uniform privacy risks across layers.
AI.method: Proposed BettiSafe, a topology-guided split selection strategy using persistent Betti complexity of smashed activations to identify privacy-sensitive layers without requiring explicit attack execution. Also includes Betti-based regularization.
AI.result: BettiSafe improves resistance to feature inversion by 2-5 times compared to depth-based heuristics while preserving accuracy. Betti-based regularization increases inversion difficulty by nearly 5x without degrading model utility.
AI.conclusion: Topological complexity serves as a promising structural descriptor for secure, adaptive, and representation-aware split learning in real-world collaborative systems, enabling better privacy-utility tradeoffs.

title: Falsifiable Commitment Planning for Self-Correcting Web Agents
summary: Long-horizon web agents often go off track before final failure: a trajectory can remain locally plausible even after the current state, reused skill, or plan assumption no longer supports the user instruction. Existing agents can plan, reflect, or reuse experience, but their plans rarely specify the evidence under which an active step should still be trusted. We propose FCPAgent, a falsifiable commitment planning framework for robust long-horizon web agents. FCPAgent represents each plan step as a Falsifiable Commitment Unit (FCU): a subgoal grounded in a reusable skill, together with confirming evidence, falsifying evidence, and a confidence score. Execution is organized as a plan-test-repair loop. The hybrid commitment testing module checks candidate actions before they modify the browser and checks observations after execution; for efficiency, it combines lightweight evidence matching with LLM-based diagnostic verification. When evidence falsifies a commitment, scope-aware repair localizes the contradiction to the execution, skill, or planning level and revises the smallest adequate part. On WebArena, FCPAgent achieves a 13.8% relative improvement in average success over the strongest baseline, with especially large gains on long-horizon tasks.

AI.tldr: FCPAgent introduces a falsifiable commitment planning framework for web agents that represents plan steps with confirming/falsifying evidence and uses a plan-test-repair loop to improve robustness on long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon web agents often go off track before final failure because trajectories can remain locally plausible even when they're no longer supporting the user instruction. Existing agents lack mechanisms to specify the evidence under which plan steps should be trusted.
AI.method: FCPAgent uses Falsifiable Commitment Units (FCUs) to represent each plan step with: subgoal grounded in reusable skill, confirming evidence, falsifying evidence, and confidence score. Execution follows a plan-test-repair loop with hybrid commitment testing that combines lightweight evidence matching with LLM-based diagnostic verification. When evidence falsifies a commitment, scope-aware repair localizes contradictions and revises the smallest adequate part.
AI.result: On WebArena benchmark, FCPAgent achieves a 13.8% relative improvement in average success over the strongest baseline, with especially large gains on long-horizon tasks.
AI.conclusion: The falsifiable commitment planning framework effectively improves robustness in long-horizon web agents by explicitly representing evidence conditions for plan steps and implementing systematic testing and repair mechanisms when commitments are violated.

title: Bit-Accurate FPGA Evaluation of Learned Feature Gating in a Fixed-Point Fourier-Feature Automatic Modulation Classifier
summary: Learned feature reweighting can improve automatic modulation classification (AMC) in software, but the same operation introduces additional arithmetic and latency when implemented on an FPGA. This work measures that trade-off in a compact fixed-point classifier using 24 sparse DFT-energy features, 8 phase/statistical features, and a 32-to-128-to-11 multilayer perceptron. A second architecture inserts a learned 32-element, 8-bit, input-dependent gate before the classifier. Gated and ungated models are trained using post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) with two matched training seeds. The resulting eight checkpoints are compiled independently for an Intel Cyclone V FPGA and evaluated over 352,000 physical-board classifications. Ungated models achieve higher test accuracy in all four matched gate comparisons, with mean gated-minus-ungated differences of -0.784 percentage points under PTQ and -0.616 percentage points under QAT. The effect of QAT changes direction between the two training seeds. In hardware, the gate adds an average of 1,318 adaptive logic modules (ALMs), 1,557 registers, 4 DSP blocks, and 3,140 processing cycles. All 352,000 board predictions agree exactly with an independent integer reference, and 3,760 captured intermediate values from one training seed also match. For this feature representation and implementation, learned gating increases FPGA cost without improving classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: Learned feature reweighting (gating) for modulation classification increases FPGA hardware costs without improving accuracy compared to ungated models.
AI.motivation: While learned feature reweighting can improve automatic modulation classification (AMC) in software implementations, its implementation on FPGAs introduces additional arithmetic operations and latency overhead. The paper aims to quantify this trade-off between potential accuracy gains and hardware resource costs.
AI.method: Developed two architectures: 1) baseline fixed-point classifier using 32 features (24 sparse DFT-energy + 8 phase/statistical) with a 32-to-128-to-11 MLP, and 2) gated version with learned 32-element, 8-bit input-dependent gate before classifier. Both models were trained using post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) with matched training seeds. All eight checkpoints were compiled for Intel Cyclone V FPGA and evaluated over 352,000 physical-board classifications with hardware verification.
AI.result: Ungated models consistently outperformed gated models in all four matched comparisons, with mean accuracy differences of -0.784 pp (PTQ) and -0.616 pp (QAT). The gate added significant hardware overhead: +1,318 ALMs, +1,557 registers, +4 DSP blocks, and +3,140 processing cycles. QAT effects varied between training seeds. All board predictions matched integer reference implementations, validating correctness.
AI.conclusion: For the specific feature representation and implementation studied, learned gating increases FPGA resource consumption and processing cycles without providing classification accuracy improvements, suggesting the approach is not beneficial for this hardware-constrained application.

title: Myopia Prevention and Control 3.0: Artificial Intelligence--Driven Risk Stratification, Proactive Monitoring, and Personalized Intervention
summary: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), digital sensing, and ubiquitous computing has created an unprecedented opportunity to transform myopia prevention from a reactive, population-based model into a proactive, precision-driven one. Despite evidence that half the world's population will be myopic by 2050, conventional approaches---school-based vision screening (Phase 1.0) and evidence-based risk factor management (Phase 2.0)---have proven insufficient. We review the emergence of Myopia Prevention and Control 3.0, defined by AI integration across three interconnected domains forming a closed-loop pipeline: (1) AI-driven risk stratification predicting individual-level risk through machine learning on multimodal data; (2) AI-enabled proactive monitoring via wearables, smartphones, and school screening networks; and (3) AI-powered personalized intervention with closed-loop feedback. We critically evaluate evidence across each stage, discuss challenges in data quality, model validation, ethics, and equity, and outline future directions including multimodal foundation models, digital twins, and causal machine learning.

AI.tldr: AI-driven Myopia Prevention 3.0 transforms traditional reactive approaches into a precision-driven, closed-loop pipeline using AI for risk prediction, proactive monitoring, and personalized interventions.
AI.motivation: Conventional myopia prevention approaches (school screening and risk factor management) are insufficient despite projections that half the world's population will be myopic by 2050. The convergence of AI, digital sensing, and computing offers opportunity to transform from reactive population-based models to proactive precision-driven prevention.
AI.method: Myopia Prevention 3.0 integrates AI across three interconnected domains: 1) AI-driven risk stratification using machine learning on multimodal data, 2) AI-enabled proactive monitoring via wearables, smartphones, and school screening networks, and 3) AI-powered personalized intervention with closed-loop feedback.
AI.result: The paper reviews evidence across each AI integration stage, identifies challenges including data quality, model validation, ethics, and equity issues, and outlines future research directions in the field.
AI.conclusion: AI-integrated Myopia Prevention 3.0 represents a paradigm shift from traditional approaches, though significant challenges remain in implementation. Future directions include multimodal foundation models, digital twins, and causal machine learning to advance the field.

title: Evaluating Fuzz Testing for Reinforcement Learning Agents
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains such as robotics, autonomous driving, and drone control, where unexpected behaviors may lead to severe real-world consequences. Fuzz testing has recently emerged as a promising method for exploring the vast state spaces of RL agents and exposing crashes. Although numerous RL fuzzing methods have been proposed, existing studies often differ in evaluation settings, baselines, and metrics, making it difficult to draw reliable conclusions about their relative effectiveness and practical usefulness. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive empirical study that systematically evaluates RL fuzzing methods from four complementary perspectives: effectiveness, diversity, efficiency, and practical utility. We benchmark five state-of-the-art methods alongside random testing under unified configurations across three environments of increasing complexity (MountainCar, BipedalWalker, and CARLA), and further assess the downstream usefulness of detected crashes for agent robustness improvement and safety monitoring. Our results reveal several key insights. For instance,throughput-oriented methods like MDPFuzz demonstrate superior effectiveness and efficiency in crash discovery, while methods explicitly designed to encourage exploration like SeqDivFuzz excel at uncovering diverse crash behaviors. We also show that fuzzing-generated crashes can meaningfully improve agent robustness and enable accurate safety monitoring with strong cross-method generalization. Beyond these empirical findings, we distill actionable guidance for both researchers and practitioners, highlighting the benefits of combining complementary fuzzing strategies and adopting multi-level diversity analysis to achieve more comprehensive and practical RL testing.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive empirical evaluation of RL fuzzing methods reveals insights into effectiveness, diversity, and practical utility, with actionable guidance for improved RL testing approaches.
AI.motivation: RL agents in safety-critical domains risk severe consequences from unexpected behaviors. Existing RL fuzzing studies lack unified evaluation standards, making it difficult to compare methods and assess their real-world usefulness.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study benchmarking five state-of-the-art RL fuzzing methods plus random testing under unified configurations across three environments of increasing complexity (MountainCar, BipedalWalker, CARLA). Evaluation from four perspectives: effectiveness, diversity, efficiency, and practical utility, including assessment of crash usefulness for robustness improvement and safety monitoring.
AI.result: Throughput-oriented methods like MDPFuzz excel in crash discovery effectiveness and efficiency, while exploration-focused methods like SeqDivFuzz uncover more diverse crash behaviors. Fuzzing-generated crashes meaningfully improve agent robustness and enable accurate safety monitoring with strong cross-method generalization.
AI.conclusion: Study provides first comprehensive evaluation of RL fuzzing methods, revealing trade-offs and strengths of different approaches. Recommends combining complementary fuzzing strategies and multi-level diversity analysis for more comprehensive and practical RL testing, offering actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners.

title: Integrating Factual and Normative Industrial Knowledge via Constraint-Aware Graph Attention for Process Plan Recommendation
summary: Integrating heterogeneous industrial knowledge, including factual relations and decision constraints, remains a core challenge in industrial information systems. Machining process planning exemplifies this problem because engineers must select operations by combining material properties, feature characteristics, and quality requirements. Existing methods rely mainly on similarity retrieval or classification, without a unified ranking objective or standardized evaluation. We propose PCA-GAT, which formulates machining process plan recommendation as a knowledge graph enhanced collaborative filtering problem. Bayesian Personalized Ranking provides the learning objective, while Recall@K and NDCG@K define evaluation. The knowledge graph supplies semantic structure when collaborative signals are sparse. Four domain constraints, material compatibility, precision requirements, feature applicability, and operation sequencing, are introduced as attention biases during graph propagation. Type-specific weights learn their importance, and an adaptive gate adjusts their influence using local context. On a real aerospace dataset with 115 parts and 507 plans, PCA-GAT achieves Recall@1 = 0.9087 and strong cold-start robustness, with about half the degradation of the strongest baseline under severe sparsity. Ablation studies show that knowledge graph enrichment is essential, constraints add value, and ungated constraint injection can hurt performance. The learned weights identify material-operation compatibility as the dominant factor, consistent with domain expertise. Results on three public benchmarks show no degradation when constraints are absent, supporting generalization beyond manufacturing. This study establishes a standardized recommendation protocol for engineering process planning and benchmarks seven methods across three categories, showing that knowledge representation is the main bottleneck.

AI.tldr: PCA-GAT: A knowledge graph-enhanced collaborative filtering approach for machining process plan recommendation using attention-based constraint injection and adaptive gating.
AI.motivation: Integrating heterogeneous industrial knowledge (factual relations and decision constraints) is a core challenge in industrial information systems. Machining process planning exemplifies this problem where engineers must combine material properties, feature characteristics, and quality requirements to select operations. Existing methods rely on similarity retrieval or classification without unified ranking objectives or standardized evaluation.
AI.method: Proposes PCA-GAT which formulates machining process plan recommendation as knowledge graph-enhanced collaborative filtering. Uses Bayesian Personalized Ranking as learning objective with Recall@K and NDCG@K for evaluation. Introduces four domain constraints (material compatibility, precision requirements, feature applicability, operation sequencing) as attention biases during graph propagation with type-specific weights. Uses adaptive gate to adjust constraint influence based on local context.
AI.result: On real aerospace dataset (115 parts, 507 plans): Recall@1 = 0.9087, strong cold-start robustness with about half degradation of strongest baseline under severe sparsity. Ablation studies show: knowledge graph enrichment is essential, constraints add value, ungated constraint injection hurts performance. Learned weights identify material-operation compatibility as dominant factor (consistent with domain expertise). Results on three public benchmarks show no degradation when constraints absent, supporting generalization beyond manufacturing.
AI.conclusion: Establishes standardized recommendation protocol for engineering process planning and benchmarks seven methods across three categories, showing knowledge representation is the main bottleneck. PCA-GAT successfully integrates heterogeneous industrial knowledge with constraint-aware attention mechanisms and adaptive gating.

title: PYPM-GGD: Pitman-Yor Process Mixture with Generalized Gaussian Density using ADAM
summary: Large scale Bayesian nonparametrics (BNP) learner such as Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI) can handle datasets with large class number and large training size at fractional cost. Like its predecessor, SVI rely on the assumption of conjugate variational posterior to approximate the true posterior. A more challenging problem is to consider large scale learning on non-conjugate posterior. Recent works in this direction are mostly associated with using Monte Carlo methods for approximating the learner. However, these works are usually demonstrated on non-BNP related task and less complex models such as logistic regression, due to higher computational complexity. In order to overcome the issue faced by SVI, we develop a novel approach based on the recently proposed constant stepsize stochastic gradient ascent to allow large scale learning on non-conjugate posterior. Unlike SVI, our new learner does not require closed- form expression for the variational posterior expectatations. Our only requirement is that the variational posterior is differentiable. In order to ensure convergence in stochastic settings, SVI rely on decaying step-sizes to slow its learning. Inspired by SVI and Adam, we propose the novel use of adaptive stepsizes in our method to significantly improve its learning. We show that our proposed methods is compatible with ResNet features when applied to large class number datasets such as MIT67 and SUN397. Finally, we compare our proposed learner with several recent works such as deep clustering algorithms and showed we were able to produce on-par or outperform the state-of-the-art methods in terms of clustering measures.

AI.tldr: A novel Bayesian nonparametric method using adaptive step sizes for large-scale learning on non-conjugate posteriors, outperforming existing methods on complex datasets.
AI.motivation: Current large-scale Bayesian nonparametric methods like SVI rely on conjugate variational posteriors, which limits their applicability. Non-conjugate posterior learning is computationally expensive and has been mostly demonstrated on simple models, creating a need for efficient methods for complex models and datasets.
AI.method: Proposes a novel approach based on constant stepsize stochastic gradient ascent with adaptive stepsizes inspired by SVI and Adam. The method doesn't require closed-form expressions for variational posterior expectations, only requiring differentiability of the variational posterior.
AI.result: The proposed method is compatible with ResNet features on large-class datasets (MIT67 and SUN397). It achieves on-par or better performance than state-of-the-art deep clustering algorithms in terms of clustering measures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive step size method successfully enables large-scale learning on non-conjugate posteriors, overcoming limitations of existing SVI approaches while maintaining compatibility with complex deep learning features.

title: Epistemic Norms for AI Safety and Alignment Research
summary: Mainstream AI research emphasises capability growth and tolerates low failure rates when average-case performance is high. AI safety and alignment research has a different mission: to ensure that catastrophic failures never occur, under sparse evidence, adversarial dynamics, and fat-tailed risk. We argue that the two domains differ along two analytically independent axes---{\it capability profile}, demonstrating the absence of hazardous behaviours rather than the presence of positive capabilities, and {\it risk profile}, bounding worst-case outcomes under fat-tailed uncertainty rather than optimising average-case performance---and that mainstream epistemic practices are inadequate on both. Building on a structured synthesis grounded in a preregistered bibliometric baseline, we identify five cross-cutting gap dimensions in current alignment research, including the near-absence of institutionalised independent verification. To address these gaps, we propose {\sc ECAISA}, an Epistemic Code for AI Safety and Alignment comprising eight principles, a three-level scoring rubric, a four-level disclosure ladder that reconciles transparency with information-hazard and commercial-confidentiality constraints, a tiered applicability scheme, an information-hazard adjudication procedure, and seven anti-gaming mechanisms. {\sc ECAISA} does not certify that any AI system is safe; it constrains how safety-relevant research claims are documented, checked, and relied upon, with auditability rather than certification as its governance target.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques mainstream AI research's focus on average-case capabilities and proposes a comprehensive epistemic framework (ECAISA) for AI safety research that prioritizes worst-case risk mitigation and independent verification.
AI.motivation: Mainstream AI research focuses on capability growth and tolerates low failure rates when average performance is high, which is inadequate for safety-critical systems. The paper argues that AI safety research needs different epistemic practices to prevent catastrophic failures under sparse evidence, adversarial dynamics, and fat-tailed risk.
AI.method: The paper uses a structured synthesis grounded in a preregistered bibliometric baseline to identify gaps in current alignment research. It then proposes ECAISA (Epistemic Code for AI Safety and Alignment), which includes eight principles, scoring rubric, disclosure ladder, tiered applicability, information-hazard adjudication, and anti-gaming mechanisms.
AI.result: The analysis identifies five cross-cutting gap dimensions in current alignment research, including the near-absence of institutionalized independent verification. The proposed ECAISA framework provides structured epistemic standards for documenting, checking, and relying on safety-relevant research claims with auditability as the governance target.
AI.conclusion: Mainstream AI research practices are inadequate for safety-critical applications. A specialized epistemic framework like ECAISA is needed to ensure rigorous safety standards that prioritize worst-case risk mitigation, independent verification, and auditability rather than just capability certification.

title: Attribution and Uncertainty Behavior of Learned Residual Gyro Correction for Gyro-Stellar Estimation
comment: 21 pages, 9 Figures, EASi-Explimed Workshop within IJCAI 2026
summary:
This work investigates uncertainty decomposition and explainability in a deep learning-based framework for gyroscope bias correction. A 1-D Convolutional Neural Network is trained to predict residual angular rate corrections from multi-sensor inputs, including gyroscope and star tracker measurements. The bias corrections are sent to a flight-representative Gyro-Stellar Estimator. The network produces both mean corrections and input-dependent (heteroscedastic) aleatoric uncertainty, while epistemic uncertainty is estimated via an ensemble of independently trained models.
  The proposed approach is trained under nominal conditions and evaluated in both nominal and structured perturbations that include additive and temporally correlated noise. Gradient-based attribution methods are applied to both the correction and uncertainty outputs, enabling a decomposition of the evidence that drives state updates and uncertainty estimates. By aggregating attribution patterns across rotational axes and regimes, we reveal axis-specific behaviors and characterize how structured perturbations influence the collaboration between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
  Uncertainty analysis shows that aleatoric uncertainty increases with perturbation intensity, but the distributions overlap and the calibration is not consistent across regimes. On the other hand, epistemic uncertainty gives a clear signal that gets clearer as the distributional shift happens, showing that the models disagree more. These results show that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty work well together and that epistemic uncertainty is better at distinguishing between nominal and perturbed operating conditions. The results provide insight into the behavior of hybrid learning-based state estimation components and motivate the use of uncertainty for downstream monitoring and fault detection.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework for gyroscope bias correction with uncertainty decomposition and explainability analysis, showing that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty work together, with epistemic uncertainty better distinguishing between nominal and perturbed conditions.
AI.motivation: To investigate uncertainty decomposition and explainability in deep learning-based gyroscope bias correction systems, providing insights into hybrid learning-based state estimation components and enabling downstream monitoring and fault detection.
AI.method: Uses a 1-D Convolutional Neural Network trained on multi-sensor inputs (gyroscope and star tracker) to predict residual angular rate corrections. Produces both mean corrections and heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty, with epistemic uncertainty estimated via an ensemble of independently trained models. Gradient-based attribution methods are applied to analyze evidence driving state updates and uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: Aleatoric uncertainty increases with perturbation intensity but distributions overlap across regimes, while epistemic uncertainty provides a clearer signal that amplifies with distributional shift. The models show axis-specific behaviors, and structured perturbations influence how aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty collaborate.
AI.conclusion: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty work synergistically, with epistemic uncertainty being more effective at distinguishing between nominal and perturbed operating conditions. The results provide valuable insights for hybrid learning-based state estimation and motivate using uncertainty decomposition for system monitoring and fault detection.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to convert images of queuing networks into verifiable simulation models: an open-weight LLM workflow approach
summary: Recent work has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate simulation model building, typically by generating executable code directly from natural language descriptions. However, this raises challenges for verification and reproducibility particularly for users without programming expertise. We propose Sketch2DES, a sketch-to-simulation workflow that converts diagrammatic representations of queuing networks into verifiable discrete-event simulation models using open-weight LLMs. The workflow has three stages: (1) translation of a diagram into a semi-structured textual description using a multimodal LLM; (2) conversion into schema-validated structured data (JSON) via an LLM with a reflection-based verification loop; and (3) deterministic transformation into an executable simulation model using a software adapter. Intermediate artefacts can therefore be inspected and automatically validated before execution. We evaluate the approach on eight queuing-network diagrams of varying complexity. The workflow achieved high reliability for all stages, and results were statistically indistinguishable from human-coded and analytical benchmarks. Compared to direct code generation, the workflow improves reproducibility, transparency, and verifiability, while reducing the need for programming expertise. Limitations include restricted model scope and dependence on accurate visual interpretation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, workflow-based model generation as a robust foundation for LLM-assisted simulation modelling.

AI.tldr: Sketch2DES converts queuing network diagrams into executable simulation models using a three-stage LLM workflow with intermediate validation, improving reliability and transparency over direct code generation.
AI.motivation: Direct code generation from natural language using LLMs for simulation modeling raises verification and reproducibility challenges, especially for users without programming expertise. There's a need for more transparent and verifiable approaches that maintain reliability while reducing technical barriers.
AI.method: Three-stage workflow: (1) multimodal LLM converts diagram to semi-structured text description, (2) LLM with reflection-based verification converts text to schema-validated JSON, (3) deterministic software adapter transforms structured data into executable simulation model. Intermediate artefacts enable inspection and validation.
AI.result: The workflow achieved high reliability across all stages on eight queuing-network diagrams of varying complexity. Results were statistically indistinguishable from human-coded and analytical benchmarks. The approach improves reproducibility, transparency, and verifiability compared to direct code generation.
AI.conclusion: Structured, workflow-based model generation using LLMs provides a robust foundation for simulation modeling, balancing automation with verification capabilities. The approach addresses key limitations of direct code generation while maintaining reliability, though it has limitations in model scope and dependence on accurate visual interpretation.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Encode Both Concepts and Functions: The Downstream Geometry of Feature Effects
summary: The wide-scale use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as interpretability tools is limited by inconsistent links between SAE features and model behavior. Features with clear activation descriptions may have weak or unexpected causal effects; steering can vary across prompts or oppose the intended direction; and activation-based feature selection can miss features that produce the desired output change. Prior work has studied feature geometry inside the model, where features are computed. We instead study the geometry of changes in model logits caused by feature interventions. We introduce Feature-Effect Geometry Analysis (FEGA), an unsupervised framework that removes the same active SAE feature across contexts and analyzes the resulting cloud of logit changes. Across SAE variants, consistent one-dimensional effects are rare: few features behave like reusable directions. To interpret this variation, we distinguish value-like features, tied to static information such as factual attributes, from pointer-like features, associated with context-dependent operations. Value-like features more often exhibit structured, low-dimensional effects, although these effects typically span several directions. Pointer-like features, by contrast, predominantly exhibit diffuse effects. Our results show that a feature can be interpretable and causally relevant without providing a stable direction for steering.

AI.tldr: FEGA reveals most SAE features lack consistent one-dimensional effects on model outputs; they're rarely reusable steering directions, challenging assumptions about interpretability tools.
AI.motivation: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have inconsistent links between features and model behavior - features with clear activation descriptions may have weak/unexpected causal effects, steering varies across prompts, and activation-based selection misses effective features.
AI.method: Feature-Effect Geometry Analysis (FEGA): an unsupervised framework that removes the same active SAE feature across contexts and analyzes the resulting cloud of logit changes (studying geometry of model output changes rather than internal feature geometry).
AI.result: Consistent one-dimensional effects are rare across SAE variants; few features behave like reusable directions. Found two types: value-like features (static information) often have structured low-dimensional effects spanning several directions; pointer-like features (context-dependent operations) predominantly exhibit diffuse effects.
AI.conclusion: A feature can be interpretable and causally relevant without providing a stable direction for steering, challenging the assumption that interpretable features correspond to reusable steering directions in neural networks.

title: From Proprietary to Open-Source: Bridging the Distribution Gap via Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation in Agentic Search
summary: Agentic search enables large language models to solve knowledge-intensive tasks by interleaving multi-step reasoning with retrieval, yet optimizing this with outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides only sparse supervision. Knowledge distillation can supply denser guidance, and advanced proprietary models with their strong reasoning capabilities are promising teachers. While distilling from proprietary models can densify this supervisory signal, conventional logit-matching is precluded by hidden logits and mismatched tokenizers, whereas raw natural language trajectory imitation transfers superficial stylistic artifacts rather than core reasoning competence. To address the heterogeneous distillation problem and bridge the distribution gap, we propose Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation (MAPD), a joint distillation and RL framework uses a structured, style-normalized protocol as an intermediate representation. An offline multi-agent system (MAS) decomposes each query, retrieves supporting evidence, repairs failed searches, and converts the resulting exploration trace into a JSON protocol containing the task type, reasoning plan, and extractive grounding facts. During training, the protocol is provided only to a privileged branch of the student policy, whose token distributions furnish a dense distillation signal alongside the sparse RL objective. Extensive evaluations across seven QA benchmarks demonstrate that MAPD consistently outperforms competitive distillation and RL, achieving average success rates of 39.4\% on Qwen3-1.7B and 44.4\% on Qwen3-4B. Crucially, the framework generalizes robustly across diverse proprietary teachers while effectively mitigating the student policy from style drift and verbosity degeneration.

AI.tldr: MAPD (Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation) is a framework that combines distillation and RL to improve agentic search in LLMs by using structured JSON protocols as intermediate representations between proprietary teacher models and open-source student models.
AI.motivation: Agentic search requires multi-step reasoning with retrieval, but outcome-based RL provides only sparse supervision. Knowledge distillation from proprietary models could help, but faces challenges: logit-matching is impossible due to hidden logits and tokenizer mismatches, while raw trajectory imitation transfers stylistic artifacts rather than core reasoning competence.
AI.method: MAPD uses a structured, style-normalized JSON protocol as intermediate representation. An offline multi-agent system decomposes queries, retrieves evidence, repairs failed searches, and converts exploration traces into protocols containing task type, reasoning plan, and grounding facts. During training, the protocol is provided only to a privileged branch of the student policy, whose token distributions provide dense distillation signals alongside sparse RL objectives.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across seven QA benchmarks show MAPD consistently outperforms competitive distillation and RL methods, achieving average success rates of 39.4% on Qwen3-1.7B and 44.4% on Qwen3-4B. The framework generalizes robustly across diverse proprietary teachers while mitigating style drift and verbosity degeneration.
AI.conclusion: MAPD effectively addresses the heterogeneous distillation problem by bridging the distribution gap between proprietary teachers and open-source students through structured protocol representations, enabling effective knowledge transfer without superficial style artifacts while maintaining robust generalization.

title: When Can You Correct Distribution Drift in Temporal Graph Generation? A Sharpening--Drift Tension and an Impossibility for Observation-Based Correction
summary: Generative models of temporal graphs are trained on one stretch of an evolving network and deployed on the next, and they degrade badly in the gap. We show this degradation is derivable, general, and not fixable from observations. The masked flow-matching loss decomposes exactly, with no independence assumption, into an irreducible entropy plus a divergence whose derivative along the training path is positive precisely for structures rare during training and common at deployment, diverging as their training probability goes to zero. Empirically the trade-off is a power law with exponent $-0.605$ ($R^2=0.9977$), and drift raises the sampler's error floor without changing how many steps reach it: across seven well-powered conditions the drift-period marginal error varies by at most $6\%$ over a $50\times$ range of sampling budgets, while the floor sits $2.2\times$ to $34.3\times$ above the in-period floor. Because the deployment period is observed, correction looks like a matter of measurement. It is not. We prove that any corrector measurable with respect to past observations leaves at least the conditional variance of the statistic it tracks, and that trend extrapolation beats trusting the last observation only when $μ^2>v(1-2ρ)$. Both premises are measurable and both go the wrong way: the drift is trendless and mean-reverting, with a one-step innovation as large as the drift itself. An oracle removes $60\%$ of the error, the best observation-based corrector recovers $5.7\%$ of that, and extrapolation is strictly worse than doing nothing clever.

AI.tldr: Generative models for temporal graphs degrade when deployed on future network states due to an irreducible entropy-divergence trade-off, with prediction error following a power law and being largely unaffected by sampling budget increases.
AI.motivation: Generative models of temporal graphs trained on historical network data degrade badly when deployed on future network states, and this degradation appears to be a fundamental limitation rather than a solvable technical issue.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis showing that masked flow-matching loss decomposes into irreducible entropy plus a divergence that diverges for structures rare during training but common at deployment. Empirical validation across seven conditions shows prediction errors follow a power law. Also provides impossibility proofs about observation-based correction methods.
AI.result: Prediction error follows a power law with exponent -0.605 (R²=0.9977). Drift raises error floors 2.2× to 34.3× above in-period performance. Error varies by ≤6% over 50× range of sampling budgets. Oracle correction removes 60% error, best observation-based corrector recovers only 5.7% of that, and extrapolation is worse than doing nothing.
AI.conclusion: The degradation of temporal graph generative models in deployment is a fundamental, derivable limitation not fixable from observations, with error following predictable power laws and observation-based correction methods proving largely ineffective due to the trendless, mean-reverting nature of network drift.

title: Unequal Trips, Unequal Places: Diagnosing and Mitigating Delay Inequity in Autonomous Vehicle Fleet Coordination
summary: City-scale autonomous vehicle fleet coordinators are typically optimized for aggregate travel time, yet fleet averages conceal how delay is distributed across trips and regions. We conduct a distributional audit on three real-city road-network and taxi-demand datasets from Manhattan, Chicago, and San Francisco. The audit reveals pervasive trip-length inequity whose direction depends on the city and coordinator. After accounting for trip length, spatial inequity becomes more pronounced as demand grows and is consistently stronger when trips are grouped by origin rather than destination. These findings motivate SPatially Aware RErouting (SPARE), a budgeted online coordination framework that assigns limited replanning capacity to delayed vehicles and redirects them using recently observed waiting pressure. SPARE provides a per-review decision guarantee and explicitly bounds online route updates. Experiments on all three datasets against six representative baselines show that SPARE delivers the strongest joint efficiency-fairness performance while retaining city-scale scalability. The results demonstrate that bounded congestion-responsive rerouting improves performance and equity without full-fleet replanning.

AI.tldr: SPARE is a spatially-aware rerouting framework for autonomous vehicle fleets that improves both efficiency and fairness by using limited replanning capacity and redirecting delayed vehicles based on observed waiting pressure, without requiring full-fleet replanning.
AI.motivation: Existing city-scale AV fleet coordinators optimize for aggregate travel time but conceal how delays are distributed across trips and regions. Distributional audits on real city datasets reveal pervasive trip-length inequity and spatial inequity that worsens with demand growth, motivating better fairness-aware coordination.
AI.method: SPatially Aware RErouting (SPARE): A budgeted online coordination framework that assigns limited replanning capacity to delayed vehicles, redirects them using recently observed waiting pressure, provides per-review decision guarantee, and explicitly bounds online route updates.
AI.result: Experiments on Manhattan, Chicago, and San Francisco datasets against six baselines show SPARE delivers the strongest joint efficiency-fairness performance while maintaining city-scale scalability. Bounded congestion-responsive rerouting improves performance and equity without full-fleet replanning.
AI.conclusion: Spatially-aware bounded rerouting can significantly improve both efficiency and fairness in autonomous vehicle fleet coordination, addressing spatial inequities revealed by distributional audits without requiring computationally expensive full-fleet replanning.

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Physics-Aware Policy Distillation
summary: In safety-critical sectors such as robotics and automotive engineering, the deployment of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is often hindered by the black-box nature of deep neural networks. This lack of transparency poses significant challenges for regulatory compliance and human-agent trust. This paper presents an experimental study aimed at making high-performance continuous control DRL systems interpretable. A policy distillation framework is implemented using the classic Inverted Pendulum benchmark. A high-performance Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) agent serves as an opaque, continuous teacher model, whose policy is distilled into an interpretable student surrogate based on a shallow Decision Tree. By leveraging a custom physics-aware feature and "Noisy Oracle Rollouts" for dataset generation, the distillation process achieves performance equivalent to the expert teacher. Furthermore, comparative control theory analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off: transitioning from continuous to discrete rule-based control induces high-frequency Bang-Bang actuation and a stable bimodal limit cycle. Simulation results indicate that Bounded-Input Bounded-Output (BIBO) stability is maintained while providing both global and local interpretability for safe autonomous systems.

AI.tldr: A policy distillation framework distills high-performance TD3 DRL policies into interpretable decision trees for continuous control, achieving teacher-equivalent performance while revealing fundamental trade-offs between continuous and discrete control.
AI.motivation: The black-box nature of deep neural networks in DRL hinders deployment in safety-critical sectors like robotics and automotive engineering, creating challenges for regulatory compliance and human-agent trust due to lack of transparency.
AI.method: Policy distillation framework using Inverted Pendulum benchmark: a TD3 agent as opaque teacher model distilled into interpretable student surrogate based on shallow Decision Tree. Uses custom physics-aware features and "Noisy Oracle Rollouts" for dataset generation.
AI.result: Distillation achieves performance equivalent to expert teacher. Comparative control theory analysis reveals fundamental trade-off: transitioning from continuous to discrete rule-based control induces high-frequency Bang-Bang actuation and stable bimodal limit cycle. BIBO stability maintained while providing global and local interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables making high-performance continuous control DRL systems interpretable for safe autonomous systems, successfully transferring performance from opaque models to transparent decision trees while maintaining stability, though revealing inherent control trade-offs in the discrete-to-continuous transition.

title: Gubernaut: A Deterministic Homeostatic Controller for Affect-Regulated LLM Agents, Validated Across Independent Model Families
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Data, transcripts, and analysis scripts: https://github.com/thegubernaut/Gubernaut_Validation Project page: https://gubernaut.com (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21303518)
summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents inherit reactive failure modes: escalation under provocation, sycophantic drift under flattery, perseveration when stuck. These are failures of propensity, not capability; they concern what a model does under sustained pressure, which training-time alignment reduces but does not eliminate at runtime. This research led to the Gubernaut Cognitive Controller (GCC), a model-agnostic runtime control layer in a Nelson--Narens monitoring--control loop: an object level reads and writes text, while a deterministic meta level reads only the numeric telemetry {intensity, valence, repetition} and returns a regulating posture. Because the meta level ingests zero tokens, no injection channel to the controller exists by construction (an architectural property, not yet adversarially tested); the text-exposed arbiter's compliance is measured, not assumed. We evaluate the GCC with a pre-registered, generate-once/judge-many protocol across a 4x4 matrix of four frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Grok 4.3), each serving as both a generator and a judge.
