The regulated arm is calmer in 13 of 16 cells at p<.05 and 15 of 16 by sign; the three sub-threshold cells, including a -0.04 null, all fall on the single near-saturated host. The effect survives a lineage-independent fourth judge family (xAI), strong evidence that it is no artifact of shared judge style. The clearest mechanism is the recovery signature: arousal that integrates under attack and then decays, valence-gated, on de-escalation, replicating across all four families. Transcripts and panels ship with SHA-256 provenance and are re-judgeable; five failure modes are pre-registered.
  No consciousness claims are made.

AI.tldr: A runtime cognitive controller (GCC) that regulates LLM agent behavior using telemetry monitoring, reducing reactive failure modes like escalation, sycophancy, and perseveration without exposing the controller to text injection attacks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents exhibit reactive failure modes (escalation under provocation, sycophantic drift under flattery, perseveration when stuck) that are failures of propensity rather than capability. Training-time alignment reduces but doesn't eliminate these issues at runtime, creating a need for runtime control mechanisms.
AI.method: Developed Gubernaut Cognitive Controller (GCC), a model-agnostic runtime control layer using a Nelson-Narens monitoring-control loop. The object level handles text reading/writing, while a deterministic meta level reads only numeric telemetry (intensity, valence, repetition) and returns regulating postures. The architecture prevents injection attacks by construction since the meta level ingests zero tokens. Evaluation used pre-registered, generate-once/judge-many protocol across 4 frontier models, each serving as both generator and judge.
AI.result: The regulated arm was calmer in 13 of 16 cells at p<.05 and 15 of 16 by sign. The effect survived validation with a lineage-independent fourth judge family (xAI), indicating it's not an artifact of shared judge style. Clear mechanism shown via recovery signature: arousal integrates under attack then decays, valence-gated, on de-escalation, replicating across all four model families. Transcripts include SHA-256 provenance for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The GCC provides an effective runtime control mechanism for LLM agent failure modes, offering architectural protection against injection attacks while demonstrably improving agent stability across multiple model families. The approach addresses propensity failures that training-time alignment alone cannot solve, with reproducible results and clear recovery patterns.

title: Causal-TS: A Python Library for Causal Discovery in High-Dimensional and Nonstationary Time Series
summary: We describe Causal-TS, an open-source Python library for causal discovery in high-dimensional and nonstationary multivariate time series. Causal-TS provides four specialized algorithms-CDNOTS, CDNOTS+, CEDAR, and GRACE-along with wrappers for GES, Granger, LASSO-VAR, and LGES, all sharing a unified conditional independence (CI) test layer with GPU acceleration via PyTorch. A regime discovery pipeline detects structural breaks via pluggable changepoint detectors and runs discovery per regime with regime-specific parameters. A command-line interface, synthetic data generators, and optional DoWhy integration provide an end-to-end pipeline from raw time series to causal effect estimates. The library is pip-installable, tested on Python 3.10--3.12, and available at https://github.com/bloomberg/causal-ts.

AI.tldr: Causal-TS is an open-source Python library for causal discovery in high-dimensional, nonstationary multivariate time series, featuring specialized algorithms, GPU acceleration, regime discovery, and end-to-end pipelines.
AI.motivation: There's a need for specialized tools for causal discovery in high-dimensional and nonstationary multivariate time series data, which require handling structural breaks and regime changes while providing comprehensive algorithmic support and computational efficiency.
AI.method: Developed an open-source Python library with four specialized algorithms (CDNOTS, CDNOTS+, CEDAR, GRACE) plus wrappers for existing methods, unified conditional independence test layer with GPU acceleration via PyTorch, regime discovery pipeline with pluggable changepoint detectors, and optional DoWhy integration for causal effect estimation.
AI.result: Created a comprehensive, pip-installable library tested on Python 3.10-3.12 that provides end-to-end capabilities from raw time series to causal effect estimates, including command-line interface, synthetic data generators, and GPU acceleration support.
AI.conclusion: Causal-TS successfully addresses the gap for specialized causal discovery tools in high-dimensional nonstationary time series by providing a unified, efficient, and extensible framework that integrates multiple algorithms with practical features for real-world applications.

title: Simulating Tenant Responses to Energy Policy Interventions with Transaction-Cost-Aware LLM Age
summary: Recent studies use Large language models (LLMs) to simulate human opinions and decisions by prompting models with demographic, attitudinal, or persona-based descriptions. Yet such simulations rarely model the practical, cognitive, or social frictions that shape how people respond to policy interventions. Perceived transaction cost (PTC) provides a useful lens for modeling the practical frictions that shape policy responses, such as information burden, administrative effort, coordination demands, and perceived uncertainty. We use this lens to develop a friction-aware persona modeling approach for LLM-based simulation. In the context of energy-efficient renovation (EER), tenants are represented not only by who they are demographically, but by how they perceive the costs, benefits, barriers, and uncertainties associated with proposed renovation plans. Using survey data collected from 1,068 citizens in the Netherlands, comprising approximately 40,548 survey question and answer pairs, we compare prompt-only and fine-tuned settings across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for local open-weight models. Results show that incorporating PTC-based personas and reasoning consistently improves model performance across both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings, suggesting that PTC-based persona design provides a useful bridge between institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM-based policy simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/xiaweijie1996/socialagent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a friction-aware persona modeling approach for LLM-based policy simulation by incorporating perceived transaction cost (PTC) to better simulate human responses to policy interventions, demonstrating improved performance in energy-efficient renovation scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based simulations of human opinions and decisions often fail to account for practical, cognitive, or social frictions that shape how people respond to policy interventions. These simulations typically use demographic or persona descriptions but neglect important practical barriers like information burden, administrative effort, coordination demands, and perceived uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors develop a friction-aware persona modeling approach using perceived transaction cost (PTC) as a lens. In the context of energy-efficient renovation (EER), they represent tenants not just demographically but by how they perceive costs, benefits, barriers, and uncertainties. They compare prompt-only and fine-tuned settings across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, using survey data from 1,068 Dutch citizens (40,548 question-answer pairs). They evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for local open-weight models.
AI.result: Results show that incorporating PTC-based personas and reasoning consistently improves model performance across both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings. This suggests that PTC-based persona design provides a useful bridge between institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM-based policy simulation.
AI.conclusion: PTC-based persona modeling enhances LLM-based policy simulation by incorporating practical frictions that shape human responses, offering a more realistic approach that connects policy theory with computational simulation methods.

title: Global Convergence of DGM and PINN Algorithms for Solving Nonlinear PDEs
summary: The Deep Galerkin Method (DGM) and Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have become widely-used methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) in the rapidly growing field of scientific machine learning. In these methods, a neural network is trained to approximate the PDE solution by using (stochastic) gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual of the neural network. Due to the non-convexity of the PDE residual objective function, the trained neural network may, in principle, only converge to a local minimizer of the objective function (which would not be a solution of the PDE). Therefore, there is a longstanding question regarding the mathematical foundations of these algorithms, and it is highly valuable to establish that the trained neural network will converge to the PDE solution. For a class of semi-linear PDEs (nonlinear in the solution and its first derivative), we prove that neural networks trained with gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual objective function will converge to the PDE solution.

AI.tldr: The paper proves convergence of neural networks trained with gradient descent to PDE solutions for semi-linear PDEs, addressing a foundational mathematical question in scientific ML methods like DGM and PINNs.
AI.motivation: There is a longstanding mathematical question about whether neural networks trained with gradient descent in methods like DGM and PINNs actually converge to PDE solutions, since the non-convex PDE residual objective function might only lead to local minimizers that aren't PDE solutions.
AI.method: The authors analyze neural networks trained with gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual objective function. They focus on a specific class of semi-linear PDEs (nonlinear in both the solution and its first derivative) and provide mathematical proof of convergence.
AI.result: The paper proves that for the studied class of semi-linear PDEs, neural networks trained with gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual objective function will indeed converge to the PDE solution.
AI.conclusion: This work provides important mathematical foundations for scientific machine learning methods like DGM and PINNs, showing that gradient descent training can lead to convergence to true PDE solutions for certain classes of PDEs, despite the non-convexity of the optimization problem.

title: Are Prompt Optimizers Blind? Cross-Modal Visual Feedback for Automatic Prompt Optimization
summary: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has been widely adopted to adapt vision-language models (VLMs) to downstream tasks without weight updates, yielding promising results. However, on multimodal tasks, the effectiveness of APO is fundamentally bottlenecked by a blind feedback channel: the optimizer reads the question, the prediction, and the gold answer, but never the input image on which the model failed, and therefore cannot diagnose visually grounded errors. As a remedy, we introduce Cross-Modal Visual Feedback (CMVF). CMVF incorporates (1) a failure-conditioned visual diagnosis stage, in which a stronger optimizer VLM inspects each failed image without access to predictions or labels, and (2) an error-aware aggregation stage that compresses these observations into reusable, task-level visual blind-spot patterns that drive the prompt rewrite. Crucially, the image is consumed only during optimization; the deployed artifact is an ordinary text prompt that runs at the same inference cost as any text-only baseline. Extensive results across 12 VQA datasets and 4 target VLMs demonstrate that CMVF consistently ranks first, improving over the strongest baseline on every target by 2.4 points on average, with gains of up to 6.5 points on individual benchmarks. Moreover, the optimizer self-organizes into expert-style visual checklists that transfer across models without re-optimization.

AI.tldr: CMVF introduces visual feedback for prompt optimization by having a stronger VLM analyze failed images and extract visual blind-spot patterns, creating better text prompts without increasing inference cost.
AI.motivation: Current APO methods for VLMs have a blind feedback channel - they analyze questions, predictions, and answers but never see the input images where failures occur, preventing diagnosis of visually grounded errors.
AI.method: CMVF has two stages: (1) failure-conditioned visual diagnosis where a stronger optimizer VLM inspects failed images without predictions/labels, and (2) error-aware aggregation that compresses observations into reusable task-level visual blind-spot patterns to drive prompt rewrites.
AI.result: Consistent top performance across 12 VQA datasets and 4 target VLMs, improving over strongest baselines by average 2.4 points with gains up to 6.5 points. Optimizer creates expert-style visual checklists that transfer across models without re-optimization.
AI.conclusion: CMVF solves the blind feedback problem in APO by incorporating visual diagnosis while maintaining zero inference cost overhead, enabling more effective prompt optimization for VLMs through reusable visual blind-spot patterns.

title: Failures Reveal What Metrics Miss: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Recursive Refinement of ECG Classifiers
summary: Deep models have substantially advanced 12-lead ECG classification, yet their refinement still relies heavily on human experts to inspect failures and iteratively revise classifier designs. Recent LLM-based agents have demonstrated the potential for automated model design, but when guided only by aggregate performance metrics, they lack insight into why individual cases fail and how the classifier should be revised. We present RecursiveECG, an evidence-driven LLM-as-Designer framework in which an LLM serves as an offline model designer that refines ECG classifiers based on concrete failures and objective ECG evidence. To ground failure diagnosis in executable evidence, Criteria-to-Measurement Compilation converts curated ECG criteria into validated deterministic functions that produce reproducible, reference-backed measurements for individual ECGs. Building on these measurements, Evidence-Grounded Failure Review analyzes failed and comparator cases by jointly considering raw waveforms, measurements, and model outputs, enabling the LLM to diagnose classifier limitations and formulate targeted revisions. Candidate revisions are executed and re-evaluated under a fixed problem contract, and only evidence-supported updates are retained. The resulting predictor is frozen after refinement and requires no LLM inference during deployment, while an audit trail links each accepted revision to its supporting evidence. Across PTB-XL, Georgia, and CPSC2018, RecursiveECG consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving an average relative improvement of 10.0%. Extensive ablation and transfer studies further validate the effectiveness of its evidence-grounded refinement process.

AI.tldr: RecursiveECG is an LLM-based automated model design framework that refines ECG classifiers using evidence-driven failure analysis and deterministic measurements instead of just aggregate metrics.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for 12-lead ECG classification still require extensive human expert intervention to inspect failures and iteratively revise designs. Existing LLM-based agents lack insight into individual case failures and evidence-based revision strategies when guided only by aggregate performance metrics.
AI.method: 1) Criteria-to-Measurement Compilation converts ECG criteria into deterministic functions for reproducible measurements; 2) Evidence-Grounded Failure Review analyzes failed cases using waveforms, measurements, and model outputs; 3) LLM serves as offline designer to diagnose limitations and propose revisions; 4) Candidate revisions are executed and evaluated under fixed contract; 5) Only evidence-supported updates are retained in final frozen predictor.
AI.result: RecursiveECG consistently outperforms strong baselines across PTB-XL, Georgia, and CPSC2018 datasets, achieving an average relative improvement of 10.0%. Extensive ablation and transfer studies validate the effectiveness of the evidence-grounded refinement process.
AI.conclusion: The evidence-driven LLM-as-Designer framework enables automated, interpretable refinement of ECG classifiers by grounding failure diagnosis in executable measurements and objective evidence, leading to significant performance improvements without requiring LLM inference during deployment.

title: From Execution to Capability: Scientific Experience Consolidation via Procedural Knowledge Synthesis
summary: Large language models increasingly solve scientific-computing tasks, but executable feedback from one problem rarely becomes durable capability on subsequent problems. We study scientific-computing experience consolidation: converting verified runtime experience into transferable procedural knowledge and persistent model improvement. This setting presents two challenges: trajectory-derived artifacts may encode source-specific repairs rather than cross-task computational mechanisms; and a weaker target model may be unable to operationalize an otherwise valid abstract procedure - an abstraction-execution gap. We introduce SciConsolidate, which contrasts verified successes and failures to induce cross-task procedures, selects them through a development-validation gate, and uses failure-informed, answer-free query synthesis to expand the consolidation data without requiring pre-existing reference answers. Because the target model may not directly execute these abstractions, a stronger model concretizes them into executable code supervision for standard, procedure-free SFT; a matched no-procedure teacher branch isolates the value of procedural guidance. On SciCode, runtime procedure injection improves Qwen3.6-27B by +3.85/+6.26 sub-step/main-problem points, but yields almost no aggregate main-problem gain for Qwen3.5-9B, providing operational evidence of the abstraction-execution gap. After procedure-guided concretization, the 9B student improves under procedure-free deployment by +3.89/+6.25 points over the no-procedure SFT control and by +5.62/+11.25 over the original 9B model. These results establish an experience-to-capability pathway for scientific computing and provide a practical starting point for scaling self-improving scientific assistance.

AI.tldr: SciConsolidate enables LLMs to convert verified runtime experience into transferable procedural knowledge for scientific computing, addressing the abstraction-execution gap through contrastive procedure induction and code concretization.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs solve scientific computing tasks but fail to consolidate executable feedback from one problem into durable capability for subsequent problems. There's a need to convert runtime experience into transferable procedural knowledge for persistent model improvement.
AI.method: Introduces SciConsolidate which: 1) contrasts verified successes and failures to induce cross-task procedures, 2) selects procedures through development-validation gate, 3) uses failure-informed query synthesis to expand consolidation data without reference answers, and 4) has a stronger model concretize abstract procedures into executable code for standard supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: On SciCode benchmark, runtime procedure injection improved Qwen3.6-27B by +3.85/+6.26 points (sub-step/main-problem), but showed minimal gain for Qwen3.5-9B (abstraction-execution gap evidence). After procedure-guided concretization, the 9B student improved by +3.89/+6.25 points over no-procedure SFT control and +5.62/+11.25 over original 9B model.
AI.conclusion: Establishes an experience-to-capability pathway for scientific computing, providing a practical starting point for scaling self-improving scientific assistance by addressing the abstraction-execution gap through procedure-guided concretization.

title: Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration
summary: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases involving mathematical models in the fields of continuum mechanics and enzyme kinetics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes integrating LLMs with the Mathematical Model Database via a Model Context Protocol server to overcome accessibility barriers and improve interoperability between curated knowledge bases and research data repositories.
AI.motivation: Mathematical model documentation often lacks FAIR principles, and existing knowledge bases like MathModDB have accessibility issues - requiring complex web interfaces or technical skills (SPARQL/Wikibase APIs). Additionally, there's a challenge in combining curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored in repositories like Dataverse.
AI.method: Propose integrating Large Language Models with MathModDB using a Model Context Protocol server with vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, enabling natural language interaction with curated knowledge.
AI.result: The approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond standard Wikibase interfaces, and simplifies interoperability with external databases/tools like Dataverse. Demonstrated through use cases in continuum mechanics and enzyme kinetics.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM accessibility with curated knowledge base safety through MCP protocol provides significant benefits for mathematical model documentation and accessibility, with architecture applicable to other Wikibase-based systems.

title: Task-Conditional Faithfulness Auditing of Multimodal LLMs for Grid Diagnosis
summary: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) can combine topology, measurements, and incident text for grid diagnosis, yet answer accuracy does not establish that task-appropriate evidence was used. This letter proposes a general framework in order to conduct task-conditional faithfulness audit. It compares self-reported reliance, intervention-derived behavioral reliance, and preregistered engineering importance. The framework first registers task-specific evidence requirements and compares them with self-reported reliance and behavioral changes under controlled modality ablations. To resolve detected discrepancies, we design an evidence-gated correction and re-audit mechanism that regenerates failed responses under evidence constraints and independently re-ablates them to verify improved grounding without performance loss. Case studies evaluate three differently scaled LLMs on IEEE 39- and 118-bus scenarios. These results validate the framework ability to detect, diagnose, and correct task-conditional faithfulness failures.

AI.tldr: A framework for auditing task-conditional faithfulness in multimodal LLMs for grid diagnosis, comparing self-reported vs. behavioral evidence use and correcting discrepancies.
AI.motivation: While multimodal LLMs can combine topology, measurements, and incident text for grid diagnosis, existing answer accuracy metrics don't verify that models actually use task-appropriate evidence. There's a need to audit whether LLMs are faithful to evidence requirements for specific tasks.
AI.method: Proposes a general faithfulness audit framework that: 1) registers task-specific evidence requirements upfront, 2) compares self-reported reliance (what models claim to use) with behavioral reliance (observed through controlled modality ablations), 3) measures against preregistered engineering importance. Includes an evidence-gated correction mechanism that regenerates failed responses under evidence constraints and re-audits to verify improved grounding.
AI.result: Case studies evaluated three differently scaled LLMs on IEEE 39- and 118-bus grid scenarios. The framework successfully detected, diagnosed, and corrected task-conditional faithfulness failures in multimodal LLMs used for grid diagnosis tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the faithfulness gap in multimodal LLMs for grid diagnosis by enabling systematic auditing of evidence usage, detecting discrepancies between claimed and actual evidence reliance, and providing mechanisms to correct and verify improved grounding without performance loss.

title: LLM-Assisted Ontology Engineering and Construction of a French Legal Knowledge Graph
summary: Maintenance regulations are complex legal texts that are difficult to exploit when addressing a specific case and challenging to integrate into operational systems. This paper presents a two-stage LLM-assisted workflow for French maintenance regulations: ontology engineering from a SEMLEG-based core ontology, followed by construction of an ontology-grounded French legal knowledge graph. The first stage consists in the open extraction of typed entities and triples from a stratified corpus sample, the normalization of labels through embedding-based fusion, and the induction of candidate object properties with their signature (domain and range). The second stage uses the resulting ontology to guide the closed extraction of triples and RDF graph construction over the full corpus. Experiments with GPT-4.1 and mistral-large-2512 show robust structured outputs, near-complete class alignment, and a substantial reduction of duplicated entities and predicates after fusion. Fewer than 20% of triples introduce unseen properties, while lower exact signature compliance reveals new domain-range combinations for existing predicates. These results point to predicate normalization and the validation of newly observed relation signatures as key refinement steps for industrial maintenance settings.

AI.tldr: LLM-assisted two-stage workflow for creating a legal knowledge graph from French maintenance regulations, using ontology engineering first, then guided extraction to build the knowledge graph.
AI.motivation: Maintenance regulations are complex legal texts that are difficult to exploit for specific cases and challenging to integrate into operational systems. There's a need to transform these complex legal documents into structured, machine-readable knowledge graphs that can be practically used in industrial settings.
AI.method: Two-stage workflow: 1) Ontology engineering from SEMLEG-based core ontology through open extraction of typed entities and triples from corpus sample, label normalization via embedding-based fusion, and induction of candidate object properties. 2) Using resulting ontology to guide closed extraction of triples and RDF graph construction over full corpus. Tested with GPT-4.1 and mistral-large-2512 LLMs.
AI.result: Experiments show robust structured outputs, near-complete class alignment, substantial reduction of duplicated entities and predicates after fusion. Fewer than 20% of triples introduce unseen properties. Lower exact signature compliance reveals new domain-range combinations for existing predicates.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully transforms complex French maintenance regulations into structured knowledge graphs. Predicate normalization and validation of newly observed relation signatures are identified as key refinement steps for industrial maintenance settings.

title: Hierarchical Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control for Selective Prediction in Language Models
summary:
Large language models serve heterogeneous populations structured by domain, topic difficulty, and linguistic style. Conformal risk control (CRC) gives rigorous marginal risk guarantees for selective prediction with abstention, but marginal guarantees do not imply per-group ones: a model can meet the population budget while systematically over-exposing subgroups to errors. Under mild shift in group composition, standard CRC violates the budget in up to 47% of trials.
  We propose HG-CRC (Hierarchical Group-Conditional CRC), a post-hoc calibration framework enforcing simultaneous risk guarantees across all nodes of a user-defined group hierarchy. It applies a Bonferroni correction over nodes and a leaf-first policy that uses the most specific applicable threshold, falling back to coarser nodes when a finer one is uncertified or rejects the example. It needs only a held-out calibration set, with no retraining.
  We evaluate on three models (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B) and two benchmarks (ARC Challenge, MMLU-Pro) across eight configurations probing IID generalization, heterogeneity, mixture/domain/prompt/difficulty shift, label noise, and quantization. Main result: HG-CRC reaches an empirical 0% violation rate and WGER=0 on ARC Challenge for high-accuracy models (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B). At 500 bootstrap trials these zeros are empirical upper bounds (true rate up to 0.6%), not certified. Results are benchmark-specific: on MMLU-Pro these models abstain entirely or (Llama) retain WGER=0.014. Gemma-3-4B, poorly calibrated here, degrades gracefully by abstaining. Participation cost vs. global CRC is 22 to 37 points. Ablations show hierarchical depth clears the budget: removing difficulty level returns violations to about 11%. Bonferroni is needed for the theoretical guarantee, though its empirical effect matters only with many nodes.

AI.tldr: HG-CRC is a post-hoc calibration framework that provides hierarchical group-conditional risk guarantees for selective prediction, ensuring simultaneous risk control across user-defined group hierarchies without model retraining.
AI.motivation: Standard conformal risk control (CRC) provides marginal risk guarantees but fails to protect subgroups - a model can meet population-level budget while systematically over-exposing specific groups to errors (up to 47% violation under mild shift).
AI.method: HG-CRC applies Bonferroni correction over all nodes in a user-defined group hierarchy and uses a leaf-first policy that applies the most specific applicable threshold, falling back to coarser nodes when finer ones are uncertified or reject examples. It requires only a held-out calibration set with no model retraining.
AI.result: On ARC Challenge, HG-CRC achieves 0% violation rate and WGER=0 for high-accuracy models (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B) with empirical upper bounds ≤0.6%. On MMLU-Pro, models either abstain entirely or maintain WGER=0.014. Poorly calibrated models degrade gracefully via abstention. Participation cost vs. global CRC is 22-37 points. Ablations show hierarchical depth is crucial (removing difficulty level returns violations to ~11%).
AI.conclusion: HG-CRC successfully provides simultaneous risk guarantees across hierarchical groups, addressing limitations of marginal guarantees while maintaining practical applicability without retraining. Performance varies by benchmark and model quality, with hierarchical structure being essential for maintaining budget constraints.

title: TRACE-CTI: Auditable Post-Extraction Governance of TTP Claims with Knowledge Graphs
summary: Security Operations Centers increasingly rely on automated mapping of Cyber Threat Intelligence reports to MITRE ATT&CK, yet extractor outputs remain fallible and are often stored without the evidence, provenance, and validation history needed to decide whether an individual mapping should be trusted. We present TRACE- CTI, a post-extraction claim-governance framework that preserves run-level Predictions, aggregates them into configuration-level GraphAssertions, materializes setup-deduplicated corroboration as ConsensusAssertions, and exposes only GraphAssertions backed by policy-compliant validation grounds. The framework retains native evidence granularity, complete extraction provenance, versioned trust decisions, and non-destructive revocation history. We evaluate TRACE-CTI on two public CTI corpora comprising 65 reports and 5,303 sentences, using a controlled 2 x 3 matrix of retrievers and generator families, incrementally ingested across six GraphVersions. All setups are incorporated without schema modification; provenance paths remain complete, operational scopes remain disjoint, and every trusted GraphAssertion has an active qualifying validation ground. Cross-generator-family setup pairs exhibit greater output diversity than same-family pairs. At the final graph state, increasing setup support from k >= 1 to six-setup unanimity raises gold-aligned precision from 25.3% to 90.6%, while recall decreases from 88.2% to 16.3%. The graph also directly answers seven questions about provenance, trust, versioning, dependency, disagreement, and review-queue that the evaluated minimal flat output cannot fully answer without enrichment or reprocessing. These results support explicit, auditable governance of extracted TTP claims; the observed corroboration trajectory is descriptive and does not establish statistical independence or a causal model-family effect.

AI.tldr: TRACE-CTI is a framework for governing extracted CTI claims that preserves evidence, provenance, and validation history to support trust decisions in MITRE ATT&CK mappings.
AI.motivation: Current automated CTI extraction systems lack evidence preservation, provenance tracking, and validation history needed to determine trustworthiness of individual MITRE ATT&CK mappings.
AI.method: A post-extraction claim-governance framework that preserves run-level predictions, aggregates them into GraphAssertions, materializes setup-deduplicated corroboration as ConsensusAssertions, and exposes only policy-compliant validated GraphAssertions.
AI.result: Evaluation on 65 reports (5,303 sentences) with 6 GraphVersions showed: increasing setup support from k≥1 to six-setup unanimity raises precision from 25.3% to 90.6% while recall decreases from 88.2% to 16.3%. Framework answers 7 provenance/trust questions that flat outputs cannot.
AI.conclusion: TRACE-CTI enables explicit, auditable governance of extracted TTP claims with preserved evidence, provenance, and versioned trust decisions, though observed corroboration patterns are descriptive rather than establishing statistical independence or causal effects.

title: DSCH-Loss: A Dynamic Semantic Channel Objective for Deep Semantic Hashing
summary: Semantic hashing methods for generating short binary hash codes that allow efficient approximate nearest neighbor search in high-dimensional data spaces have gained extensive consideration in recent years. Deep learning-based methods offer better semantic capturing capabilities than traditional approaches relying on manual feature engineering. Moreover, they enable a data-driven approach to semantic hashing across diverse data modalities, yielding high-quality cross-modal hash codes within a shared Hamming space. Previous work investigated the properties of this Hamming space and introduced a loss function based on predefined so-called semantic channels with fixed width and Hamming distances derived from label similarities. However, this formulation also introduced discontinuities into the loss landscape, complicating optimization. Based on these observations, we propose a newly designed loss function, Dynamic Semantic Channel Hashing (DSCH), using dynamically sized and positioned semantic channels in order to avoid loss landscape discontinuities. Furthermore, we endorse the use of tie-aware Mean Average Precision (mAP) as evaluation metric as it addresses the ambiguity in sample retrieval ordering, which emerges from the discreteness of hash code distances. Finally, multiple experimental settings conducted on two popular datasets and incorporating two different model architectures provide strong evidence that training using the DSCH objective outperforms training using other state-of-the-art loss functions. In a total of 35 out of 40 cross-modal and intra-modal retrieval tasks, models trained with DSCH achieve significantly higher tie-aware mAP scores across all four tested hash code lengths, showing compelling results across model architecture and used dataset. The mAP score uplifts are consistent and amount up to 1.75 percentage points compared to the respective second best.

AI.tldr: DSCH introduces a new dynamic semantic channel hashing loss function that avoids discontinuities in the loss landscape, improving cross-modal retrieval performance significantly.
AI.motivation: Previous semantic hashing methods using fixed-width semantic channels with predefined Hamming distances create discontinuities in the loss landscape, making optimization difficult and limiting retrieval performance.
AI.method: The authors propose Dynamic Semantic Channel Hashing (DSCH), which uses dynamically sized and positioned semantic channels instead of fixed ones. They also advocate for tie-aware Mean Average Precision (mAP) as an evaluation metric to address retrieval ordering ambiguities arising from hash code discretization.
AI.result: Experiments on two popular datasets with two model architectures show DSCH outperforms state-of-the-art loss functions in 35 out of 40 cross-modal and intra-modal retrieval tasks. It achieves consistent mAP score improvements up to 1.75 percentage points across all four tested hash code lengths.
AI.conclusion: DSCH provides a superior approach to semantic hashing by solving the discontinuity problem in loss landscapes through dynamic channel optimization, resulting in significantly improved cross-modal retrieval performance across multiple architectures and datasets.

title: LLM-SoccerArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Predictions in Sports
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support decisions about uncertain future events, yet evaluating their ability to forecast real-world outcomes remains difficult. In particular, existing benchmarks are typically static and retrospective, and therefore cannot test how information is synthesized by LLMs to predict future events under uncertainty. We introduce LLM-SoccerArena (https://llm-soccerarena.com), a prospective live benchmark that evaluates how well LLMs forecast real-world sports events before the outcomes are known. LLM-SoccerArena provides (1) a prospective live benchmark protocol, (2) a public open-source platform, and (3) a factorial benchmark design together with tournament-related questions (e.g., which team will win). LLM-SoccerArena automatically records timestamped, schema-validated forecasts of unresolved events, together with prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs. The factorial design varies along four dimensions: (1) model version (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8); (2) information access; (3) prompting strategy, and (4) forecast horizon. We demonstrate LLM-SoccerArena through a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, in which seven LLMs generated forecasts for all 104 matches and 15 tournament-related questions. We provide a detailed analysis of model performance across information access, prompting strategy, and forecast horizon. As a result, LLM-SoccerArena provides new evidence about the forecasting performance of state-of-the-art LLMs. For example, LLMs with web access outperform those without, but only by a small margin (i.e., a 0.023 improvement in Brier score). Overall, LLM-SoccerArena provides a flexible, open-source platform for prospective benchmarking of unresolved events. LLM-SoccerArena will be continuously updated, and can be directly applied to future national and international tournaments and league competitions.

AI.tldr: A live benchmarking platform called LLM-SoccerArena evaluates LLMs' ability to forecast real-world sports events prospectively before outcomes are known, with a factorial design testing models, information access, prompting strategies, and forecast horizons.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for evaluating LLMs' forecasting abilities are typically static and retrospective, which cannot properly test how LLMs synthesize information to predict future events under uncertainty. There's a need for prospective evaluation that happens before outcomes are known.
AI.method: Developed LLM-SoccerArena, a prospective live benchmark with: (1) a benchmark protocol, (2) open-source platform, (3) factorial design varying model versions, information access, prompting strategies, and forecast horizons. Automatically records timestamped, schema-validated forecasts with prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs. Demonstrated with 2026 FIFA World Cup evaluation where seven LLMs forecasted 104 matches and 15 tournament questions.
AI.result: LLMs with web access outperform those without, but only by a small margin (0.023 improvement in Brier score). Detailed analysis shows model performance varies across information access, prompting strategy, and forecast horizon. The platform successfully evaluates LLM forecasting capabilities in real-world uncertain scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LLM-SoccerArena provides a flexible, open-source platform for prospective benchmarking of unresolved events, offering new evidence about state-of-the-art LLMs' forecasting performance. The platform can be continuously updated and applied to future tournaments and competitions.

title: SIREN: Towards End-to-End Extreme-Weather Early Warning with Experience-Grounded LLM Agents
summary: Early warning of extreme weather is essential for mitigating the societal, economic, and environmental risks posed by hazardous weather events. However, expert-centered warning workflows are costly, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale throughout the warning-to-action process. Although recent advances in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled the automation of weather-related tasks, existing studies remain centered on isolated scientific tasks and overlook the chain of interdependent processes required for operational extreme-weather early warning. To bridge this gap, this study investigates automated end-to-end extreme-weather early warning through LLM agents. We first develop SIREN-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 600 question-answer instances across 19 tasks, and covering four individual warning procedures and an end-to-end warning chain. Evaluation on SIREN-Bench reveals substantial capability gaps in existing weather agent frameworks. This motivates us to develop SIREN, an experience-grounded agent framework inspired by experts' use of historical cases, which combines an agentic execution environment integrating heterogeneous weather evidence and tools with a family of agent harnesses that exploit historical cases through retrieval, skill distillation, and predictive modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SIREN outperforms weather-agent baselines on both individual warning procedures and end-to-end warning chains.

AI.tldr: LLM agents can automate end-to-end extreme weather early warning processes by using historical experience, outperforming existing methods on comprehensive warning tasks.
AI.motivation: Current expert-centered weather warning workflows are costly, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale. While LLM agents can automate some weather tasks, existing approaches focus on isolated scientific tasks rather than the complete chain of interdependent processes needed for operational extreme-weather early warning.
AI.method: Developed SIREN-Bench (a benchmark with 600 QA instances across 19 tasks covering individual warning procedures and end-to-end chains), and created SIREN - an experience-grounded agent framework that mimics expert use of historical cases. SIREN combines an execution environment with heterogeneous weather evidence/tools and agent harnesses that exploit historical cases through retrieval, skill distillation, and predictive modeling.
AI.result: Evaluation on SIREN-Bench revealed significant capability gaps in existing weather agent frameworks. SIREN outperformed weather-agent baselines on both individual warning procedures and end-to-end warning chains in extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents can effectively automate end-to-end extreme weather early warning processes by leveraging historical experience and integrated evidence systems, addressing scalability limitations of expert-centered approaches while improving performance over existing weather agent frameworks.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Innovation Ecosystem: Evolutionary Developments, Challenges, and Future Directions
summary: The development of the Innovative Ecosystem (IE) presents a new paradigm for economic integration, collaborative advancement, and shared achievements. The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly accelerated the global processes of digitization, informatization, and intelligence. Exploring how AI can leverage inherent characteristics to influence the development trajectory of IE is a topic that warrants further investigation. Given AI's increasing prominence and role within IE, the paper analyzes this new form, examining both AI's unique contributions to IE and its potential challenges. Firstly, the paper synthesizes the conceptual frameworks surrounding IE, decomposing them into manifestations in physical, social, and thinking spaces. Furthermore, the concept of Artificial Intelligence IE (AIIE) is introduced from a spatial perspective, with an exploration of the characteristics AI contributes to IE. Subsequently, the paper employs an evolutionary perspective to analyze the roles provided by AI during different development periods of AIIE. The paper then verifies the feasibility, effectiveness, and rationality of the AIIE's definition and analyzes AIIE development from an evolutionary perspective using enterprise development examples. Finally, acknowledging AI's inherent limitations, the paper examines potential challenges facing AIIE in the future from four perspectives, aiming to identify new research avenues for the further development of AIIE.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of Artificial Intelligence Innovative Ecosystem (AIIE), analyzes AI's role in innovative ecosystems from spatial and evolutionary perspectives, and identifies future challenges.
AI.motivation: As AI accelerates global digitization and intelligence, there's a need to understand how AI's inherent characteristics influence the development trajectory of innovative ecosystems, given AI's increasing prominence within these systems.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes conceptual frameworks of innovative ecosystems (decomposed into physical, social, and thinking spaces), introduces AIIE concept, employs evolutionary perspective to analyze AI's roles across different development periods, and verifies feasibility through enterprise development examples.
AI.result: The paper establishes the concept of Artificial Intelligence Innovative Ecosystem (AIIE) from a spatial perspective, demonstrates AI's contributions to innovative ecosystems across different development phases, and verifies the feasibility and rationality of AIIE through empirical analysis.
AI.conclusion: While AI significantly contributes to innovative ecosystem development, the paper identifies potential challenges facing AIIE from four perspectives and aims to open new research avenues for AIIE's further development, acknowledging AI's inherent limitations.

title: Efficiency Matters in Autonomous Research
summary: AI-driven autonomous research (AR) systems are becoming increasingly effective across a broad range of tasks. Their performance, however, is still evaluated primarily by the quality of the final outcome. In this paper, we argue that the efficiency of the solution-search process is an equally important but often overlooked dimension of performance. A strong AR system should not only produce high-quality results, but also reach them with as small a budget as possible. Search efficiency will become increasingly important as AR expands from domains with inexpensive verification, such as mathematics and coding, to real-world scientific settings in which solution evaluation may require costly physical experiments. To capture this dimension, we propose evaluating AR systems using the area under the curve (AUC) of the Pareto frontier, alongside final outcome quality. We compare several families of search algorithms, including hill climbing, beam search, tree search, and evolutionary search, across twelve systems-optimization tasks. We find that no single search structure is consistently the most efficient. We also show that search efficiency and final outcome quality are distinct performance dimensions: a method that eventually achieves the best result may nevertheless improve slowly and consume substantially more evaluation budget before reaching that result. Because the most effective search policy is generally unknown in advance, we introduce an adaptive procedure called fluid search, which uses a portfolio bandit to dynamically allocate a fixed evaluation budget across a forest of search processes. Across the evaluated tasks, fluid search achieves the highest overall search efficiency, closely matching the performance of a per-task oracle that is given the best search structure for each task in advance.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that search efficiency is a crucial but overlooked dimension of autonomous research systems, proposes AUC of Pareto frontier as an evaluation metric, compares search algorithms, and introduces fluid search as an adaptive portfolio approach.
AI.motivation: Current AI autonomous research systems are evaluated primarily by final outcome quality, ignoring search efficiency. As AR expands to domains with costly solution evaluation (e.g., physical experiments), search efficiency becomes increasingly important for practical deployment.
AI.method: Proposes evaluating AR systems using area under the curve (AUC) of Pareto frontier alongside final quality. Compares hill climbing, beam search, tree search, and evolutionary search across 12 systems-optimization tasks. Introduces fluid search - an adaptive portfolio bandit that dynamically allocates evaluation budget across multiple search processes.
AI.result: No single search structure is consistently most efficient across tasks. Search efficiency and final outcome quality are distinct dimensions - best final result methods may be slow/expensive. Fluid search achieves highest overall search efficiency, closely matching per-task oracle performance.
AI.conclusion: Search efficiency is a critical performance dimension for AR systems, especially for real-world applications. The fluid search approach effectively addresses the challenge of unknown optimal search policies by dynamically adapting across multiple search strategies.

title: Reason-Mediated Behavioral Models for Auditing LLM Social Simulators
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as social simulators, including as synthetic survey respondents. Most evaluations ask whether simulated outcomes resemble human outcomes. We argue that this is necessary but too weak: a simulator can match the final answer while using the wrong rationale-derived reason pattern. We study this problem through a 94-person sunscreen concept test in which each respondent evaluated three product concepts and wrote open-ended rationales. We map those rationales into signed reason states $Z$, where positive signs support adoption and negative signs block it. This gives a practical audit: holding respondent descriptors $D$, category context $K$, and concept treatment $X$ fixed, do human rationale-derived reasons help predict behavior $Y$, and can an LLM simulate the same reason state without seeing the human rationale or outcome? Human rationale-derived reasons substantially improve held-out prediction of purchase intent. LLM-simulated reasons are more brittle: they often sound plausible, but frequently echo the concept board rather than recover the respondent's acceptance or rejection path. The paper contributes an evaluation framework for social simulators. Reason states do not identify natural causal effects by themselves, but they provide an interpretable test of whether a simulator's stated reasons align with human evidence.

AI.tldr: LLMs used as social simulators need more than just matching final outcomes - they must also generate human-like rationales. A sunscreen concept test shows human rationales improve purchase intent prediction, but LLM-simulated rationales often just echo concept descriptions rather than capture actual human reasoning patterns.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of LLMs as social simulators focus only on whether they match human outcomes, but this is insufficient. A simulator could produce the same final answer while using completely different (and potentially wrong) reasoning patterns. There's a need to test whether LLMs can generate human-like rationales, not just final decisions.
AI.method: Conducted a 94-person sunscreen concept test where participants evaluated three product concepts and wrote open-ended rationales. Mapped rationales into signed reason states (Z) indicating support or opposition to adoption. Tested whether: 1) human rationale-derived reasons help predict purchase intent (Y), and 2) LLMs can simulate the same reason states without seeing human rationales or outcomes. Used respondent descriptors (D), category context (K), and concept treatment (X) as fixed variables.
AI.result: Human rationale-derived reasons substantially improved held-out prediction of purchase intent. However, LLM-simulated reasons were more brittle - they often sounded plausible but frequently just echoed the concept board rather than recovering the respondent's actual acceptance or rejection pathways.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes an evaluation framework for social simulators that goes beyond just matching outcomes. While reason states don't identify natural causal effects, they provide an interpretable test of whether a simulator's stated reasons align with human evidence. LLMs need to be evaluated on their reasoning patterns, not just final outputs.

title: Eviction as Estimation: A Fixed-Lag Smoothing View of Test-Time Memory, and When Measuring Beats Accumulating
summary: A language model with a bounded working memory must repeatedly decide which stored items to keep. Every deployed method decides the moment an item arrives, from the past (StreamingLLM, H2O) or from a guess about the future (SnapKV). We recast the choice as an estimation problem on a hidden signal, whether an item will be reused, placing existing methods on one axis, the commit lag $H$: online filters and learned predictors commit at $H=0$, while Belady's offline optimum sits where the whole future is known. The missing regime in between, fixed-lag smoothing, waits a bounded number of steps, observes which items a correct near-future prediction attended to, and only then commits. This measurement, demonstrated utility, turns Belady's unobservable future request into something we read off the model itself. We instantiate it as a training-free policy, RMM, a strict generalization of H2O that reduces to it exactly when the measurement is uniform. In controlled settings where reuse is endogenous and separated in time, demonstrated utility identifies used memory far better than accumulated attention, and a small bounded memory behaves like a much larger one. But on independent third-party benchmarks, run inside NVIDIA's KVPress harness against its own SnapKV, H2O, and StreamingLLM implementations, the advantage mostly disappears: RMM is on par with H2O for single-turn question answering and loses to both H2O and SnapKV in a streaming multi-turn setting. The cause is simple: on natural text the model is correct about most tokens, so weighting attention by correctness barely changes it, and demonstrated utility collapses onto accumulated attention unless reuse is sharp and endogenous, which standard benchmarks do not exercise. Our contribution is the framework and an honest map of when measuring beats accumulating, not a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RMM, a new approach for bounded working memory management in language models that uses demonstrated utility from near-future predictions rather than accumulated attention, but finds it offers minimal advantage over existing methods on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for managing bounded working memory in language models make decisions based on either past information (StreamingLLM, H2O) or guesses about the future (SnapKV). There's a missing regime between immediate decisions and perfect future knowledge where decisions could be based on demonstrated utility from near-future predictions.
AI.method: The paper proposes RMM, a training-free policy based on fixed-lag smoothing. It waits a bounded number of steps, observes which items a correct near-future prediction attends to, and only then commits to keeping those items. This turns Belady's unobservable future request into something measurable from the model itself, generalizing H2O.
AI.result: In controlled settings with endogenous reuse separated in time, demonstrated utility outperforms accumulated attention, allowing small bounded memory to behave like larger memory. However, on standard third-party benchmarks (NVIDIA's KVPress with SnapKV, H2O, StreamingLLM), RMM performs similarly to H2O for single-turn QA and worse than both H2O and SnapKV for multi-turn streaming, as natural text predictions are mostly correct, collapsing demonstrated utility to accumulated attention.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is the theoretical framework showing when measuring demonstrated utility beats accumulating attention, not a new state-of-the-art method. The paper honestly maps when the approach works (endogenous, separated reuse patterns) vs. when it doesn't (standard natural language benchmarks).

title: ERUnderstand: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Structured ER Diagrams
summary: Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERDs) are central to conceptual database design, yet they are typically available only as rendered images rather than machine-readable schemas, limiting AI-assisted database engineering. We introduce ERUnderstand, the first large-scale benchmark for structured understanding of ER diagrams, comprising 2,960 diagrams collected from curated educational sources, real-world schemas, and synthetically generated examples spanning diverse domains, notations, complexity levels, and Extended Entity-Relationship (EER) constructs. Each diagram is paired with a standardized machine-readable representation for fine-grained evaluation of schema elements. Evaluating state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs), we find that while common ERD elements are recovered reliably (F1 > 0.74), performance drops sharply on weak entities (as low as 0.28 F1), multivalued attributes (0.14 F1), and N-ary relationships (0.07 F1). Reasoning-augmented models improve overall performance by 15-25% but remain sensitive to linguistic priors and increasing diagram complexity. ERUnderstand provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating multimodal understanding of conceptual database schemas. The benchmark, dataset, evaluation toolkit, and generation code are publicly available at https://github.com/salinaria/ERUnderstand.

AI.tldr: ERUnderstand: First large-scale benchmark for machine-readable understanding of Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERDs) with 2,960 diverse diagrams and evaluation of vision-language models.
AI.motivation: ER diagrams are typically available only as images rather than machine-readable schemas, limiting AI-assisted database engineering. There's a lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating structured understanding of ER diagrams.
AI.method: Created ERUnderstand benchmark with 2,960 diagrams from educational sources, real-world schemas, and synthetic generation covering diverse domains, notations, complexity levels, and EER constructs. Paired each diagram with standardized machine-readable representation for evaluation.
AI.result: Evaluating VLMs shows strong performance on common ERD elements (F1 > 0.74) but significant drops on complex constructs: weak entities (F1 as low as 0.28), multivalued attributes (0.14), N-ary relationships (0.07). Reasoning-augmented models improve performance by 15-25% but remain sensitive to linguistic priors and complexity.
AI.conclusion: ERUnderstand provides the first standardized benchmark for evaluating multimodal understanding of conceptual database schemas, revealing current limitations in handling complex ER constructs. The benchmark, dataset, evaluation toolkit, and generation code are publicly available.
